The following morning, I recounted the incident to Poirot over the breakfast table. He was at the moment engaged in the delicate operation of precisely aligning his toast-rack with the edge of the table. He listened with more interest than I had expected, his egg-shaped head tilted slightly to one side. When I had finished, he remained silent for a moment, twirling his moustache with an air of profound abstraction. “It is a small thing, Hastings,” he remarked at last, “but the small things, they are often the most interesting. Why should a flat in Montagu Mansions, a most desirable neighbourhood, be offered at a price so ridiculously low? And why should your friend, this Mrs. Ferguson, believe it was already let when it was not? One does not usually make such a mistake when one is hunting for a home with the desperation of a tiger. No, there is something here that does not ring true—a dissonance in the melody of the commonplace.”

It was on the following morning that I recounted the circumstances of the cheap flat to Poirot. He was at the moment engaged in an elaborate task of symmetry, rearranging the contents of my bookshelf which I had somewhat disarranged the night before, but he paused, his eyes kindling with a sudden interest. I had expected him to dismiss the matter as a piece of feminine gossip, but instead he leaned back in his chair and regarded me with a look of profound meditation. “Tell me once more, Hastings,” he said, “about this friend of the lady—this Elsie Ferguson. She was quite sure the flat was let, you say? And yet, when Mrs. Robinson arrived but a few minutes later, she found it still available? It is curious, my friend, most curious. A flat in Montagu Mansions for eighty pounds—it is an impossibility!”

I repeated the story to Poirot on the following morning. He was delicately singeing a stray hair from his moustache with a pair of miniature spirit-lamps. He listened with his head on one side, his eyes shining with that peculiar green light which meant that his interest was aroused. “It is a small thing, Hastings,” he remarked, “but it is a curious thing. Eighty pounds? It is not a rent; it is a gift. And why was this Elsie Ferguson told that the flat was let, when your friends the Robinsons found it otherwise? People do not usually refuse a tenant for the pleasure of it. There is a lack of logic here that I find most intriguing.”

The following morning I related the whole matter to Poirot. He was drying his moustache with meticulous care after his second cup of chocolate, and he listened with an air of polite boredom which I found somewhat damping. When I had finished, however, he laid down his napkin and leaned back in his chair, his eyes twinkling with a sudden green light which I knew of old meant that his interest was at last aroused. “It is a little problem of the most charming,” he murmured. “A young couple find a flat in an expensive quarter for a price that is—how do you say?—a song. And a friend, who arrives but a few minutes before them, is told that the flat is already let. It is a paradox, Hastings, and I have a great weakness for paradoxes.”

The following morning, I recounted the whole matter to Poirot. He was intensely interested. I had expected him to be dismissive of what I considered a mere piece of social gossip, but on the contrary, he sat up in his chair, his eyes shining with that peculiar green light that always betokened his mental excitement. "A flat in Montagu Mansions for eighty pounds a year?" he murmured. "It is incredible, Hastings. There is no such thing in London today. And this Mrs. Ferguson, you say she was told it was already let? There is a discrepancy there, a little knot in the thread. One does not give away money for nothing, even in this England of yours where the bargains are so sought after. There must be a reason, and a very good reason, why that particular flat is being disposed of at such a price. I should like to see this Mrs. Robinson; she sounds a most charming and, more importantly, a most lucky young woman."

The whole thing was rather amusing, and I propounded the thing as
a mock problem to Poirot on the following morning. He seemed
interested, and questioned me rather narrowly as to the rents of
flats in various localities.

“A curious story,” he said thoughtfully. “Excuse me, Hastings, I
must take a short stroll.”

When he returned, about an hour later, his eyes were gleaming with
a peculiar excitement. He laid his stick on the table, and brushed
the nap of his hat with his usual tender care before he spoke.

“It is as well, _mon ami_, that we have no affairs of moment on
hand. We can devote ourselves wholly to the present investigation.”

“What investigation are you talking about?”

“The remarkable cheapness of your friend’s, Mrs. Robinson’s, new
flat.”

“Poirot, you are not serious!”

“I am always serious, Hastings, when I am confronted by a fact that defies the laws of the universe—and in London, a cheap flat is a very great defiance indeed. I have made a few little inquiries of my own. It appears that the flat in question, Number 4, was previously tenanted by a lady named Elsa Hardt, who departed with a most suspicious suddenness. Then we have the curious matter of Elsie Ferguson. You say she told her friend the flat was let? Yet the Robinsons found it vacant. Why should she lie, unless she had a reason to keep them away? And finally, we have the charming Mrs. Robinson herself, who is perhaps not as simple as she appears. When the rent is low, the motive is usually high. We shall go to Montagu Mansions, Hastings. We shall observe this ‘dirt cheap’ bargain with our own eyes, for I have a little idea that the furniture is not the only thing that was left behind by Mademoiselle Hardt.”

“I am always serious when it concerns the use of the little grey cells, Hastings. I have been to the house agents, Stosser and Paul. It is as I thought. The rent is indeed eighty pounds, but the agents were as surprised as I was. They had orders from the owner—a certain Elsa Hardt—to let it at that figure only to a young couple of a particular description. Now, why should a woman like Elsa Hardt, who I discover is a singer of some note, be so anxious to find a specific type of tenant that she sacrifices two hundred pounds a year? And why was your friend Elsie Ferguson told the flat was let, while Mrs. Robinson was accepted immediately? There is a precision there, a selection, that does not suggest the haphazard. It suggests, rather, a most deliberate plan. We shall call upon Mrs. Robinson this afternoon and see this bargain for ourselves.”

“I am always serious when it comes to the unusual, Hastings. Consider the facts which you have so kindly provided. A flat in Montagu Mansions, for which the market price is easily three hundred and fifty pounds a year, is offered for eighty. No premium is asked. The furniture is sold for a song. And then, there is the curious matter of the friend, Mrs. Ferguson. She is told it is let; your friends are told it is not. Is it that Mrs. Ferguson is a woman of a density incomparable? Or is there some other reason why she, specifically, was turned away? I have been to the house agents, Stosser and Paul, Hastings. I represented myself as a potential tenant for a similar flat. It seems there have been many applicants for No. 4, yet for some reason, they have all been rejected until the Robinsons arrived. Why the Robinsons? What is it that distinguishes them from the others?”

“I am of the most serious, Hastings. Figure to yourself: eighty pounds for a flat in Montagu Mansions! It is an absurdity, a thing that does not happen in this London of yours. I have been to the agents, Stosser and Paul. I have made inquiries. There have been many applicants for No. 4, and to all of them, the same story was told—that it was let. Yet to the Robinsons, it was not let. Why? Because they were the ones desired. There is a reason, Hastings, and when there is a reason for such a departure from the normal, Poirot is interested. We shall see, my friend, what the move to-morrow brings forth. I have a little idea that the charming Mrs. Robinson and her husband are being used as pawns in a game of which they know nothing.”

“I am always serious when it comes to the unusual, Hastings,” Poirot replied, his eyes twinkling with that green light that signified his brain was working at full speed. “Consider the facts. A flat in such a fashionable quarter for eighty pounds? It is not merely a bargain; it is a miracle. And as our friend Gerald Parker remarked, miracles in London real estate are as rare as a politician who speaks only the truth. I have taken the liberty of visiting the agents, Stosser and Paul. They were most—how shall we say—evasive. They confirmed that the flat has been on their books for some time, yet they could not explain why so many prospective tenants, like your friend Elsie Ferguson, were turned away when the flat was, in fact, available. It is a mystery of the most intriguing, and where there is a mystery, there is a reason—usually a very dark one. Does it not strike you as significant that the Robinsons were accepted so instantly, where others were rebuffed?”

“I am most serious. Figure to yourself, my friend, that the real
rent of those flats is £350. I have just ascertained that from the
landlord’s agents. And yet this particular flat is being sublet at
eighty pounds! Why?”

“There must be something wrong with it. Perhaps it is haunted, as
Mrs. Robinson suggested.”

Poirot shook his head in a dissatisfied manner.

“Then again how curious it is that her friend tells her the flat
is let, and, when she goes up, behold, it is not so at all!”

“But surely you agree with me that the other woman must have gone
to the wrong flat. That is the only possible solution.”

“You are of a touching simplicity, Hastings! To go to the wrong flat—it is possible, yes. But observe: Mrs. Ferguson is also searching for a home; she would not be so careless. And why, I ask you, should the flat be ‘let’ to her and ‘not let’ to the Robinsons? There is a discrepancy there that pleases me not. Moreover, I have been busy. I find that the tenant who is vacating so precipitately is a certain Mademoiselle Elsa Hardt, a lady of the stage. She has left behind her a most charming set of furniture for a mere fifty pounds. Does that not strike you as being—how shall we say—a little too good to be true? In this world, Hastings, one seldom gets something for nothing without a reason.”

“You are of an ingenious mind, Hastings,” Poirot remarked, a small smile playing around his lips. “But observe, the flat is No. 4. Is it likely that Mrs. Ferguson, looking for No. 4, should enter No. 14 or No. 24 by mistake? No, there is something here that does not leap to the eye. I have been to the agents, Stosser and Paul. I represented myself as a gentleman seeking a flat in Montagu Mansions. They told me there were none available—not one! And yet, our charming Mrs. Robinson obtained hers with the ease of a magician pulling a rabbit from a hat. Furthermore, I have made inquiries regarding the previous tenant—a lady who left in some haste. Her name, it appears, was Elsa Hardt. A young woman of foreign extraction, who lived there with a companion. It is curious, is it not?”

“It is the easy explanation, Hastings. But me, I do not like the easy explanation. If Mrs. Ferguson went to the wrong flat, she is a very stupid woman, and the English, they are not usually stupid about their own comforts. No, there is something more. Why were they so anxious to let the flat to the Robinsons? Why the low rent? Why the cheap furniture? It is like a trap, is it not? A trap baited with a very small rent to catch a very specific kind of mouse. We must discover why the Robinsons are so desirable as tenants. Let us go and see these gentlemen, Stosser and Paul. I have a little idea that I wish to verify.”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “It is certainly the simplest, and as such it would appeal to you. But I, I find it a little too simple. Consider, Hastings, there are many people looking for flats. Why should this one be given to Mrs. Robinson? Why not to the first person who applied? And then the furniture—fifty pounds! It is a gift! No, there is something here that is not natural. There is a design. Let us go and call upon your friends. I should like to see this flat for myself, and I should like to meet this Mrs. Robinson.”

“Did she go to the wrong flat?” Poirot murmured. “That is the easy explanation, the one that leaps to the eye. But consider, Hastings, the names. Your friend’s friend is a Mrs. Ferguson. Your new acquaintance is a Mrs. Robinson. These are names most ordinary, most unremarkable. But there is a third name involved. I have been to the agents, Stosser and Paul, and I have discovered who it is that is subletting this flat so cheaply. It is a certain Madame Elsa Hardt. She is a singer, I believe, who has been in London for only a short time. Why should she be in such a desperate hurry to depart that she sacrifices her money so ruthlessly? It is not the way of the world, Hastings. People do not give away hundreds of pounds for the pleasure of seeing Mrs. Robinson settled in a fashionable neighborhood. There is a reason, and I confess I find myself most intrigued by it.”

“You may or may not be right on that point, Hastings. The fact
still remains that numerous other applicants were sent to see it,
and yet, in spite of its remarkable cheapness, it was still in the
market when Mrs. Robinson arrived.”

“That shows that there must be something wrong about it.”

“Mrs. Robinson did not seem to notice anything amiss. Very curious,
is it not? Did she impress you as being a truthful woman, Hastings?”

“She was a delightful creature!”

“_Évidemment!_ since she renders you incapable of replying to my
question. Describe her to me, then.”

“Well, she’s tall and fair; her hair’s really a beautiful shade of
auburn——”

“Always you have had a penchant for auburn hair!” murmured Poirot.
“But continue.”

“Blue eyes and a very nice complexion and—well, that’s all, I
think,” I concluded lamely.

“And her husband?”

“Oh, he’s quite a nice fellow—nothing startling.”

“Dark or fair?”

“I don’t know—betwixt and between, and just an ordinary sort of
face.”

Poirot nodded.

“Yes, there are hundreds of these average men—and, anyway, you
bring more sympathy and appreciation to your description of women.
Do you know anything about these people? Does Parker know them
well.”

“They are just recent acquaintances, I believe. But surely, Poirot,
you don’t think for an instant——”

Poirot raised his hand.

“_Tout doucement, mon ami_. Have I said that I think anything? All
I say is—it is a curious story. And there is nothing to throw light
upon it; except perhaps the lady’s name, eh, Hastings?”

“Her name is Stella,” I said stiffly, “but I don’t see——”

Poirot interrupted me with a tremendous chuckle. Something seemed
to be amusing him vastly.

“And Stella means a star, does it not? Famous!”

“What on earth——”

“And stars give light! _Voilà!_ Calm yourself, Hastings. Do not
put on that air of injured dignity. Come, we will go to Montagu
Mansions and make a few inquiries.”

We reached Montagu Mansions, a block of some pretension, and Poirot led the way to the porter’s office. With an air of grandiloquence and the judicious use of a ten-shilling note, he extracted a wealth of information. The flat, No. 4, had indeed been taken by the Robinsons, who had moved their effects in that morning. Before them, the tenant had been a lady of foreign extraction, a Mademoiselle Elsa Hardt. She had occupied the flat for only a few weeks, paying the rent in advance, and had departed with equal suddenness. Poirot’s interest seemed particularly piqued by this Mademoiselle Hardt. He questioned the porter closely as to her appearance, and whether she had received many visitors. The porter mentioned a tall, dark gentleman who had called frequently, but he could tell us little more. As we left the building, Poirot walked in silence for a few moments, his brow furrowed in thought, before remarking that the plot was thickening in a most satisfactory manner.

We arrived at Montagu Mansions—a handsome building indeed. Poirot’s interest seemed to center on the porter, a man of stolid appearance and many medals, who was standing at the entrance. After a few preliminary remarks and the discreet passage of a coin, Poirot managed to elicit a good deal of information. It appeared that Flat No. 4 had been occupied for some months by a lady of foreign extraction, a certain Mademoiselle Elsa Hardt. She was, according to the porter, a singer of some renown, though she lived a very quiet life. She had left quite suddenly a few weeks ago, and since then, the flat had been on the market. The porter's brow darkened slightly as he mentioned that there had been many applicants, but none seemed to suit until the Robinsons arrived; he remarked that several ladies, including a Mrs. Ferguson who visited frequently, had seemed most disappointed. He seemed particularly struck by the fact that the agents had sent so many people to see it, only to have them turned away for reasons he could not fathom.

We reached Montagu Mansions, a handsome and imposing block of buildings. Poirot, with his usual finesse, approached the porter. By means of a few well-placed questions and a discreetly offered half-crown, he soon elicited several interesting facts. The most remarkable of these was that the previous tenants of No. 4 had also been named Robinson. They had occupied the flat for barely six months and had departed with almost no notice. The porter described them as a quiet couple, though he mentioned that a young woman, a foreigner by her accent, had been a frequent visitor of late. “A Mademoiselle Elsa Hardt, I believe her name was,” the man added, scratching his head. “A very striking young lady, if I may say so, sir.”

The mansions were a handsome block of red brick, well-appointed and modern. A gold-braided porter was on duty, and to him Poirot addressed himself with that mixture of authority and confidential charm which he knows so well how to employ. We learned that No. 4 had indeed been the object of much coming and going of late. The previous tenant, it appeared, was a foreign lady, a Mademoiselle Elsa Hardt, who had left somewhat precipitately some weeks ago. Since then, the flat had been seen by dozens of people, but according to the porter, there had been a singular reluctance on the part of the agents to actually close a deal—until, as if by magic, the Robinsons had been accepted without delay. “A very pleasant young couple, sir,” the porter added, “though it did seem a bit sudden-like, considering how many others were turned away for no reason at all.”

Upon our arrival at the impressive portals of Montagu Mansions, Poirot did not at once ascend to the second floor. Instead, he sought out the porter, a man whose official dignity was easily thawed by the sight of a silver coin. From him, we gleaned several interesting facts. The flat, No. 4, had seen a rapid succession of tenants. Before the present occupants, it had been held by a young couple, also named Robinson, who had stayed but a few months and departed with almost no luggage. But more significant still was the tenant before them: a Mademoiselle Elsa Hardt. The porter’s eyes narrowed as he spoke of her; she was, it seemed, a lady of many foreign visitors and much luggage, who had vanished quite suddenly, leaving the furniture behind—the very furniture for which the new Mrs. Robinson had paid her fifty pounds.

I accompanied him, nothing loath. The Mansions were a handsome
block of buildings in excellent repair. A uniformed porter was
sunning himself on the threshold, and it was to him that Poirot
addressed himself:

“Pardon, but could you tell me if a Mr. and Mrs. Robinson reside
here?”

The porter was a man of few words and apparently of a sour or
suspicious disposition. He hardly looked at us and grunted out:

“No. 4. Second floor.”

“I thank you. Can you tell me how long they have been here?”

“Six months.”

I started forward in amazement, conscious as I did so of Poirot’s
malicious grin.

“Impossible,” I cried. “You must be making a mistake.”

“Six months.”

“Are you sure? The lady I mean is tall and fair with reddish gold
hair and——”

“That’s ’er,” said the porter. “Come in the Michaelmas quarter,
they did. Just six months ago.”

He appeared to lose interest in us and retreated slowly up the
hall. I followed Poirot outside.

“_Eh bien_, Hastings?” my friend demanded slyly. “Are you so sure
now that delightful women always speak the truth?”

I did not reply.

Poirot had steered his way into Brompton Road before I asked him
what he was going to do and where we were going.

“To the house agents, Hastings. I have a great desire to have a
flat in Montagu Mansions. If I am not mistaken, several interesting
things will take place there before long.”

We were fortunate in our quest. No. 8, on the fourth floor, was to
be let furnished at ten guineas a week. Poirot promptly took it
for a month. Outside in the street again, he silenced my protests:

“But I make money nowadays! Why should I not indulge a whim? By
the way, Hastings, have you a revolver?”

“Yes—somewhere,” I answered, slightly thrilled. “Do you think——”

“That you will need it? It is quite possible. The idea pleases you,
I see. Always the spectacular and romantic appeals to you.”

The following day saw us installed in our temporary home. The flat
was pleasantly furnished. It occupied the same position in the
building as that of the Robinsons, but was two floors higher.

The day after our installation was a Sunday. In the afternoon,
Poirot left the front door ajar, and summoned me hastily as a bang
reverberated from somewhere below.

“Look over the banisters. Are those your friends. Do not let them
see you.”

I craned my neck over the staircase.

“That’s them,” I declared in an ungrammatical whisper.

“Good. Wait awhile.”

About half an hour later, a young woman emerged in brilliant and
varied clothing. With a sigh of satisfaction, Poirot tiptoed back
into the flat.

“_C’est ça_. After the master and mistress, the maid. The flat
should now be empty.”

“What are we going to do?” I asked uneasily.

Poirot had trotted briskly into the scullery and was hauling at
the rope of the coal-lift.

“It is a very useful invention, this coal-lift,” murmured Poirot, his eyes twinkling with a mischievous light. “It allows for a certain... discretion in one’s movements. We shall descend, Hastings, not by the grand staircase where the eyes of the world might behold us, but by this humble conduit of combustible material.” I stared at him in genuine consternation. “You mean to enter their flat? Poirot, it’s housebreaking! We could be arrested!” He shrugged his shoulders with a characteristic Gallic flourish. “Housebreaking? Such a robust word for a simple visit of inspection. Besides, did not the charming Mrs. Robinson invite your professional interest? No, no, do not argue. The lift is small, but for one of my slight build and agile movements, it is quite sufficient. You, my friend, will remain here to act as the sentinel. If any person should approach the service entrance below, you will whistle—not too loudly, but with distinctness. One must always be prepared for the unexpected return of the ‘star’ and her satellites.”

“It is a most useful contrivance, this coal-lift,” observed Poirot, gesturing toward the dark shaft. “It connects the sculleries of all the flats in this tier. Since the maid has gone out, and your friends—if they are your friends—have also departed, the way is clear. We shall descend, Hastings, not by the stairs where the eyes of the porter might be upon us, but by this humble route of the domestic world. It is not, perhaps, a very dignified proceeding, and I fear for the state of my attire, but necessity, she is a hard mistress.” He stepped into the wooden box and motioned for me to join him. I hesitated, for the lift looked both precarious and soot-stained, but Poirot’s imperative nod allowed for no delay. Slowly, he began to pay out the rope, and we sank into the gloom of the shaft.

He beckoned to me with a finger. “The coal-lift, Hastings! It is not perhaps the most dignified mode of progression for a detective of my standing, but it has the advantage of being unexpected. The back door into the kitchen will, I fancy, be found unbolted. It is a common negligence of the domestic class when they go out for an hour’s recreation.” I followed him into the cramped, somewhat sooty compartment. With a dexterity that surprised me, Poirot manipulated the ropes, and we descended slowly through the dark shaft until we reached the level of the second floor. As he had surmised, the service door was merely latched; he pushed it open with a flourish, and we stepped into the silent, shadowed kitchen of the flat below.

“See you, Hastings,” Poirot remarked as he stepped gingerly into the small wooden compartment of the lift, “the service elevator is a most convenient invention for the private investigator. While the front door remains locked against the world, the back entrance—the way of the coals—is often neglected. I shall descend to the second floor and conduct a small inspection of our friends' ‘new’ home. You will remain here, at the top of the shaft, and should you hear a signal—two sharp whistles—you will descend by the stairs and join me at the front door of Number 4. But remember, keep a sharp eye upon the street; we do not wish for the return of the charming Mrs. Robinson to catch us at our domestic duties.” With a wink that combined mischief and gravity, he began to lower himself into the gloom of the shaft, his patent leather shoes disappearing last into the dusty depths.

“We are going to pay a visit to our neighbors below,” Poirot announced, his eyes twinkling with a mischievous light. “The coal-lift, Hastings, is a most convenient invention for the discreet investigator. Since the maid has departed for her afternoon of ‘the cinema,’ and the master and mistress are likewise absent, we shall take the liberty of an inspection. It is narrow, yes, and perhaps not entirely suited to your English ideas of dignity, but for the ‘little grey cells’ to function, one must sometimes descend to the level of the scullery.” He stepped into the small wooden box of the lift and beckoned me to follow. With a series of rhythmic tugs on the rope, we sank slowly past the third floor until the opening of the second-floor scullery came into view. Poirot stepped out with the agility of a cat, his face set in an expression of intense concentration as he began to survey the seemingly ordinary kitchen of the mysterious Mrs. Robinson.

“We are about to descend after the method of the dustbins,” he
explained cheerfully. “No one will observe us. The Sunday concert,
the Sunday ‘afternoon out,’ and finally the Sunday nap after the
Sunday dinner of England—_le rosbif_—all these will distract
attention from the doings of Hercule Poirot. Come, my friend.”

He stepped into the rough wooden contrivance and I followed him
gingerly.

“Are we going to break into the flat?” I asked dubiously.

Poirot’s answer was not too reassuring:

“Not precisely to-day,” he replied.

Pulling on the rope, we descended slowly till we reached the second
floor. Poirot uttered an exclamation of satisfaction as he perceived
that the wooden door into the scullery was open.

“Step out, Hastings,” he commanded.

“But what if they return? What if they see us?”

“_Tais-toi, mon ami_. They will not return for at least two hours.”

He stepped across the threshold and I followed him.

“Ah,” he remarked, glancing round him. “Everything is as I had
imagined. The kitchen of the Robinsons. Very nice, and very well
fitted—but for the small detail that there are no coals. See, the
bunker is quite empty.”

“Is that all you have come to find out?” I asked, with a touch of
sarcasm.

“Wait. Now let us go into the hall. Ah, a telephone! I must see if
the number is the same as ours.”

He noted it down on his cuff, and then proceeded into the drawing-room.
It was a charmingly furnished room, and the furniture looked as
if it had cost considerably more than fifty pounds.

Poirot’s eyes were everywhere. He peered into the bedrooms and
even into the cupboards. I followed him, feeling more than a little
ashamed of our proceedings.

Finally he returned to the drawing-room and stood for a moment or
two in the middle of it.

“And now, Hastings, let us go back.”

“Well,” I said, as we regained our own flat once more. “And what
have we discovered?”

Poirot shrugged his shoulders.

“Nothing—and everything. But we will have a little tea, and then,
since it is a fine afternoon, we will go for a walk.”

I was about to suggest a more exciting occupation when the telephone
rang. Poirot took up the receiver and listened.

“_Bon_,” he said, when he had hung up. “That was Gerald Parker.
He tells me that the Robinsons have just telephoned to him to say
that they are moving in to-morrow.”

“But the porter said they had been there six months!” I cried.

“Exactly, Hastings. There is some mystery about these Robinsons.
And I mean to find out what it is.”

He was silent for a few minutes, then he added:

“You know, Hastings, I have a feeling that we are on the track of
something much bigger than we imagine. The Robinson mystery is only
a part of it.”

“What do you mean?”

“I don’t know yet. But we shall see. In the meantime, we will go
for our walk.”

We went out and strolled along the Brompton Road. As we were
passing a small restaurant, Poirot suddenly stopped.

“Let us go in here and have some tea,” he suggested.

The restaurant was almost empty. We sat down at a small table in
the corner. Poirot ordered tea and then leaned across the table
to me.

“Do you see those two women at the table over there, Hastings?
The one with her back to us is Elsie Ferguson. And the other—the
one with the dark hair—is Elsa Hardt.”

“Elsa Hardt!” I exclaimed. “The famous singer?”

“The same. She is a very beautiful woman, is she not? And a very
talented one. But she is also a very dangerous one.”

“Dangerous? In what way?”

“She is a spy, Hastings. One of the most dangerous spies in
Europe. And I have a feeling that she is mixed up in this
Robinson business.”

“But how?”

“That is what we have to find out. But look, they are getting
up to go. We must follow them.”

We followed them out of the restaurant and along the street. They
walked quickly and we had some difficulty in keeping them in
sight. Finally they turned into a small side street and entered
a house at the end of it.

“That is Elsa Hardt’s house,” Poirot whispered. “We must find
out what they are doing there.”

He led the way to the back of the house and we managed to climb
over the wall into the garden. There was a large window on the
ground floor and we crept up to it and peered in.

The room was luxuriously furnished, and Elsa Hardt and Elsie
Ferguson were sitting on a sofa talking earnestly. We could
not hear what they were saying, but they both looked very
agitated.

Suddenly the door opened and a man entered the room. It was
Gerald Parker!

I gasped in astonishment. What was Parker doing here?

He went up to Elsa Hardt and took her hand.

“It’s all right,” he said. “The Robinsons are moving in
to-morrow. Everything is going according to plan.”

Elsa Hardt sighed with relief.

“Thank God!” she said. “I was beginning to get worried.”

“There was no need to be,” Parker replied. “Everything is
under control. Now, we must get ready for the meeting.”

The meeting! What meeting? And what had the Robinsons to do
with it?

Poirot touched my arm and we crept away from the window.

“We have seen enough for now, Hastings,” he whispered. “We must
get back to the flat and think this over.”

We made our way back to Montagu Mansions in silence. I was
bewildered by what I had seen. Parker, our friend Parker,
was mixed up in some kind of plot with a spy! It seemed
incredible.

When we reached the flat, Poirot sat down in his armchair and
closed his eyes. I knew he was thinking deeply, so I did not
disturb him.

After a long time, he opened his eyes and looked at me.

“Hastings,” he said. “The mystery of the Robinsons is even
more complicated than I thought. But I think I am beginning
to see the light.”

“Tell me!” I cried.

“Not yet, _mon ami_. I must be sure of my facts first. But
I can tell you this: the Robinsons are not Robinsons at all.
They are being used as pawns in a very dangerous game.”

“And Parker?”

“Parker is the brain behind the whole thing. He is a very
clever man, Hastings, and a very dangerous one.”

I could hardly believe it. Parker, the man I had known for
years, a criminal!

“But what about Elsie Ferguson and Elsa Hardt?” I asked.

“They are his accomplices. They are all working together to
carry out a daring robbery.”

“A robbery? What are they going to rob?”

“The Italian Embassy, Hastings. It is just around the corner
from Montagu Mansions. And tomorrow night, there is to be
a big reception there. That is when they plan to strike.”

“But why the Robinsons? Why do they need them?”

“Because the Robinsons’ flat is the key to the whole operation.
From there, they can gain access to the Embassy without being
seen.”

“How?”

“That is what I have to find out. But I think I know. And if
I am right, we must act quickly to stop them.”

He stood up and began to pace the room.

“Tomorrow night, Hastings, we will go to the Italian Embassy.
And we will catch them red-handed!”

I felt a thrill of excitement. This was what I had been waiting
for! A real case, with danger and intrigue!

“But what about the Robinsons?” I asked. “What will happen
to them?”

“They will be safe, Hastings. I will see to that. But for
now, we must prepare for tomorrow night.”

And with that, he went into his bedroom and closed the door.

I sat there for a long time, thinking about what he had told
me. It seemed like something out of a detective story. And
yet, I knew that with Poirot, anything was possible.

The next day passed slowly. Poirot was busy with his preparations,
and I spent the time reading and trying to calm my nerves.

Finally, evening came. Poirot and I dressed in our evening
clothes and made our way to the Italian Embassy.

The building was brilliantly lit, and a crowd of people was
streaming in. We joined them and were soon inside the
magnificent ballroom.

Poirot’s eyes were everywhere. He was looking for Parker,
Elsa Hardt, and Elsie Ferguson.

Suddenly, he gripped my arm.

“There they are!” he whispered.

I looked in the direction he was pointing. There, standing
near the buffet, were Parker, Elsa Hardt, and Elsie Ferguson.
They were talking and laughing, as if they hadn't a care
in the world.

“Wait here, Hastings,” Poirot said. “I must speak to the
Ambassador.”

He disappeared into the crowd, and I was left alone. I watched
Parker and his accomplices closely. They seemed to be
waiting for something.

Suddenly, Parker looked at his watch and nodded to the two
women. They began to move towards the door.

I followed them at a distance. They went up the stairs and
into a small room at the end of the hall.

I crept up to the door and listened. I could hear them
talking in low voices.

“Is everything ready?” Parker asked.

“Yes,” Elsa Hardt replied. “The ladder is in place.”

“Good. Then let’s go.”

I heard the sound of a window being opened. I knew I had to
act.

I burst into the room and shouted, “Stop! You’re under arrest!”

They all turned and looked at me in astonishment.

“Hastings!” Parker cried. “What are you doing here?”

“I know all about your plot, Parker,” I said. “And I’m not
going to let you get away with it.”

He laughed. “You’re too late, Hastings. We’ve already got
what we came for.”

He held up a small leather bag.

“The Italian Crown Jewels!” he exclaimed. “And now, if you’ll
excuse us, we have a plane to catch.”

He moved towards the window, but I blocked his way.

“You’re not going anywhere, Parker!” I said, reaching for
my revolver.

But before I could pull it out, Elsa Hardt stepped forward
and knocked it out of my hand.

“Don’t be a fool, Hastings,” she said. “You can’t stop us.”

She and Elsie Ferguson grabbed me and held me fast. Parker
climbed out of the window and disappeared into the night.

“Now, what are we going to do with you?” Elsie Ferguson asked.

“I think we should take him with us,” Elsa Hardt suggested.
“He might be useful as a hostage.”

They dragged me towards the window, but just as they were
about to push me out, the door burst open and Poirot
entered the room, followed by the Ambassador and several
policemen.

“Stop!” Poirot cried. “In the name of the law!”

Elsa Hardt and Elsie Ferguson were quickly overpowered and
handcuffed. Poirot went to the window and looked out.

“He’s gone!” he said. “Parker has escaped!”

“But we’ve got the jewels!” the Ambassador cried, picking up
the leather bag which Parker had dropped in his haste.

Poirot turned to me and smiled.

“Well done, Hastings! You played your part perfectly.”

“But Parker got away!” I said, feeling a little disappointed.

“Not for long, _mon ami_. I have already informed the police,
and they are waiting for him at the airport. He will not
get far.”

And indeed, Parker was arrested as he was about to board a
plane for South America.

The mystery of the Robinsons was finally solved. It turned
out that they were indeed being used by Parker. He had
rented the flat for them, and then used it as a base for
his operations.

The Robinsons themselves were completely innocent. They had
no idea what was going on, and were shocked to find out
the truth.

As for Elsa Hardt and Elsie Ferguson, they were both
sentenced to long terms in prison.

And so, once again, Hercule Poirot had triumphed. He had
unravelled a complex web of intrigue and brought a gang
of dangerous criminals to justice.

As we were sitting in our flat the next day, I asked him
how he had figured it all out.

“It was simple, Hastings,” he said, with a twinkle in his
eye. “I just used my little grey cells.”

I had to smile. After all, that was Poirot. Always the
same, always brilliant, and always right.

“The first step, Hastings, is to establish whether the Robinson who lives here is indeed the Robinson you met at Gerald Parker's,” Poirot whispered as we stepped cautiously out of the lift and into the quiet, dim kitchen of Flat No. 4. The air smelled faintly of furniture polish and lavender. Poirot moved with the silent agility of a cat, his eyes darting from side to side, noting every detail with that meticulous precision I knew so well. He led the way into the drawing-room, which was indeed tastefully furnished, just as Mrs. Robinson had described. On a small mahogany table lay a silver-framed photograph. Poirot picked it up and held it out to me. "Is this the lady of the auburn hair, Hastings?" I looked at the portrait of the beautiful woman I had seen only a few nights before. "Yes, that's her," I confirmed. Poirot nodded, his expression unreadable, then replaced the frame exactly where it had been. "And yet the porter says they have lived here for six months, while she told you they were only moving in tomorrow. Someone, my friend, is lying with great deliberation."

“Is this the Robinson’s flat?” I inquired.

“Exactly. You are sure you will not be seen?”

“Nobody. It is empty.”

Poirot hopped out. I followed him into the small and well-kept
scullery.

The kitchen lay beyond it. It was clean and neat. Poirot gazed
around him with a satisfied air. He seemed to be looking for
something in particular.

At length his eyes fell upon a large cupboard. He went towards it,
turning the key. It was empty.

“You see?” he said.

“I see it is empty.”

“And it is large! Large enough to hold—shall we say—a man?”

“A man?” I exclaimed.

“_Certainement_. Is it not so? Now we will go. Do not forget to
shut the door after you.”

We reascended in the coal-lift. Once more in our own flat, Poirot
rubbed his hands with glee.

“The plot thickens,” he remarked. “The plot thickens! Let us go
out for a walk, my friend.”

We spent a pleasant evening in the Park. On our return we were met
by the porter.

“A lady for you, sir,” he said to Poirot. “She’s in No. 8. Went
up about half an hour ago.”

Poirot’s eyes flashed.

“Come, Hastings,” he said, and led the way up the stairs.

A lady was waiting for us. She was tall and slender, and her face
was heavily veiled. As we entered, she rose and came towards us.

“M. Poirot?” she said in a low, musical voice.

“At your service, Madame.”

“I have come to you on a matter of the most urgent importance.”

“Will you not sit down, Madame? This is my friend, Captain
Hastings.”

The lady bowed to me and then turned to Poirot again.

“I am Elsa Hardt,” she said, and her voice shook with emotion. “I
think you may have heard of me.”

I had indeed. Elsa Hardt was a well-known actress.

“And you have come to me because——” Poirot paused.

“Because I am in trouble—terrible trouble. My jewels have been
stolen.”

“Your jewels?”

“Yes. They were taken last night from my flat—No. 4, Montagu
Mansions.”

I started.

“But No. 4 is the Robinsons’ flat,” I cried.

Elsa Hardt looked at me in surprise.

“The Robinsons? I do not know any Robinsons. I have lived there
for two years.”

“Then you are the mistress of the flat?”

“I am.”

“And you have a maid?”

“I have—a girl named Annie. She has been with me for some time.”

“Then who are the Robinsons?” I asked Poirot in bewilderment.

Poirot smiled.

“That is what we have to find out,” he said. “Now, Mlle. Hardt,
will you tell us all about the robbery?”

“The Robinsons are really most careless people,” he murmured, as
he stepped into the kitchen.

I followed him, somewhat shamefacedly.

“We have no business to be here,” I began.

“_Peut-être pas, mon ami_. For the moment, we will explore the
unknown.”

He made his way into the hall and began a systematic search of the
rooms.

The flat was as Mrs. Robinson had described it. One bedroom was
handsomely furnished, but the second one, smaller and darker, had
hardly anything in it. Poirot, however, seemed particularly
attracted to this room. He paced its length several times,
frowning heavily as he did so.

Suddenly he stooped. A small, dark object lay on the carpet near
the window. He picked it up and held it for me to see. It was a
single black hair—short and stiff.

“This did not come from the golden-haired Mrs. Robinson,” he
observed.

He continued his search, and presently from under the bed he
produced a small, square cardboard box. On the lid was the name
of a well-known firm of chemists. Inside there was a small bottle
half-full of some white powder.

“What’s this?” I asked.

Poirot sniffed it cautiously.

“Arsenic,” he said laconically.

“Good heavens!” I cried. “You don’t mean that the Robinsons——”

Poirot replaced the box and shook his head.

“No, no, Hastings. I do not think it was the Robinsons who left
the arsenic here. But come, we have seen enough. Let us return to
our own domain.”

We made our way back as we had come. Poirot was silent for the rest
of the evening. He seemed to be thinking deeply.

The following morning he was out early. When he returned he was
triumphant.

“I have seen my friend of the CID, Japp,” he announced. “He will
be with us this evening. Also we shall have a visitor.”

“Who?”

“Mrs. Robinson.”

“But how did you manage it?”

“I sent her a note. I asked her to come and see me. I said I had
found something she had lost.”

“But she hasn’t lost anything!”

“On the contrary, she has lost a great deal. She has lost her
identity, Hastings!”

“What do you mean?”

“You will see. You will see. It is all very interesting.”

He refused to say any more, and the day passed slowly.

At half-past eight Japp arrived. He was a small, alert man, with
a keen eye and a somewhat cynical expression.

“Well, Poirot,” he said, as he settled himself in an armchair,
“what’s this mystery of yours? I hope it’s worth the journey.”

“I think you will find it so, my friend. But here is our visitor.”

The bell had rung, and a moment later Mrs. Robinson was ushered
into the room. She was as I had seen her on the previous evening,
tall and fair, with her beautiful auburn hair. She seemed a little
nervous.

“You have found something of mine, Monsieur Poirot?” she asked,
looking from one to the other of us.

Poirot rose and bowed.

“Will you not sit down, Madame?” he said. “Yes, I have found
something of yours. I have found—your predecessor.”

The woman’s face went white. She stared at him with wide,
frightened eyes.

“My predecessor?” she whispered.

“Exactly. The woman who lived in No. 4 before you.”

“I—I don’t understand.”

“Oh, I think you do, Madame. I think you understand very well.
But perhaps I had better explain. You see, I am a very inquisitive
person. I like to know why things happen. And it seemed to me very
strange that a flat in Montagu Mansions should be let for eighty
pounds a year when the real rent was three hundred and fifty. It
seemed even more strange that so many people had been sent to see
it and yet it was still to let. And then, when you told my friend
Hastings your story, I began to see a light.”

“I don’t know what you mean,” she said, her voice trembling.

“Let me continue. I went to the flat. I found it empty. And in the
small bedroom I found two things. A black hair and a bottle of
arsenic.”

The woman gave a little cry and buried her face in her hands.

“And then,” Poirot went on, his voice soft and relentless, “I
remembered something. I remembered a case that had happened about
six months ago. A man had murdered his wife. He had poisoned her
with arsenic. He had been caught and hanged. But his accomplice,
the woman who had helped him, had disappeared. She had never been
found.”

He paused, and for a moment there was a dead silence in the room.

“The man’s name,” Poirot said, “was Gerald Parker.”

I started up in amazement.

“Parker!” I cried. “But—but Parker is my friend!”

Poirot looked at me with a strange expression.

“Is he, Hastings? Are you sure? You met him, you say, at a party.
He was your host. But did you know him before that?”

“No—no, I didn’t. But he seemed such a nice fellow.”

“Ah, Hastings, you are always so easily deceived by a ‘nice
fellow.’ But it was not Gerald Parker who murdered his wife. It
was his brother, James Parker. And the woman who helped him—the
woman who disappeared—was his wife’s maid, Elsa Hardt.”

He turned back to the woman in the chair.

“And you, Madame, are Elsa Hardt!”

With a sudden movement, the woman sprang to her feet. Her face
was no longer pale; it was distorted with rage and fear.

“It’s a lie!” she screamed. “It’s a lie! I am Mrs. Robinson! I
have never heard of Elsa Hardt!”

“Then how do you explain the auburn hair, Madame?” Poirot asked
quietly. “Elsa Hardt was a dark-haired woman. But you—you have
beautiful auburn hair. Only, you see, it is not your own hair. It
is a wig. And underneath it, I think we shall find that your hair
is black—short and stiff, like the hair I found on the floor.”

With a swift movement, he reached out and snatched the wig from
her head. Underneath, her hair was indeed black and closely
cropped.

The woman stood for a moment, her eyes flashing fire. Then, with
a sudden spring, she was at the door. But Japp was too quick for
her. He caught her by the arms and held her fast.

“No you don’t, my beauty!” he said. “You’re coming with me.”

He led her out of the room, and Poirot and I were left alone.

“So it was Elsa Hardt,” I said, sinking back into my chair. “But
how did you know, Poirot?”

“It was the rent, Hastings. The rent of the flat. It was so low
because it was being used as a hiding-place. Elsa Hardt had
remained in the flat after the murder. She had hidden herself there,
relying on the fact that no one would think of looking for her in
the very place where the crime had been committed. But she needed
money. And so she hit upon the plan of subletting the flat at a
nominal rent. She would choose people who were unlikely to ask
questions, and who would be grateful for their good fortune. And
to make sure that she got the right people, she arranged that her
friend, Mrs. Ferguson, should meet them at the door and tell them
the flat was already let. Only the people she wanted would be
admitted.”

“But the arsenic?” I asked. “Why was that there?”

“That was the mistake, Hastings. The one mistake that every
criminal makes. She had kept it by her, perhaps as a last resort,
and she had forgotten to hide it. And then, there was the hair.
She had been cutting her hair to change her appearance, and she
had been careless.”

He sighed and shook his head.

“It is always the same. They are so clever, and yet they are so
stupid. But come, Hastings, let us go and have some dinner. I
think we have earned it.”

I followed him out of the room, my mind still dazed by the events
of the evening. But as we walked down the street, I couldn’t help
feeling a certain pride in my friend. Once again, Hercule Poirot
had triumphed.

And as for Gerald Parker, I never saw him again. Whether he was
really involved in the business, or whether he was just another
victim of Elsa Hardt’s cleverness, I never knew. But I have a
feeling that Poirot could have told me—if he had wanted to.

He stepped out of the lift and I followed. The scullery was small,
very small indeed. Through the doorway I could see into a very
neat and modern kitchen.

Poirot examined the scullery window.

“Ah! A most excellent point for a burglar. These blocks of flats
have their weak points. It is as I thought.”

He stood for some moments lost in thought, and then he suddenly
wheeled round.

“Hastings, did you say that this was a furnished flat?”

“The Robinsons said so.”

“And you believed them?”

“Well, it seemed quite natural.”

“And it seemed quite natural that they should have it for eighty
pounds a year? And it seemed quite natural that they should have
remained there six months? And it seemed quite natural that Mrs.
Ferguson should say it was let, when it wasn’t?”

I was silent.

“I tell you, Hastings, it is all very natural! Let us leave this
place before the return of the maid.”

We regained our own flat without further incident. Poirot seemed
much more cheerful than I had seen him for some time.

“And now, Hastings,” he said, as he sat down in a big armchair,
“what have you to say for yourself? Does your theory of the ‘other
flat’ still hold good?”

“I don’t know what to think,” I confessed. “What do you think
about it?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that it is a very interesting case—very
interesting indeed. It has points—yes, it has points. And now,
Hastings, if you will be so good as to reach me that small blue
book from the shelf—no, not that one—the other—the one on the
left.”

I handed it to him. It was a recent number of the _Daily Gazette_.
Poirot turned over the pages with a certain deliberation.

“Ah! Here we are. ‘Missing—a young lady of the name of Elsa Hardt.
Last seen leaving her home in South Kensington. Tall, fair,
reddish-gold hair, blue eyes.’ It is a description that might
apply to many, is it not?”

“Elsa Hardt!” I exclaimed. “The German girl who was supposed to
have been kidnapped?”

“The same. You remember the case? A very mysterious business.”

“But what has that to do with the Robinsons?”

“That is what we have to find out, Hastings.”

I stared at him.

“You don’t mean to say——”

“I mean to say nothing. But it is a curious coincidence, is it not?
Two young women with auburn hair—one of them missing, the other
living in a flat at a ridiculously low rent.”

“But Mrs. Robinson is an Englishwoman.”

“Is she? Are you sure of that?”

“Well, she seemed so.”

“Wait and see, my friend. Wait and see.”

I was about to ask him further questions when there was a ring at
the bell.

“Ah!” cried Poirot. “Our first visitor! I wonder who it can be.”

It was Gerald Parker. He looked somewhat surprised to see us.

“Hullo!” he exclaimed. “What are you two doing here?”

“We have taken this flat for a month,” Poirot explained. “A little
whim of mine, you understand.”

Parker laughed.

“Well, you’ve picked a good place. It’s a very comfortable block
of flats. By the way, have you heard the news about the Robinsons?”

“What news?” I asked eagerly.

“They’ve gone!”

“Gone!” I cried. “Where?”

“Nobody knows. They left this morning—bag and baggage. The porter
says they went off in a taxi about eleven o’clock.”

Poirot and I looked at each other.

“This is very interesting,” said Poirot softly. “Very interesting
indeed.”

“I thought you’d be interested,” said Parker. “It’s a queer
business, isn’t it? First they get the flat for a song, and then,
after a few days, they clear out without a word to anyone.”

“And the furniture?” asked Poirot.

“They took it with them. At least, they took some of it. The rest
is still there.”

“I see. And the maid?”

“She went too. The whole party vanished into thin air.”

“Well,” said Poirot, “it is certainly a very remarkable occurrence.
And now, Mr. Parker, if you will excuse us, I think we will go
down and have a look at No. 4.”

“I’ll come with you,” said Parker. “I’m interested in this
business myself.”

We went down to the second floor. The door of No. 4 was locked, but
Poirot produced a bunch of keys from his pocket and, after a few
minutes’ work, the door flew open.

We entered the flat. It was, as Mrs. Robinson had said, very
nicely furnished. But there was a certain air of desolation about
it.

Poirot went straight to the kitchen.

“Ah!” he cried. “As I thought!”

He pointed to the scullery window. It was wide open.

“They didn’t go out by the front door,” he said. “They went out
this way—by the coal-lift.”

“But why?” I asked.

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we have to find out.”

He began to search the flat thoroughly. In one of the bedrooms he
found a small piece of paper lying on the floor. He picked it up
and examined it closely.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is a piece of a letter,” said Poirot. “And it is written in
German.”

He handed it to me. It was only a fragment, but I could make out
the words: “...will be at the usual place... Elsa.”

“Elsa!” I exclaimed. “Then it _was_ Elsa Hardt!”

“It would seem so,” said Poirot. “And now, Hastings, I think we
had better go back to our own flat and think things over. There
is a great deal that I do not understand.”

We left the flat and went upstairs. Parker went back to his own
place, promising to let us know if he heard anything further.

As soon as we were alone, I turned to Poirot.

“What does it all mean?” I asked. “Who is this Elsa Hardt, and
what has she to do with the Robinsons?”

“Elsa Hardt,” said Poirot, “is a very dangerous young woman. She
is a spy, Hastings—a very clever and successful spy. And she is
also a murderess.”

“A murderess!” I cried. “Who has she murdered?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to tell you.”

He sat down in his armchair and began to speak in his usual
methodical way.

“You remember the case of the late Sir James Bond? He was found
dead in his study about six months ago. It was supposed to be a
case of suicide, but I have always had my doubts about it. Sir
James was a very wealthy man, and he had many enemies. He was also
in possession of certain important state secrets.”

“And you think Elsa Hardt murdered him?”

“I am sure of it. She was seen leaving his house on the night of
the murder. But she disappeared completely, and the police were
never able to find her.”

“And what about the Robinsons?”

“The Robinsons,” said Poirot, “were her accomplices. They took
the flat in Montagu Mansions as a hiding-place for her. They chose
that particular flat because of the coal-lift, which provided a
convenient means of escape.”

“But why did they leave so suddenly?”

“Because they realized that I was on their track. They knew that
I had taken the flat upstairs, and they guessed that I was
investigating the case. So they decided to clear out before I
could catch them.”

“And where are they now?”

“That I do not know. But I have a very good idea where they are
likely to be found.”

“Where?”

“At the house of a certain Mrs. Ferguson—the same Mrs. Ferguson
who told Mrs. Robinson that the flat was let.”

“Elsie Ferguson!” I exclaimed. “But she is a friend of Mrs.
Robinson’s.”

“Precisely. And she is also a member of the same gang of spies.
She was the one who arranged the whole business.”

“But what about the fragment of the letter? What does that mean?”

“It means,” said Poirot, “that Elsa Hardt is planning another
murder. And we must stop her before it is too late.”

“Another murder! Who is she going to murder?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we are going to find out. Come,
Hastings, we have no time to lose.”

We left the flat and went down to the street. Poirot hailed a taxi
and gave the driver an address in South Kensington.

“Where are we going?” I asked.

“To the house of Mrs. Ferguson,” said Poirot. “I have a feeling
that we shall find Elsa Hardt there.”

When we arrived at the house, Poirot told the driver to wait. We
went up to the front door and Poirot rang the bell.

The door was opened by a maid.

“Is Mrs. Ferguson at home?” asked Poirot.

“Yes, sir. Will you come this way?”

We were shown into a large and elegantly furnished drawing-room.
A few minutes later, Mrs. Ferguson entered the room. She was a
tall, dark woman with a very determined expression.

“Good evening,” she said. “What can I do for you?”

“We have come to see Miss Elsa Hardt,” said Poirot.

Mrs. Ferguson started.

“Elsa Hardt! I don’t know any Elsa Hardt.”

“I think you do,” said Poirot quietly. “She is staying here with
you, is she not?”

“I don’t know what you are talking about,” said Mrs. Ferguson
angrily. “And now, if you will excuse me, I have a great deal to
do.”

She turned to leave the room, but Poirot stepped in front of her.

“One moment, Mrs. Ferguson. I have a warrant for the arrest of
Elsa Hardt. And I also have a warrant for your arrest, as her
accomplice.”

Mrs. Ferguson’s face went white.

“This is ridiculous!” she cried. “You can’t prove anything!”

“I think I can,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will be so good as
to tell me where Elsa Hardt is, it will be much better for you.”

Mrs. Ferguson looked at him for a moment, and then she realized
that the game was up.

“She is upstairs,” she said in a low voice. “In the bedroom on the
second floor.”

Poirot and I went upstairs. We found the bedroom door locked, but
Poirot soon managed to open it.

Inside the room, we found a young woman with auburn hair. She was
sitting at a desk, writing a letter.

When she saw us, she started up and tried to escape, but Poirot
was too quick for her.

“Miss Elsa Hardt,” he said, “I am arresting you for the murder of
Sir James Bond.”

The girl didn’t say a word. She just stared at him with a look of
defiance in her eyes.

Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of our little investigation?”

“It’s amazing!” I said. “I would never have believed it.”

“It was all very simple,” said Poirot. “Once I had the clue of the
auburn hair, everything else followed logically.”

“But what about the Robinsons? What has happened to them?”

“They have also been arrested,” said Poirot. “They were caught
trying to leave the country this afternoon.”

“And what about Mrs. Ferguson?”

“She will also be dealt with,” said Poirot. “She was the mastermind
behind the whole business.”

“Well,” I said, “it’s a great relief to know that the case is
finally settled.”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “It is a very satisfactory conclusion. And now,
Hastings, I think we had better go back to our own flat and have
a nice cup of tea.”

I agreed. As we walked back to Montagu Mansions, I couldn't help
thinking what a remarkable man Hercule Poirot was. He had solved
one of the most mysterious cases of the century, and all because
of a chance remark about a cheap flat.

It was indeed a most unusual case.

“You observe? Never do they bolt these doors in the daytime. And
yet anyone could mount or descend as we have done. At night
yes—though not always then—and it is against that that we are going
to make provision.”

He took from his pocket a small steel wedge, which he proceeded
skilfully to insert between the bottom of the door and the floor.

“That will hold it—firmly! And now, Hastings, to return as we came.
The little exercises of the coal-lift are somewhat exhausting, are
they not?”

“But Poirot,” I gasped when we were once more in our own flat.
“What—what is it you are expecting to happen?”

Poirot’s face grew suddenly grave.

“I am expecting that what happened six months ago will happen
again, Hastings. A woman who is tall and fair with auburn hair and
blue eyes, and her husband who is quite a nice fellow—nothing
startling—dark or fair—just an ordinary sort of face.”

“But I don’t understand! The Robinsons have been there six
months——”

“My poor Hastings! You do not yet see? It is not the same Mrs.
Robinson—it is another Mrs. Robinson. And before that, I doubt not,
there was another still! Stella—the star! The Star of the Morning!
Does that say nothing to you?”

“Not a thing.”

“I will tell you, then. Stella was the name of the girl who was
murdered in the coal-cellar at Plumpton’s. You remember? Her
husband—the ‘ordinary sort of fellow’—was never caught. That was
six months ago. Six months before that there was another murder—the
‘West-end mystery.’ The victim was a woman, tall and fair, with
auburn hair and blue eyes. In each case the flat had been taken
recently, and in each case the furniture had been ‘bought for a
mere song.’”

“Poirot!” I cried. “You mean——”

“I mean that the man we are looking for is a ‘man of the world,’
Hastings. He knows the ways of women. He knows that no woman can
resist a ‘bargain.’ He knows that a woman who is tall and fair
with auburn hair and blue eyes is—well, a type. And he knows that
there are many such women in London. So he baits his trap. A
flat—at a rent that is ‘dirt cheap’—furnished. What woman can
resist it? He gets them there, one after another—the Stella
Robinsons of this world. And then——”

Poirot’s voice dropped to a whisper.

“Then, Hastings, he kills them. He kills them for the sake of their
clothes—their jewels—the few poor sticks of furniture they have
brought with them. It is a ‘business,’ you see. A ‘paying
proposition.’”

“But the bodies?”

“The coal-lift, Hastings! The coal-lift! What more simple? Down to
the basement—and then? Who knows? There are many ways of disposing
of a body in London if one is clever—and this man is very clever.
He has been doing it for years, I shouldn’t wonder. One every six
months. It is a ‘regime,’ you see.”

“But the porter? He said they had been there six months.”

“Exactly! To him they are always ‘the Robinsons.’ One ‘Mrs.
Robinson’ goes—another ‘Mrs. Robinson’ comes. She is always the
same type—tall and fair with auburn hair. Why should he notice any
difference? He is a man of few words, as you saw. He does not
trouble himself about the tenants.”

“But the agents? Stosser and Paul?”

“Ah, there we come to the most clever part of the whole business.
I have no doubt that ‘Stosser and Paul’ is—just the man himself!
He has a little office somewhere—a ‘dummy’ office—and it is there
that he lures his victims. He tells them the flat is already ‘let,’
knowing well that that will only make them more anxious to get it.
Then he pretends to ‘relent.’ It is a beautiful ‘system,’
Hastings—beautiful!”

“But Mrs. Robinson? Our Mrs. Robinson? Is she——”

“She is in the most imminent danger, Hastings! At any moment—this
very night perhaps——”

“We must warn her!” I cried, starting up.

“Wait! We do not know when he will strike. We must watch—and wait.
That is why I have taken this flat. That is why I have ‘wedged’
the door of the coal-lift. He will not be able to use it to-night!”

“And the husband? Is he in it too?”

“I think not. He is probably just a ‘dummy’ like the rest. A
convenient ‘stalking horse.’ The man we want is the man who
poses as the ‘agent’—the man who ‘sells’ the furniture—the man who
is behind the whole ‘system.’”

“But who is he?”

“That, Hastings, is what we are going to find out!”

The evening wore away. We sat in the dark, watching the door of
the flat below. Twice the porter passed along the corridor, but
there was no other sign of life.

At eleven o’clock, the lights in the Mansions were put out. Still
we watched.

It must have been about midnight when I heard a faint sound from
below—the sound of a door being softly opened.

“Poirot!” I whispered.

He gripped my arm.

“_Silence!_”

A figure emerged from No. 4. It was the figure of a man. He carried
a large suitcase. He moved stealthily towards the lift.

“Now!” hissed Poirot.

We dashed down the stairs. The man turned, saw us, and dropped the
suitcase. He made a bolt for the stairs, but I was too quick for
him. I tackled him round the waist, and we came down together in
a heap.

Poirot was beside us in an instant. He had a small electric torch
in his hand. He flashed it into the man’s face.

I uttered a cry of astonishment.

It was Gerald Parker!

“Parker!” I gasped. “You!”

Poirot’s voice was cold and hard as steel.

“Yes, Hastings. Mr. Gerald Parker—the man who ‘loves’
house-hunting! The man who is ‘always moving’! The man who knows
all about ‘flats’ and ‘maisonnettes’!”

“But—but I don’t understand! The bodies—the ‘Mrs. Robinsons’——”

“There are no bodies, Hastings! And there are no ‘Mrs.
Robinsons’—except the ones that Mr. Parker has ‘invented’ for your
benefit!”

“Invented?”

“Precisely! It was a ‘plot,’ you see. A ‘plot’ to get rid of
certain—shall we say, ‘incriminating’ documents? Documents that
were hidden in the furniture of No. 4, Montagu Mansions! Mr. Parker
knew they were there, but he did not know how to get them. So he
‘invented’ the story of the ‘cheap flat’ and the ‘mysterious
disappearances’ to account for his interest in the place. He even
‘invented’ the ‘Mrs. Robinson’ who told you the story—oh, she was
a real woman, of course, a ‘friend’ of his who was in the plot!
And he hoped that you, Hastings, would ‘investigate’ the matter,
and—well, ‘pull the chestnuts out of the fire’ for him!”

“But the porter? He said they had been there six months.”

“A little matter of a ‘bribe,’ Hastings! A very small ‘bribe’
will go a long way with a man like that!”

Parker had struggled to his feet. He was white to the lips, and
his eyes were full of a baffled rage.

“You—you——” he sputtered.

“_Precisely_, Monsieur!” Poirot’s voice was bland and polite. “I
am Hercule Poirot! And I am not quite so—shall we say, ‘simple’—as
my friend Hastings here!”

He turned to the suitcase which lay on the floor.

“And now, Monsieur Parker, we will see what it is that you were
so anxious to—‘remove’ from No. 4!”

He knelt down and opened the suitcase. It was full of papers—legal
documents, letters, and blueprints.

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes gleamed. “The ‘treaty,’ I think! The ‘secret
treaty’ that was stolen from the Foreign Office last month! A
very valuable ‘commodity,’ Monsieur Parker! One for which certain
‘Foreign Powers’ would be willing to pay a very high price!”

He rose to his feet and looked at Parker.

“It was a clever ‘plot,’ Monsieur—very clever! But you made one
mistake. You forgot that Hercule Poirot has a ‘nose’ for these
things! And now, Hastings, if you will be so good as to fetch a
policeman——”

I did so. And as I led the way back to the Mansions, I couldn’t
help thinking that, after all, Poirot was right. I am a little
‘simple’ sometimes!
