The next morning, Poirot was in a thoughtful mood.

“A curious case, Hastings,” he said, as he sipped his chocolate.
“A very curious case.”

“But it’s all over now,” I said. “Parker is in prison, and the
treaty is safe.”

“Is it?” Poirot’s eyes were fixed on the ceiling. “I wonder.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, Hastings, that there is one thing that I do not quite
understand. Why did Parker ‘invent’ the story of the ‘Mrs.
Robinsons’? Why did he not just—take the flat himself?”

“He said he was ‘always moving.’ It would have looked suspicious.”

“Perhaps. And yet——”

He was silent for a moment. Then he turned to me.

“Hastings, do you remember the woman you saw—the ‘Mrs. Robinson’
who told you the story?”

“Of course.”

“And you said she was ‘tall and fair with auburn hair and blue
eyes’?”

“Yes.”

“And the woman we saw yesterday—the one who went out for the
‘Sunday concert’—she was also ‘tall and fair with auburn hair and
blue eyes’?”

“Yes.”

“And the ‘Elsie Ferguson’ that Mrs. Robinson mentioned—she was
also ‘looking for a flat’?”

“Yes.”

“It is a ‘type,’ you see, Hastings! A ‘type’ that Monsieur Parker
seems to be very fond of!”

“Well, what of it?”

“Nothing—except that I have a feeling, Hastings—a very strong
feeling—that we have not yet seen the end of this ‘Mrs. Robinson’
business!”

And as it turned out, he was right. But that is another story.

Poirot took from his pocket a small and extremely sharp chisel,
and before I could speak he had begun to work upon the door of the
scullery. For some minutes he worked in silence, his fingers
deftly prying at the wood. When he had finished, the latch would
still hold, but the least pressure from outside would cause the
door to fly open.

“There,” said Poirot, surveying his handiwork with pride. “Now we
will return to our own flat and wait. It is a very simple trap,
_mon ami_, but it is the simple traps that often catch the
biggest rats.”

We returned as we had come, and once back in our own quarters,
Poirot became unusually silent. He sat in his favorite armchair,
his eyes closed, his fingertips joined, the very picture of a
man deep in thought. I knew better than to disturb him, for I
could see that the little grey cells were working at high pressure.
Whatever mystery lay behind the cheap flat of the Robinsons, Poirot
was determined to solve it. For my part, I was still puzzled by
the conflicting stories—the Robinsons’ claim of having just moved
in and the porter’s insistence that they had been there for six
months. Who was lying, and why? And where did Elsie Ferguson, the
friend who had supposedly been mistaken, fit into the puzzle? 

The hours of the Sunday evening crawled by. Poirot remained
immobile, and I found myself jumping at every sound from the
corridor outside. At last, as the clocks of the neighborhood
struck eleven, Poirot stirred and opened his eyes.

“The time has come, Hastings,” he said softly. “The actors are
taking their places upon the stage. Let us see what the play
will be.”

As we reached the second floor, Poirot stepped out onto the narrow
landing of the service stairs. He did not attempt to enter the 
Robinson's flat, but instead, he began to examine the doorframe of 
the service entrance with a tiny magnifying glass. "You see, 
Hastings," he whispered, his eyes dancing with that peculiar green 
light I knew so well, "the wood here has been recently disturbed. 
A new bolt, perhaps? Or something more... ingenious?" He ran 
a finger along a faint, almost invisible scratch near the lock. 
"The Robinsons, they move in yesterday, yet the porter says they 
have been here six months. And our charming Mrs. Robinson, she 
tells a tale of luck that defies the laws of London real estate. 
Someone is playing a very clever game, and this door, it is the 
backstage entrance to the theater." He straightened up, 
gesturing for us to ascend once more. "We have seen enough for 
one afternoon. Tomorrow, we shall pay a formal call upon our 
'neighbors' and see if the lady with the auburn hair recognizes 
the man she met at Mr. Parker's."

He drew from his pocket a small and very sharp-looking knife, and
deftly cut through several of the ropes of the lift.

“It will take some time to mend,” he commented, “and meanwhile the
only way into No. 4 will be by the hall door. Now, Hastings, we will
ascend to our own flat once more.”

The rest of the evening Poirot spent in a large armchair, gazing
intently at the ceiling and occasionally muttering to himself in
his native tongue.

“I cannot understand it!” he broke out at last. “What was the
motive?”

“I don’t follow you,” I said.

“Listen. Mrs. Robinson has told us that she has just taken the
flat. The porter, on the contrary, says that they have been there
six months. Why did she lie? She had no reason to do so—it was a
gratuitous piece of fiction. There must be some motive behind it.”

“I can only suppose,” I said, “that she wished to make herself
out more interesting than she was. You know how these women are.”

“_Mon ami_, I have the highest opinion of women, but I do not
flatter myself that I understand them as you do. Still, let us
consider the facts. Mrs. Robinson told us a story of a flat let
at a ridiculously low rent. Is it true? I find it is not. The flat
is let at its proper value. Therefore the whole of her story is
false. Why?”

“She must have been pulling our legs,” I suggested.

“No, no, Hastings. There is something more than that. Something
deep and sinister. And I am going to find out what it is.”

He sat for some time longer in silence, then rose and went to the
window.

“Look, Hastings. There is a man watching the house.”

I joined him at the window. A tall, dark man was standing on the
opposite pavement, his eyes fixed on the entrance to Montagu
Mansions.

“Who is he?” I asked.

“I do not know, but he has been there for the last hour. And I
fancy that he is not the only one.”

“What do you mean?”

“Look there—at the corner of the street. There is another man.
And see, there is a third further down.”

“It’s a regular siege!” I exclaimed.

“It looks like it. And the objective is No. 4.”

“Do you think they are after the Robinsons?”

“I am sure of it. But why? What have they done? Or what have they
got that these men want?”

He turned away from the window and began to pace the room.

“I must think, Hastings. I must think. There is something here
that I do not understand.”

He continued to pace the room for some time, then suddenly he
stopped and a look of triumph came into his eyes.

“I have it!” he cried. “I have it at last!”

“What is it?” I asked eagerly.

“The name, Hastings! The name! Robinson! Do you not see?”

“I’m afraid I don’t.”

“But it is so simple! Robinson—the most common name in England!
And what was the name of the lady? Stella—a star! Do you not see
now?”

“I’m afraid I’m as far off as ever,” I confessed.

Poirot sighed.

“Never mind, my friend. All will be revealed in time. For the
present we must wait and watch.”

He went back to the window and stood there looking out into the
gathering darkness.

“The plot thickens, Hastings,” he murmured. “The plot thickens.”

The next few days passed without any further developments. Poirot
spent most of his time at the window, watching the men in the
street. They were always there, sometimes one, sometimes two,
sometimes three. They never seemed to do anything, but they never
relaxed their vigilance.

As for the Robinsons, they went about their business as usual.
Mrs. Robinson went out shopping, and Mr. Robinson went to his
office in the City. They seemed quite unaware of the men who were
watching them.

Then, on the Thursday evening, something happened.

We were sitting in the drawing-room after dinner, when there was
a ring at the bell. I went to the door and found a young woman
standing there. She was dressed in a nurse’s uniform and looked
pale and agitated.

“Is Mr. Poirot in?” she asked.

“Yes,” I said. “Will you come in?”

I showed her into the drawing-room, where Poirot was waiting for
her.

“Monsieur Poirot?” she said.

“I am Hercule Poirot, mademoiselle. What can I do for you?”

“I am Elsa Hardt,” she said. “I am a nurse at the hospital near
by. I have come to you because I am in great trouble.”

“Sit down, mademoiselle, and tell me all about it.”

She sat down and began to tell her story.

“It’s about a patient of mine,” she said. “A Mr. Parker. He was
brought in a few days ago, suffering from a severe head injury.
He has been unconscious most of the time, but this evening he
regained consciousness for a few minutes and he told me to come
to you.”

“Gerald Parker!” I exclaimed. “But I saw him only a few days ago!”

“He said you would know him, Captain Hastings,” said Elsa Hardt.
“He told me to tell you that he had found out the secret of No. 4,
and that his life was in danger.”

“Where is he now?” asked Poirot.

“He’s at the hospital. But I’m afraid he’s very ill. The doctors
don’t think he’ll last the night.”

“We must go to him at once!” cried Poirot.

He seized his hat and stick and hurried out of the room. I followed
him, and in a few minutes we were in a taxi on our way to the
hospital.

When we arrived, we were shown into a small private room. Gerald
Parker was lying in bed, his head swathed in bandages. He looked
ghastly pale and his eyes were closed.

Poirot went up to the bed and spoke to him.

“Mr. Parker,” he said. “It is I, Hercule Poirot. Can you hear me?”

Parker opened his eyes and looked at him.

“Poirot,” he whispered. “Thank God you’ve come.”

“What happened, Mr. Parker?” asked Poirot.

“I was—I was attacked,” said Parker. “In the street—near Montagu
Mansions. They—they hit me on the head.”

“Who were they?”

“I don’t know. But I saw them—the men who were watching the
house. They—they followed me.”

“And what did you find out about No. 4?” asked Poirot.

Parker’s voice was growing weaker.

“The flat,” he whispered. “It’s—it’s not what it seems. The
Robinsons—they’re not—they’re not who they say they are.”

“Then who are they?” asked Poirot.

But Parker did not answer. His eyes closed and he slipped back
into unconsciousness.

The nurse, Elsa Hardt, came forward.

“I’m afraid he can’t tell you any more now,” she said. “He must
rest.”

Poirot nodded.

“We will come back in the morning,” he said.

We left the hospital and drove back to Montagu Mansions in silence.
Poirot was deep in thought, and I did not care to disturb him.

When we reached the flat, Poirot went straight to the window and
looked out.

“They are still there, Hastings,” he said. “The watchers. But
there is something new. Look.”

I joined him at the window. A large black car was drawn up at the
curb, and two men were standing beside it.

“What does it mean?” I asked.

“It means that the crisis is approaching, Hastings. We must be
prepared.”

He went to the table and picked up his revolver.

“Is it loaded?” he asked.

“Yes,” I said.

“Good. Keep it ready. We may need it before the night is out.”

He sat down in his armchair and waited. I sat opposite him, my
revolver in my hand. The hours passed slowly. The silence of the
night was broken only by the occasional sound of a passing car or
the distant chiming of a clock.

Suddenly, there was a sound from the scullery. A faint, scraping
sound, as if someone were trying to open the door.

Poirot was on his feet in an instant. He signalled to me to be
silent and crept towards the scullery. I followed him, my heart
thumping against my ribs.

We reached the scullery door and Poirot peered through the keyhole.

“It is as I thought,” he whispered. “They are coming up the lift.”

He turned to me, his eyes gleaming with excitement.

“Now, Hastings! Now is the time!”

He threw open the scullery door and we burst into the room.

Two men were just stepping out of the lift. They were both tall and
powerfully built, and they were armed with revolvers.

“Hands up!” cried Poirot.

The two men were so taken by surprise that they dropped their
revolvers and held up their hands.

“Who are you?” demanded Poirot. “And what are you doing here?”

The men did not answer. They stood there, sullen and defiant.

“I see,” said Poirot. “You will not speak. Very well. Hastings,
will you be so good as to telephone for the police?”

I went to the telephone and gave the alarm. In a few minutes, the
sound of a police siren could be heard in the distance.

The two men were led away by the police, and Poirot and I were
left alone in the flat.

“Well, Poirot,” I said. “You were right after all. But what does
it all mean? Who are these men, and what were they after?”

Poirot smiled.

“It is very simple, my friend. These men were members of a gang of
international thieves. They were after the Robinson diamonds.”

“The Robinson diamonds!” I exclaimed. “But I’ve never heard of
them!”

“No, because they were stolen some months ago from the Duchess of
Abercrombie. The thieves were never caught, but the diamonds were
traced to London. It was believed that they were hidden in a flat
in Montagu Mansions.”

“And were they?”

“Yes. In No. 4. The thieves had taken the flat under the name of
Robinson, and they had hidden the diamonds there. But then they
became aware that the police were watching them, and they were
afraid to move the diamonds. So they hit upon a very clever plan.
They decided to let the flat to someone else, and to hide the
diamonds in the furniture.”

“But why did they let it to the Robinsons?”

“Because of the name, Hastings! They wanted someone with the same
name, so that if the police made inquiries, they would find that
Mr. and Mrs. Robinson were still living there. And they chose a
young couple who were looking for a cheap flat, so that they would
be less likely to ask questions.”

“But what about the fifty pounds for the furniture?”

“That was the master-stroke! The furniture was worth far more than
that, but the thieves wanted to make sure that the Robinsons took
it. And they knew that if they offered it at a very low price, the
Robinsons would jump at it.”

“I see. But how did you find out all this, Poirot?”

“By using my ‘little grey cells,’ Hastings! The story of the cheap
flat was so improbable that I knew there must be something behind
it. And when I found out that the Robinsons had been there for six
months, I knew that they were lying. Then I remembered the Duchess
of Abercrombie’s diamonds, and everything became clear.”

“But what about Elsie Ferguson? And Elsa Hardt? And Gerald Parker?”

Poirot’s face clouded.

“Ah, that is the sad part of the story. Elsie Ferguson and Elsa
Hardt were both members of the gang. They were sent to watch the
Robinsons and to make sure that they didn’t find the diamonds.
And poor Gerald Parker—he must have stumbled upon the truth and
they tried to silence him.”

“It’s a terrible business,” I said.

“Yes, it is. But at least justice has been done. The thieves are in
custody, and the diamonds will be restored to their rightful
owner.”

He turned away from the window and smiled at me.

“And now, Hastings, I think we have earned our dinner. Let us go
and find a good restaurant.”

As we left the flat, I couldn’t help thinking how lucky I was to
have a friend like Hercule Poirot. He might be a little conceited
at times, but there was no denying his genius.

He stepped into the scullery, where a row of empty milk bottles
stood on a dresser. Opening the little window, he carefully
extracted the inner pane of glass. Then he examined the fastening
on the scullery door.

“_Bon!_” he ejaculated. “The simplest way.”

With a pocket knife, he cleverly picked the lock. It was child’s
play to him.

I followed him into the flat, which was exactly like our own above
it. Poirot appeared to have some definite end in view. He searched
the little hall, then went into the dining-room.

“Ah! Here we are!”

He was pointing to a heavy oak sideboard, a handsome piece of
furniture.

“You see?”

“I see a sideboard,” I said. “Is there anything remarkable about
it?”

“Look closer.”

I looked, but could see nothing special.

“Open the left-hand cupboard.”

I did so. It was empty.

“Open the right-hand one.”

This also was empty.

“Look inside.”

I did so, and noticed that the back was of some dark-coloured wood.

“Feel it.”

I ran my hand over the wood. It was smooth and cold.

“Wait!” Poirot produced a small electric torch. He directed the
beam into the cupboard.

I saw now that the wood at the back was not part of the sideboard
at all. It was a thin piece of three-ply wood which had been
skilfully fitted in.

“You see? A false back. Why? For what purpose? To hide something?
Possibly. We shall see.”

He replaced the plywood and we left the flat by the way we had
come.

“What does it mean?” I asked, as we were once more in our own
abode.

“It means, my friend, that the Robinsons have a reason for taking
this flat—a reason which they have not seen fit to disclose.”

“But the furniture—they bought it for fifty pounds!”

“Exactly. And the furniture—or at any rate a part of it—belongs
to the previous tenant.”

“But who _was_ the previous tenant?”

“That is what I am going to find out,” replied Poirot. “It will
be interesting, I think.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“Tell me, Hastings, when you saw Mrs. Robinson at Parker’s, did
she mention a friend of hers—a woman?”

“Yes—Elsie Ferguson. She said she was looking for a flat too.”

“Elsie Ferguson. I wonder—I wonder if she is the same person as
a certain Elsa Hardt?”

“Elsa Hardt? Who is she?”

“A very clever and dangerous woman, Hastings. She is an
international spy. At the beginning of the War she was in England,
but she managed to escape to Holland, and from there to Germany.
Since then she has been heard of in various parts of Europe. She
is supposed to have a genius for disguise. If Elsie Ferguson is
Elsa Hardt——”

He broke off.

“But what has that to do with the Robinsons?”

“Everything, my friend. If the Robinsons are what they seem to
be—just a young couple looking for a flat—then Elsie Ferguson may
be just a friend of theirs. But if the Robinsons are—well, not
exactly what they seem to be—then the matter is different.”

“You think they are in league with Elsa Hardt?”

“It is a possibility. We must be prepared for anything. That is
why I asked you if you had a revolver. One never knows.”

He was silent again, and I did not care to interrupt his thoughts.
I was beginning to realize that what I had taken for a simple
mystery was likely to prove a much more complicated affair.

The next few days passed without any further developments. Poirot
seemed to have lost interest in the Robinsons. He spent most of
his time in the flat, reading or writing. He did not go out much,
and when he did, he was always back before dark.

On Thursday afternoon, however, he received a letter which seemed
to excite him.

“Aha!” he exclaimed. “This is what I have been waiting for!”

“What is it?” I asked.

“A letter from a friend of mine in Paris. He has been making
inquiries for me. It seems that Elsa Hardt was in Paris last week.
She was seen in the company of a man who is known to be an agent
of the Soviet Government.”

“The Soviet Government! Then it is a political matter?”

“It may be. But we shall see. In the meantime, Hastings, I want
you to do something for me.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to go to the office of Stosser and Paul, the house
agents, and find out what you can about the previous tenant of
No. 4, Montagu Mansions. Do not mention my name. Just say you are
interested in the flat and would like to know who lived there
before the Robinsons.”

“I’ll go at once,” I said.

I found the office of Stosser and Paul without difficulty. It was
in a small street off Mayfair. A clerk came forward to attend to
me.

“I am interested in a flat in Montagu Mansions,” I said. “No. 4,
to be precise. I understand it was recently let to a Mr. and Mrs.
Robinson.”

“That is correct, sir,” said the clerk.

“I was wondering if you could tell me who the previous tenant was?”

The clerk looked a little surprised.

“The previous tenant was a Mr. Gerald Parker,” he said.

“Gerald Parker!” I exclaimed. “Are you sure?”

“Perfectly sure, sir. He had the flat for about six months.”

I was so surprised that I could hardly speak. Gerald Parker! The
very man who had been my host on the evening when I first heard
about the flat!

“Thank you,” I said, and hurried out of the office.

I found Poirot waiting for me in our flat.

“Well?” he asked.

“The previous tenant was Gerald Parker!” I cried.

Poirot did not seem surprised.

“I thought as much,” he said. “It is very interesting.”

“But what does it mean? Parker never mentioned that he had lived
in Montagu Mansions. In fact, he seemed quite surprised when Mrs.
Robinson spoke about it.”

“Exactly. He was very surprised. And yet he was the person who
told them about the flat in the first place—or rather, he was the
person who introduced them to the subject of flat-hunting.”

“But why should he lie about it?”

“That is what we have to find out. But I think I can guess. Gerald
Parker is a very clever man, Hastings. He has a ‘shrewd business
head,’ as you said. And he is also a man who is very fond of—what
did you call it?—the ‘sport’ of house-hunting.”

“You mean he is involved in this?”

“I think it is more than likely. But we must be careful. We are
dealing with very clever people.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I think it is time we paid another visit to No. 4. But this time
we will not go by the coal-lift. We will go in by the front door.”

“But the Robinsons will be there!”

“I do not think so. I have reason to believe that they are out.”

“How do you know?”

“I have been watching the flat. They went out about half an hour
ago. And the maid has also gone out.”

“Then the flat is empty?”

“Exactly.”

We went down to the second floor and Poirot rang the bell. There
was no answer. He rang again, and then, after a moment’s wait, he
produced a bunch of keys from his pocket and proceeded to try them
one by one in the lock.

At last one of them turned and the door swung open. We stepped
inside and Poirot closed the door behind us.

The flat was quiet and still. We went into the dining-room and
Poirot went straight to the sideboard. He opened the right-hand
cupboard and felt for the plywood back.

“It is still here,” he said.

He began to feel around the edges of the plywood with his fingers.
Suddenly there was a sharp click and the plywood swung open like
a door.

Behind it was a small cavity, and in the cavity was a small steel
box.

Poirot took out the box and carried it to the table. He produced
another bunch of keys and after a few moments the box was open.

Inside was a mass of papers—mostly letters and documents. Poirot
began to look through them quickly.

“Aha!” he exclaimed. “This is what I wanted!”

He held up a letter. It was written in German and was addressed to
Elsa Hardt.

“What does it say?” I asked.

“It is a letter from her employer in Berlin. It gives her
instructions for her work in England. It seems she was to obtain
certain secret plans of a new type of submarine which the British
Admiralty is building.”

“And did she get them?”

“I think so. Look at this.”

He held up another document. It was a set of technical drawings.

“These must be the plans!” I cried.

“They are. And they were hidden in this sideboard all the time.”

“But why did she leave them here?”

“I think I can explain that. She knew she was being watched, and
she didn’t want to be caught with the plans on her. So she hid them
in the sideboard, intending to come back for them later. But then
something happened—perhaps she had to leave the country in a hurry—and
she wasn’t able to get them.”

“But what about the Robinsons? Where do they come in?”

“The Robinsons are not Robinsons at all. They are agents of Elsa
Hardt. They were sent here to get the plans.”

“And Gerald Parker? What about him?”

“I think Gerald Parker is the person who was supposed to receive
the plans from Elsa Hardt. But he was also being watched, so he
couldn’t get them himself. That’s why he had to use the Robinsons.”

“But why did he pretend not to know about the flat?”

“Because he didn’t want anyone to suspect him. He wanted it to
look like a complete coincidence that the Robinsons had taken the
flat.”

“But then why did he tell me about it?”

“Because he wanted to use you as an alibi. He knew that if you
were there when the Robinsons talked about the flat, it would look
even more like a coincidence.”

“It’s incredible!” I said. “And to think that I actually liked the
man!”

“He is a very charming man, Hastings. That is one of his greatest
assets.”

Suddenly Poirot stiffened.

“Hark!” he whispered. “Someone is coming!”

We heard the sound of a key in the front door.

“Quick!” said Poirot. “Behind the curtain!”

We hurried behind the long velvet curtains that hung at the window.
A moment later the door opened and someone entered the room.

It was Gerald Parker.

He was alone. He went straight to the sideboard and opened the
cupboard. He seemed surprised to find the plywood door open.

He reached into the cavity and then uttered a cry of rage.

“Gone!” he shouted.

At that moment Poirot stepped out from behind the curtain.

“Looking for these, Monsieur Parker?” he asked, holding up the
plans.

Parker turned, his face white with fury.

“You!” he gasped.

“Yes, it is I, Hercule Poirot. I think you have some explanations
to make, Monsieur Parker.”

Parker’s hand went to his pocket, but before he could draw his
revolver I was upon him. We struggled for a moment, and then I
managed to wrest the weapon from his hand.

“Well done, Hastings!” said Poirot. “I think we have our man.”

He turned to Parker.

“It was a very clever scheme, Monsieur Parker. But you made one
mistake. You forgot that Hercule Poirot is not easily deceived.”

Parker did not speak. He stood there, his face a mask of hatred.

“And now,” said Poirot, “I think we had better call the police.”

He went to the telephone and began to dial.

As he did so, the door opened and Mrs. Robinson entered the room.

She looked from Poirot to Parker, and then her eyes fell on the
plans.

“So,” she said, her voice cold and hard. “You have found them.”

“Yes, Madame,” said Poirot. “We have found them. And I think we
have found out a good many other things as well.”

She looked at him for a moment, and then she turned to Parker.

“I told you we should have been more careful,” she said.

“It was your fault!” Parker snarled. “You should have gotten the
plans sooner.”

“Enough!” said Poirot. “The police will be here in a few minutes.
I think it would be better if you both remained quiet.”

He turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, I think we can congratulate ourselves. It has been
a most interesting case.”

“It certainly has,” I said. “But there’s one thing I don’t
understand. Why did Mrs. Robinson tell us about the flat in the
first place? If she wanted to keep it a secret, why did she talk
about it at Parker’s?”

“That was a very clever move, Hastings. She knew that if she talked
about it openly, it would look less suspicious. And she also knew
that you would be there, and that you would probably tell me about
it. She wanted me to think that it was just a simple case of a
cheap flat, so that I wouldn’t look any further.”

“But it backfired!”

“Exactly. It backfired. She forgot that Hercule Poirot is always
interested in anything that is unusual. And the cheapness of the
flat was very unusual indeed.”

He smiled at me.

“And now, my friend, I think we have earned our dinner. Let us go
and celebrate our success.”

We left the flat and went down to the street. As we walked away, I
couldn’t help thinking about Gerald Parker. I had always liked him,
and it was hard to believe that he was a spy.

“You know, Poirot,” I said, “I’m almost sorry for him.”

“Do not be sorry for him, Hastings. He is a dangerous man. And he
would have had no mercy on you if he had had the chance.”

“I suppose you’re right.”

“Of course I am right. I am always right.”

We walked on in silence for a while, and then Poirot said:

“You know, Hastings, there is one thing that I am very glad of.”

“What is that?”

“I am glad that Elsie Ferguson was not Elsa Hardt. It would have
been a pity if such a charming young woman had turned out to be
a spy.”

“But who was she, then?”

“She was just what she seemed to be—a friend of Mrs. Robinson’s
who was also looking for a flat. And she did go to the wrong flat,
just as you said.”

I felt a glow of satisfaction.

“So I was right about something after all!”

“Yes, Hastings. You were right about that. And I am very happy to
be able to say so.”

We reached the restaurant and went inside. It had been a long and
tiring day, but as we sat down to our meal, I felt a sense of great
accomplishment. We had solved the mystery of the cheap flat, and
we had caught a dangerous spy.

It was a good day’s work for Hercule Poirot and his friend,
Captain Hastings.

He had drawn some tools from his pocket as he spoke, and at once
set deftly to work, his object being to arrange the bolt so that
it could be pulled back from the lift. The operation only occupied
about three minutes. Then Poirot returned the tools to his pocket,
and we reascended once more to our own domain.

On Monday Poirot was out all day, but when he returned in the
evening he flung himself into his chair with a sigh of satisfaction.

“Hastings, shall I recount to you a little history? A story after
your own heart and which will remind you of your favourite cinema?”

“Go ahead,” I laughed. “I presume that it is a true story, not one
of your efforts of fancy.”

“It is a story of three people,” began Poirot, “all three of whom
are well known to the police of two continents. There is first of
all a woman, beautiful, blonde, and, let us say, a trifle
adventurous. She has for some years been known as Elsa Hardt. Then
there is her friend and colleague, a young American of the name of
Gerald Parker. He was originally what you call a ‘con man’ but
subsequently became more ambitious and associated himself with a
clever but unscrupulous Italian, and together they had many
schemes to their credit. But their latest and greatest exploit was
the theft of some very valuable diamonds, which were on their way
from South Africa to a firm of London merchants. The robbery took
place on the high seas, and the stones were successfully smuggled
into this country.”

“But why did they choose this particular flat?” I asked, much
interested.

“That is what I was coming to. After the robbery, which was
remarkably well planned, the three people in question came to
London. They took this flat under an assumed name, but they had
not been in residence many days when they became aware that they
were being watched by the police. In fact, a warrant was out for
their arrest. It was then that they devised their ingenious scheme.
The girl, Elsa Hardt, would stay in the flat, and they would find
some young couple to take it off their hands, a couple who would
exactly resemble the descriptions of themselves, and would thus
unconsciously act as their substitutes. You see the idea,
Hastings? The police would watch the flat, and, when they were
ready to strike, they would arrest the innocent couple. In the
meantime, the real criminals would have had time to get away.”

“But what about the rent?” I asked. “They couldn’t hope to get a
couple to pay three hundred and fifty pounds a year for a flat
that was only worth eighty.”

“No, but they could sublet it at a loss! It was a small price to
pay for their safety. And they must have known that any young
couple would be only too glad to get such a bargain. They had only
to wait for the right people to come along. Mrs. Robinson was
exactly what they wanted. She was tall and fair, and her husband
was just an ordinary young man.”

“But how did they get Mrs. Robinson to go there?” I asked.

“That was easy enough. They simply put an advertisement in the
papers, offering the flat at a ridiculously low rent. They knew
it would be snapped up at once.”

“But the agents? Surely they would know that the rent was too
low?”

“They would not know the real rent of the flat. The criminals
would have seen to that. They would have represented themselves as
the owners, and would have given the agents all the necessary
information.”

“But what about Elsie Ferguson?” I asked. “Why did she tell Mrs.
Robinson that the flat was let?”

“That was all part of the scheme. They wanted to make Mrs. Robinson
more anxious than ever to get the flat. They knew that if she
thought someone else was after it, she would be all the more
likely to take it at once.”

“It’s a most ingenious story, Poirot,” I said, “but what has
happened to the criminals? Have they escaped?”

“Not yet, Hastings. They are still in London, and I have reason to
believe that they are planning another robbery. But this time they
will not find it so easy to escape.”

“And the diamonds? Where are they?”

“Ah, that is what I should like to know. But I think I have a clue.”

“What is it?” I asked eagerly.

“Do you remember the coal-lift, Hastings? I have a suspicion that
the diamonds are hidden somewhere in that lift. That is why I took
this flat. I wanted to have an opportunity of examining it.”

“But why the coal-lift?”

“Because it is the only place in the flat where they could have
hidden them without any fear of their being discovered. No one
ever uses the coal-lift nowadays, and even if they did, they would
not be likely to find the diamonds.”

“It’s a possible theory, Poirot,” I said, “but it seems a bit far-fetched.”

“We shall see, Hastings. We shall see.”

“Listen. One day last autumn, a certain lady—we will call her Elsa
Hardt—became suddenly extremely popular. She was a lady who lived
under several names and in several different countries. In this
country she was known as Elsa Hardt. She was a young lady of
singular beauty, and possessed of a most delightful personality.
Her hair was of a very lovely auburn tint. Do you follow me,
Hastings?”

“Is it possible?” I gasped.

“Quite possible. For the first time in her life, however, Elsa
Hardt felt she was in some danger. The police of two countries
were very anxious to see her. They had many things to discuss with
her. And Elsa Hardt did not wish to see them. There was only one
way of safety. She must disappear. She must find a sanctuary. It
must be a sanctuary where she would not be known, and where she
could live in peace and quiet until the clouds had rolled by. Now,
think, Hastings, what was the best thing for her to do?”

“Go to the country,” I suggested.

Poirot shook his head.

“No, that would be a mistake. She would be noticed at once. No,
the best place to hide is in a crowd. But it must be a place where
no one would dream of looking for her. And where could she find
such a place? In a small flat, Hastings! In a small flat where she
could live as a quiet, respectable married woman with her husband.
But there were several difficulties. First of all, she must find
the husband; and then she must find the flat. The husband was easy.
She knew many men who would be only too glad to play the part.
But the flat! That was more difficult. It must be a flat in a large
block of buildings where no one would know her. And it must be a
flat that she could get quickly, and without many questions being
asked. Now, you see, Hastings, the importance of the flat.”

“I see,” I said. “But what has all this to do with Mrs. Robinson?”

“Wait. Elsa Hardt had a friend. Her name was Elsie Ferguson. Elsie
Ferguson was also a lady who lived under several names. She was
not so beautiful as Elsa Hardt, but she was very clever. She was
the ‘brain’ of the organization. It was she who thought of the
flat. She found the flat in Montagu Mansions. It was a flat that
was to be let furnished. Elsa Hardt and her ‘husband’ took it. They
took it for six months. They paid the rent in advance. They were
very quiet, very respectable. No one suspected them. They were just
Mr. and Mrs. Robinson. They were very happy. But then, after six
months, the clouds began to roll away. Elsa Hardt could come out
of her sanctuary. But there was one difficulty. If she and her
husband just disappeared, it might cause inquiry. They must find
someone to take their place. Someone who would be glad to get a
cheap flat. And they found—the real Robinsons!”

“But how did they know that they were called Robinson?” I asked.

Poirot smiled.

“They didn’t. They just waited until someone of that name came to
look at the flat. They knew that sooner or later someone called
Robinson would come. And then they would tell them that the flat
was let—to another Robinson! You see, Hastings? It was very simple.
And the real Robinsons would be so pleased at getting a cheap flat
that they wouldn’t ask any questions. They would just move in, and
the other Robinsons would move out. And no one would ever know the
difference!”

“But why go to all that trouble?” I asked. “Why not just leave?”

“Because, my friend, Elsa Hardt was still a little afraid. She
wanted to be sure that no one was following her. And if she could
show that ‘Mr. and Mrs. Robinson’ were still living in the flat,
no one would look for her anywhere else. It was a very clever
plan.”

“And what happened then?”

“That is what we are going to find out, Hastings. Tonight we will
visit the flat of Mr. and Mrs. Robinson!”

“It is as true as most stories told to Poirot are. You know of
the ‘Star of the East’? No? It is the great diamond of the
De Be Beers, one of the famous stones of the world, and it was
brought home to England some three weeks ago by its owner, Lady
Hardt, a young and lovely American. You are perhaps aware that
the Hardts are one of the richest and most powerful families in the
States. It was reported that the Star of the East had been stolen
on the night of Lady Hardt’s arrival in London. But it was
recovered later on, though I believe its recovery was not generally
known, and I was even asked to look into the matter by Lady Hardt’s
agent here. Since then I have had it under my eye, and for the last
ten days it has been in the care of its owner, Lady Hardt, herself,
at her house in Mayfair.”

Poirot’s eyes had become very small and bright as he reached this
point of his narrative. He leaned forward and lowered his voice
impressively:

“Wait, Hastings! Here is the point of my story. Last night Lady
Hardt was again robbed. The Star of the East has disappeared
once more. Only this time it is a very different affair. There
can be no doubt about it this time. It has been stolen.”

“You are sure of that?”

“Positive. I have just come from Lady Hardt’s. The stone was
removed from her dressing-table during the night.”

“And you have no clue? Who was in the house at the time?”

“Everyone is under suspicion—her husband, her maid, her
secretary, and her cousin, Elsa Hardt, who is staying with her.
She is a very beautiful girl, Hastings, but she has a somewhat
eccentric reputation.”

“I see. And you suspect——”

“I suspect no one. I have merely looked at the case from the
outside. Now we must see what the inside has to say to us. This
evening we will visit No. 4, Montagu Mansions.”

“You mean——”

“I mean that the Star of the East is there.”

“But how do you know?”

“I do not know—I deduce. I told you that ‘Stella’ means a star,
did I not? And what is more likely than that the Star of the
East should be found in a flat whose mistress is named Stella? It
is a little joke of mine, Hastings, but I believe it will turn out
to be a very good one.”

“But, Poirot, this is incredible!”

“Wait and see, my friend. Wait and see.”

I could get nothing more out of him, and I had to be content to
wait for the evening with what patience I could muster. It was
about nine o’clock when Poirot rose and signed to me to follow
him. We descended in the coal-lift as before, and Poirot soon
had the door of No. 4 open. The flat was in darkness, and we
crept cautiously into the hall.

“Listen!” whispered Poirot.

A low murmur of voices came from the drawing-room. We stole towards
it, and Poirot cautiously opened the door an inch or two. I
peered over his shoulder.

The room was lit only by a small lamp on a table in the centre.
Two people were sitting there—a man and a woman. The man I
recognized as Robinson, but the woman was a stranger to me. She
was dark and very handsome, and she was dressed in a way that
suggested she was about to go out.

“It’s all right, Elsa,” Robinson was saying. “The car will be here
in five minutes. You’ve got the stone?”

“Yes, I’ve got it,” replied the woman. “But I don’t like it, John.
It’s too dangerous. Why can’t we wait a bit?”

“Because we can’t. We’ve got to get it away tonight. If we don’t,
Poirot will be on our track.”

“Poirot! What do you mean?”

“I mean that he’s in this building. I saw him this afternoon.”

“You did? Then why did you come back here?”

“Because I had to get the stone. And besides, he doesn’t know
anything yet. He’s only suspicious. If we can get away now, we’re
safe.”

“But where are we going?”

“To Paris. I’ve got the tickets. Come on, we haven’t a moment to
lose.”

They rose and moved towards the door. Poirot and I retreated into
the shadows of the hall. As they passed us, I saw the woman’s
face clearly. It was a face I shall never forget—beautiful,
but with a look of terror and desperation that was haunting.

They went out of the flat and down the stairs. Poirot and I followed
them at a distance. When they reached the street, they got into a
large car that was waiting for them.

“Quick, Hastings!” cried Poirot. “A taxi!”

We were fortunate enough to find one almost immediately, and Poirot
gave the driver instructions to follow the car in front.

The chase led us through the streets of London, out into the
suburbs, and finally on to the main road to Dover. The car in front
was a fast one, and it was all our driver could do to keep it in
sight.

“Where are they going, Poirot?” I asked.

“To the coast, of course. They hope to catch the midnight boat
to Calais.”

“But we must stop them!”

“We shall, my friend. We shall.”

As he spoke, the car in front suddenly swerved and came to a
standstill. We pulled up behind it, and Poirot and I jumped out.

The man and woman were already out of the car and were running
towards a small cottage that stood by the side of the road.

“Stop!” cried Poirot. “In the name of the law!”

They paid no attention to him, but disappeared into the cottage.
We followed them, and as we entered the small living-room, we saw
them standing by the fireplace.

“It’s no use, Robinson,” said Poirot calmly. “The game is up. Give
me the Star of the East.”

The man looked at him with a look of defiance.

“I don’t know what you’re talking about,” he said.

“Oh, yes, you do. And if you don’t give it to me, I shall be forced
to take it from you.”

He moved towards the man, but the woman stepped between them.

“No!” she cried. “You shan’t have it!”

She reached into her bosom and drew out a small leather case. She
opened it, and there, lying on a bed of white velvet, was the
most magnificent diamond I have ever seen. It was truly a star—a
shining, brilliant star of light.

“It’s mine!” she cried. “It belongs to me!”

“It belongs to Lady Hardt,” said Poirot quietly. “And you are
going to give it back to her.”

He reached out his hand, but the woman drew back.

“Never!” she cried. “I’d rather die first!”

And before we could stop her, she had snatched a small pistol from
the table and pointed it at her own head.

“Stop!” cried Poirot.

But it was too late. There was a loud report, and the woman fell
to the floor.

Robinson uttered a cry of despair and threw himself beside her.

“Elsa! Elsa!” he cried.

But she did not answer. She was dead.

Poirot moved towards the body and picked up the leather case. He
opened it and looked at the diamond for a moment. Then he closed
the case and put it in his pocket.

“Come, Hastings,” he said. “Our work here is done.”

As we walked back to the taxi, I asked him:

“Who was she, Poirot? And how did she get the diamond?”

“She was Elsa Hardt,” he replied. “Lady Hardt’s cousin. And she
stole the diamond because she was in love with Robinson, and they
needed the money to start a new life together in Paris.”

“But how did you know she was at the flat?”

“I didn't know for certain. But when I heard the name Robinson, and
learned that the flat was being sublet at such a low rent, I
became suspicious. And when I found out that Elsa Hardt was
staying with Lady Hardt, and that she was a friend of the
Robinsons, the pieces of the puzzle began to fall into place.”

“And what about the other woman—the one who told Mrs. Robinson
the flat was let?”

“That was Elsie Ferguson, Elsa’s sister. She was in on the plot,
too. She wanted to make sure that no one else took the flat, so
that Elsa and Robinson could use it as a hideout.”

“I see. And the fifty pounds for the furniture?”

“That was just a ruse to make the whole thing look legitimate. The
furniture was actually worth much more than fifty pounds, but
the Robinsons didn't care about that. They just wanted to get
settled in the flat as quickly as possible.”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “you’ve done it again. You’ve solved
another mystery.”

“It was nothing, my friend,” he replied with a smile. “Just a
matter of logic and deduction. And a little bit of luck, of
course.”

As the taxi drove us back to London, I couldn't help but marvel at
the brilliant mind of Hercule Poirot. He had once again proved
himself to be the greatest detective in the world.

“Listen then, Hastings. Some months ago, certain important papers—plans of a new type of coastal defense, to be precise—were stolen from the Ministry. The thief was a woman, a very clever woman of international reputation, known as Elsa Hardt. She was known to be in league with a certain foreign power. The police were hard on her heels, but she vanished into thin air. She and her accomplice were traced to a certain house in London, but after that—nothing. They disappeared as if the earth had swallowed them up. It was a most remarkable disappearance, one that has intrigued the Secret Service for months. And now, I believe, we are on the track of the lady who calls herself Elsa Hardt, and I have a little idea that our ‘cheap flat’ is the key to her whereabouts.”

“It is a true story, and it is a most interesting one. Some
months ago, a certain lady, a Mrs. Ferguson, was looking for a
flat. She was a beautiful woman, with auburn hair and blue
eyes, and her husband was a man of about thirty-five, dark,
with a small black moustache. They went to various agents, and
finally they heard of a flat in Montagu Mansions, the rent of
which was only eighty pounds a year. They went to the flat, and
saw the maid, and then the mistress, and the thing was
concluded. They were to move in on the following Tuesday.”

“But, Poirot, this is the story of the Robinsons! You have
forgotten the name.”

“On the contrary, I have remembered it. These people’s name was
Ferguson. They moved in, and remained for about three weeks. At
the end of that time, the lady became ill, and her husband
decided that they must leave London at once for the country.
They left, taking with them all their belongings. And then,
behold, about a month later, the flat is again in the market,
and another young couple, also with auburn hair and blue eyes,
arrive and take it. They also remain for about three weeks, and
then the lady becomes ill, and they also leave for the
country.”

“Poirot! What does it mean? Are you serious?”

“I am most serious. I have been to various agents to-day, and I
have found that this has happened no less than four times in the
last six months. Each time the couple is the same—a young woman
with auburn hair and blue eyes, and a husband who is dark and
not too tall.”

“But the Robinsons—they are there now!”

“Precisely. They have been there for three weeks. And to-day,
Mrs. Robinson has become ill, and they are leaving for the
country to-morrow.”

“Poirot! Is there some devilry at work? What is the meaning of it
all?”

“That is what we are going to find out, Hastings. To-night, we
will pay a visit to No. 4. We will go down by the coal-lift, as
we did before, and we will see what we can find.”

“But won’t they be there?”

“The flat will be empty. They are leaving this evening, instead
of to-morrow. I have seen the van at the door. We will wait
until they have gone, and then we will make our investigation.”

“But why the coal-lift, Poirot? Why not go in by the front door?”

“Because, my friend, the front door will be locked. And besides,
it is more—how you say?—spectacular to go by the coal-lift. It
appeals to your romantic nature, does it not?”

I could not help smiling, though I felt a certain amount of
trepidation at the prospect of our midnight adventure.

“Very well,” I said. “I am with you. But I hope we don’t get
caught!”

“We shall not be caught, Hastings. I have seen to that. And now,
let us have some dinner, and then we will prepare for our
expedition.”

We dined at a small restaurant in Soho, and then returned to our
flat to wait for the appointed time. At eleven o’clock, Poirot
rose and beckoned to me.

“Come,” he said. “The time has arrived. We will go down.”

We descended by the coal-lift as we had done before, and soon
reached the second floor. Poirot deftly manipulated the bolt,
and we stepped into the scullery of No. 4. The flat was in total
darkness, and the air was heavy with the smell of stale tobacco
and some sweet, sickly perfume.

“Wait here a moment,” whispered Poirot. “I will get my
flashlight.”

He disappeared into the darkness, and I waited, my heart beating
fast with excitement. A few moments later, he returned with a
small electric torch.

“Now,” he said. “Let us see what we can find.”

We moved cautiously through the flat, our footsteps muffled by the
thick carpets. Everything seemed to be in order. The furniture
was all there, and there was no sign of any struggle or
violence. We went into the bedroom, and there, on the dressing-table,
we saw a small bottle of medicine.

“Aha!” said Poirot. “What have we here?”

He took the bottle and held it up to the light. It was half full
of a clear, colourless liquid.

“What is it?” I asked.

“I do not know, Hastings. But we will have it analyzed. It may
be the key to the mystery.”

We continued our search, but found nothing else of interest.
Finally, we went into the drawing-room, and there, on the floor
near the window, we saw a small piece of paper. Poirot picked it
up and examined it by the light of his torch.

“What is it?” I asked again.

“It is a telegram,” replied Poirot. “And it is addressed to
someone named Elsa Hardt.”

“Elsa Hardt!” I exclaimed. “Who is she?”

“That is what we must find out, Hastings. But look at the
message. It says: ‘Everything ready. Come at once. G.’”

“G!” I cried. “Gerald Parker!”

“Perhaps, Hastings. Perhaps. But we must not jump to
conclusions. There are many names beginning with G.”

“But Parker was the one who told us about the flat!”

“True. But that does not prove that he is involved in this
business. We must have more evidence before we can accuse anyone.”

We left the flat as we had entered it, by the coal-lift, and
returned to our own quarters. Poirot was silent and thoughtful for
the rest of the evening, and I could see that he was hard at
work on the problem.

The next morning, he sent the bottle of medicine to be analyzed,
and then he went out again. He did not return until late in the
afternoon, and when he did, his face was grave.

“Hastings,” he said. “I have news. The medicine contained a
powerful sedative, enough to make anyone sleep for several hours.
And I have found out who Elsa Hardt is.”

“Who is she?” I asked eagerly.

“She is a well-known German spy,” replied Poirot. “She has been
active in this country for some time, and the police have been
looking for her for months.”

“A spy!” I cried. “But what has she to do with the Robinsons and
the other couples?”

“That is what we are going to find out to-night, Hastings. We are
going back to No. 4, and this time, we are going to wait for
our friends to arrive.”

“But who are they?”

“I do not know, Hastings. But whoever they are, they are up to no
good. And we must be ready for them.”

We went back to the flat at eleven o’clock, and took up our
positions in the drawing-room. We waited in the darkness for
several hours, and then, just as I was beginning to think that
nothing was going to happen, we heard a sound at the front door.

Someone was turning a key in the lock. The door opened, and we
heard footsteps in the hall. Two people were coming into the
flat.

“Stay where you are,” whispered Poirot. “And don't make a
sound.”

The two people came into the drawing-room, and one of them turned
on the light. It was Gerald Parker and a woman I had never seen
before. She was tall and dark, with a hard, cruel face.

“Well,” said Parker. “Everything is ready. We can leave as soon
as she arrives.”

“Good,” replied the woman. “I am glad it is almost over. I am
tired of this business.”

“So am I,” said Parker. “But it will be worth it in the end. Once
we have the plans, we can leave the country and never look back.”

“And what about the girl?” asked the woman.

“She will be safe enough,” replied Parker. “The sedative will
keep her quiet until we are well away. And by the time she
wakes up, it will be too late.”

“I hope so,” said the woman. “I don't like the idea of leaving her
here. Someone might find her.”

“No one will find her,” said Parker. “The flat is supposed to be
empty. And besides, who would ever think of looking for her
here?”

At that moment, Poirot stepped out from behind the curtain, his
revolver in his hand.

“I would, Mr. Parker,” he said quietly.

Parker and the woman both started in surprise, and Parker
reached for his pocket.

“I wouldn't do that if I were you, Mr. Parker,” said Poirot. “My
friend Hastings has his revolver as well, and he is a very
good shot.”

I stepped out from behind the other curtain, my revolver at the
ready.

“What is the meaning of this?” demanded Parker, trying to put a
bold face on it.

“The meaning is very simple, Mr. Parker,” replied Poirot. “You
and your accomplice, Elsa Hardt, are under arrest for
espionage and kidnapping.”

“You’re crazy!” cried Parker. “I don't know what you’re talking
about!”

“Oh, I think you do,” said Poirot. “I have been following your
movements for some time, and I know all about your little
scheme. You used the cheap flat as a lure to find young women
who looked like Elsa Hardt, so that she could use their
passports to leave the country. And when you found a suitable
candidate, you drugged her and took her place.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Elsa Hardt. “You have no proof!”

“I have all the proof I need,” said Poirot. “Including the
telegram you sent to Mr. Parker, and the bottle of sedative I
found in the flat. And I have also found the real Mrs.
Robinson, who is at this moment being cared for by the
police.”

Parker and Elsa Hardt both turned pale, and I could see that they
knew the game was up.

“You’re too clever for us, Poirot,” said Parker, with a bitter
laugh. “I should have known better than to try and fool you.”

“Yes, Mr. Parker,” said Poirot. “You should have. And now, if you
will both come with us, we will hand you over to the proper
authorities.”

We took them to the police station, where they were charged with
their crimes. And then Poirot and I went back to our flat, where
we had a long talk about the case.

“It was a clever scheme, Poirot,” I said. “But how did you know
it was Parker?”

“It was the telegram, Hastings,” replied Poirot. “The ‘G’ could
only have stood for Gerald. And when I found out that he was the
one who had told you about the flat, I knew he must be involved.”

“And Elsa Hardt?”

“She was the woman who had been taking the place of the young
women who took the flat. She was a perfect match for them, and
with their passports, she could easily have left the country
without being detected.”

“It was a brilliant piece of work, Poirot,” I said. “I don't know
how you do it.”

“It is simple, my friend,” replied Poirot, with a smile. “It is all
a matter of using the little grey cells. And now, let us have
some tea, and then we will go to bed. It has been a long and
exciting day.”

I agreed, and we spent the rest of the evening in quiet
conversation, as the mystery of the cheap flat was finally
laid to rest.

“It is true enough. Inspector Japp of Scotland Yard will vouch for
its accuracy, since it was through his kind offices that it came
to my ears. Listen, Hastings. A little over six months ago some
important Naval plans were stolen from an American Government
department. They showed the position of some of the most important
Harbour defences, and would be worth a considerable sum to any
foreign Government—that of Japan, for example. Suspicion fell upon
a young man named Luigi Valdarno, an Italian by birth, who was
employed in a minor capacity in the Department and who was missing
at the same time as the papers. Whether Luigi Valdarno was the
thief or not, he was found two days later on the East Side in New
York, shot dead. The papers were not on him. Now for some time past
Luigi Valdarno had been going about with a Miss Elsa Hardt, a young
concert singer who had recently appeared and who lived with a
brother in an apartment in Washington. Nothing was known of the
antecedents of Miss Elsa Hardt, and she disappeared suddenly about
the time of Valdarno’s death. There are reasons for believing that
she was in reality an accomplished international spy who has done
much nefarious work under various _aliases_. The American Secret
Service, whilst doing their best to trace her, also kept an eye
upon certain insignificant Japanese gentlemen living in Washington.
They felt pretty certain that, when Elsa Hardt had covered her
tracks sufficiently, she would approach the gentlemen in question.
One of them left suddenly for England a fortnight ago. On the face
of it, therefore, it would seem that Elsa Hardt is in England.”
Poirot paused, and then added softly: “The official description of
Elsa Hardt is: Height 5 ft. 7, eyes blue, hair auburn, fair
complexion, nose straight, no special distinguishing marks.”

“Mrs. Robinson!” I gasped.

“Precisely, Hastings,” said Poirot, his eyes twinkling at my excitement. “The description is identical. But consider the discrepancy. The porter at Montagu Mansions insists that Mrs. Robinson has resided there for six months. Our charming friend, on the other hand, tells us she has only just secured the lease at a miraculously low rent. Does it not strike you as significant? If one wished to vanish, what better way than to install a double in one’s own apartment—a double who bears the same name and the same appearance, and who has a perfectly legal right to be there? The ‘cheap flat’ was the bait, Hastings. A bait designed to attract a couple of a certain appearance and, shall we say, a certain financial standing, who would jump at the chance to live in Knightsbridge for a pittance.”

“But the porter said they had been there six months!” I cried. “And Mrs. Robinson told us only the other night that they had just taken the flat.”
“Exactly,” said Poirot. “The ‘Robinsons’ who have been there for six months are the spies. The ‘Robinsons’ you met are the innocent doubles, chosen for their name and their appearance, and lured by the bait of a ‘cheap flat’ to take the place of the others. The real Elsa Hardt and her companion wish to vanish, but they also wish to provide a substitute—someone to receive any... shall we say, ‘unpleasantness’ that might be intended for them. The Japanese gentleman, he will come to No. 4 Montagu Mansions. He will find a man and a woman who answer to the name and the description. It is very simple—and very villainous.”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “The description tallies. But there is a small difficulty. Our Mrs. Robinson—the ‘delightful creature’—says she has just taken the flat. The porter says she has been there six months. If she is Elsa Hardt, she has been in Washington until recently; she could not have been here six months ago. Therefore, either she is not Elsa Hardt, or the woman the porter saw six months ago was someone else entirely—someone who perhaps resembles her. And then there is the matter of the ‘cheap’ rent. Why offer a flat at eighty pounds when it is worth three hundred and fifty? To attract a particular type of tenant, Hastings? A tenant like the Robinsons? Or perhaps to ensure the flat was never truly ‘on the market’ for long? Let us not forget the mysterious Elsie Ferguson, who tried to discourage her friend from even visiting the place.”

"Precisely," murmured Poirot, "the description, it fits like a glove. But let us not march too quickly. If you were a dangerous spy with a king’s ransom in your pocket, would you risk everything for a saving of two hundred pounds a year in rent? It is not logical. And what of the others in this little drama? Our friend Gerald Parker, who is so ‘shrewd’ a business head and yet so obsessed with these flats? Or the mysterious Elsie Ferguson, who vanished as quickly as she appeared? No, Hastings, there is a deeper play here. Someone desired that the Robinsons—or people who *looked* like the Robinsons—should occupy No. 4 Montagu Mansions. Why? Because the real Elsa Hardt is expected there, and it is better to have a double in her place to draw the fire, or perhaps to act as a shield while the real bird flits away."

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “But observe the ingenuity of the plan. The real Elsa Hardt and her accomplice have been living in that flat for six months under the name of Mr. and Mrs. Robinson. But they are known to be under surveillance. What do they do? They decide to provide themselves with ‘doubles.’ They find a real couple named Robinson, of similar appearance, and through the medium of a ‘philanthropic’ house agent, they lure them to the very flat they themselves have occupied. The newcomers take over the flat, the name, and the reputation of the previous tenants. If the secret agents come for ‘Mrs. Robinson,’ they find—your charming and innocent friend! Meanwhile, the real Elsa Hardt, having successfully ‘shed’ her identity, is free to complete her negotiations for the sale of the papers.”

“Well, there is a chance of it, anyhow,” amended Poirot. “Also, I
learn that a swarthy man, a foreigner of some kind, was inquiring
about the occupants of No. 4 only this morning. Therefore, _mon
ami_, I fear that you must forswear your beauty sleep to-night,
and join me in my all-night vigil in the flat below—armed with that
excellent revolver of yours, _bien entendu_!”

“Rather,” I cried with enthusiasm. “When shall we start?”

“The hour of midnight is both solemn and suitable, I fancy. Nothing
is likely to occur before then.”

I was as good as my word. When midnight arrived I was ready and
waiting. We descended the lift, and when we reached the second
floor Poirot deftly unbolted the door. We had no difficulty in
entering the flat. It was pitch-dark, and our only light was a small
electric torch.

“Where shall we wait?” I asked in a whisper.

“The dining-room, I think,” answered Poirot.

We made our way there and sat down behind the heavy plush curtains.
A long and weary wait began. I began to feel very drowsy.
Suddenly Poirot’s hand gripped my arm.

“_Écoutez!_” he hissed.

For a moment I could hear nothing. Then, away in the distance, I
heard a low, scratching sound.

“The coal-lift,” whispered Poirot. “Someone is coming up.”

Nearer and nearer came the sound. There was a faint thud as the
lift reached the second floor. Then came the sound of the scullery
door opening. A moment later, a man stepped into the kitchen.
I could hear his breathing as he moved cautiously.

Suddenly there was a flash of light. The man had turned on an
electric torch. By its light I saw him quite clearly. He was a
small, swarthy man, and he was carrying a large, heavy-looking
bag. He moved across the kitchen and into the hall.

“Now!” whispered Poirot.

We sprang out from behind the curtains.

“Hands up!” I cried, leveling my revolver at the man’s head.

The man dropped his bag with a crash. He was a small, dark-skinned
man, and his face was distorted with fear.

“Don’t shoot!” he cried. “I—I am only a poor man. I have done
nothing wrong.”

“Who are you?” I demanded.

“My name is—is—Giuseppe,” the man stammered. “I—I am a waiter.”

“A waiter, eh?” said Poirot, stepping forward. “And what is a waiter
doing in a private flat at two o'clock in the morning? And what
is in that bag of yours?”

The man did not answer. Poirot picked up the bag and opened it.
Inside were several sets of heavy, old-fashioned silver.

“Aha!” said Poirot. “A common thief, it would seem. But I think
not. Tell me, my friend, why did you come to this particular flat?”

“I—I was told there was money here,” the man whispered.

“By whom?”

“I—I do not know. A man in a cafe. He told me the flat would be
empty to-night.”

“And you believed him? You are a very foolish man, Giuseppe.
But I do not think you are a thief. I think you are something
much more dangerous.”

“I—I do not understand,” the man stammered.

“We shall see,” said Poirot. “In the meantime, Hastings, I think
we had better take this gentleman to our own flat and wait for
the morning. I have a feeling that we shall have other visitors
before long.”

At twelve o’clock, we accordingly descended to the second floor
by our coal-lift, and Poirot, with his usual dexterity, unbolted
the door from the outside and we entered the kitchen of No. 4.
The flat was as silent as the grave. The Robinsons were apparently
sound asleep.

“I only hope,” whispered Poirot, as he led the way along the
passage, “that they have not provided themselves with a watchdog.”

He seemed to know his way about the flat as though he had lived
there all his life. He chose the small room at the end of the
passage for our vigil. In this room there was a large sofa and
on this we both ensconced ourselves. For some time we sat there in
complete silence. Then Poirot nudged me. I had been nearly asleep.
A light was shining under the door. Then there came the sound of
low voices in the next room. They seemed to be speaking in some
foreign tongue.

“Our friends have arrived!” breathed Poirot. “Wait!”

The light in the next room was suddenly extinguished, and then I
heard the cautious opening and shutting of the door. The next
moment, a hand was on our door-handle and someone was entering the
room. My heart was beating like a sledge-hammer. My hand tightened
on my revolver.

The person, whoever it was, did not seem to be aware of our presence.
He moved across the room in the direction of the window. A moment
later there was a sharp click, and the beam of a pocket torch
swept the floor. It stopped at the sofa where we were sitting.

“Don’t move!” I cried, springing to my feet and pointing my revolver.
“Or I’ll fire!”

The man uttered a low cry of alarm and dropped his torch.

“Switch on the light, Poirot,” I commanded.

Poirot did so. The man was a dark, foreign-looking individual,
certainly not Robinson. He was cowering in the corner, his hands
above his head.

“Who are you?” I demanded. “And what are you doing here?”

He did not reply. Poirot stepped forward and addressed him in
French.

“Will you be so good as to tell us your name?”

“I—I am Luigi Valdarno!” gasped the man.

“Valdarno!” I cried. “But I thought you were dead!”

“I am not dead,” he replied in a trembling voice. “I—I was only
wounded. I—I managed to escape.”

“And what are you doing here?”

“I—I came for the papers. Elsa Hardt has them. She—she stole them
from me.”

“And where is Elsa Hardt?” asked Poirot.

“She is in the next room. She—she is with her brother.”

Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? I was right. Elsa Hardt is indeed in England.
And now, I think we had better have a little talk with her.”

He moved towards the door, but at that moment it was flung open
and a woman stood on the threshold. She was tall and fair, with
auburn hair and blue eyes. In her hand she held a revolver.

“Hands up!” she cried. “Both of you!”

I saw Poirot’s hands go up at once. I followed suit, though with
a feeling of intense chagrin. We were fairly caught!

“So,” she said, her eyes flashing with anger. “You thought you
could catch Elsa Hardt, did you? Well, you were mistaken. And now,
what are we going to do with you?”

She looked from one to the other of us with a mocking smile. Then
her gaze fell upon Valdarno.

“So you are here too, are you, Luigi? I thought I had finished with
you in New York. Well, this time I will make sure!”

She raised her revolver and pointed it at Valdarno’s heart.

“Stop!” cried Poirot. “For God’s sake, don’t fire!”

At that moment, there was a sudden sound of heavy footsteps in the
passage. The door was flung open and Inspector Japp, followed by
two other men, burst into the room.

“Drop that revolver, Elsa Hardt!” he cried. “The game’s up!”

The woman hesitated for a moment, then she dropped her revolver
and burst into a fit of hysterical weeping.

“It’s no use,” she sobbed. “It’s no use! You’ve got me!”

Japp stepped forward and handcuffed her. Then he turned to Poirot.

“Well, Poirot,” he said with a grin. “You’ve done it again! I don’t
know how you do it, I’m sure!”

“It was quite simple, my friend,” replied Poirot with a modest air.
“A little matter of deduction, that is all.”

“And what about the papers?” asked Japp.

“They are in that bureau,” replied Poirot, pointing to a small
writing-desk in the corner. “I found them there this morning when
I was—er—making a few inquiries.”

Japp went over to the bureau and opened it. Inside were several
large envelopes. He tore one open and looked at the contents.

“Yes, these are they right enough,” he said with a sigh of relief.
“Well, Poirot, I must be getting along. I’ve got a taxi waiting
outside. Coming, Hastings?”

“In a moment,” I replied. I was still feeling a little dazed by the
rapidity with which events had moved.

When we were alone, I turned to Poirot.

“But I don’t understand,” I said. “Who was the man who came into
the room first? And how did Japp know we were here?”

Poirot smiled.

“The man was, as he said, Luigi Valdarno. He had followed Elsa
Hardt to England, and was determined to get the papers back. As
for Japp, I telephoned him this afternoon and told him where we
should be. I thought it better to have the official police at hand
in case of any unpleasantness.”

“But how did you know that Mrs. Robinson was Elsa Hardt?”

“My dear Hastings, did I not tell you that the official description
of Elsa Hardt was: Height 5 ft. 7, eyes blue, hair auburn, fair
complexion, etc.? And did you not yourself describe Mrs. Robinson
to me in almost identical terms? The rest was easy. I merely had
to find out if there was anyone in Montagu Mansions who answered
to that description. And there she was—in No. 4!”

“But what about the rent?” I asked. “Why was the flat so cheap?”

“Because,” replied Poirot with a twinkle in his eye, “it was
necessary for Elsa Hardt to have a safe hiding-place where she
could be sure of not being disturbed. And what better hiding-place
could there be than a flat in a respectable neighborhood like
Knightsbridge? By letting it at a ridiculously low rent, she
insured that there would always be plenty of applicants for it,
and she could then pick and choose whom she would. In this way,
she was able to keep an eye on everyone who came to the building,
and to make sure that no one suspicious was hanging about. It was
really a very clever scheme.”

“But what about the real Robinsons?” I asked. “Who were they?”

“There were no ‘real’ Robinsons,” replied Poirot. “The whole thing
was a fabrication. Elsa Hardt and her brother simply took the name
of Robinson and moved into the flat. They were the people who had
been there for six months, as the porter told us.”

“And what about Elsie Ferguson?” I asked. “The friend who told Mrs.
Robinson that the flat was let?”

“She was, I imagine, a confederate,” replied Poirot. “Her job was
to discourage any likely applicants so that Elsa Hardt could have
the pick of them. It was all very neatly arranged.”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “I must take my hat off to you. You really
are a wonder!”

Poirot smiled.

“It was nothing, my friend,” he said. “A mere trifle. But come, let
us go home. I am tired, and I think we both need a good night’s
rest.”

And so ended the mystery of the Cheap Flat.

We took our places in the coal-lift, and Poirot, who was as excited
as a schoolboy, soon had the bolt drawn back and the scullery door
opened. We entered the flat, and Poirot made a careful tour of
the rooms. He was evidently well-satisfied. He selected the
bedroom—the door of which he stood slightly ajar—as our hiding-place.

“There are two of them, you see—the Robinsons,” I whispered. “What
about them?”

“The woman whom you saw on Sunday was an American, Elsa Hardt. She
was staying here as Mrs. Robinson for some months. But she was
afraid of being watched, so she stayed on as Mrs. Robinson and
pretended to let the flat. She had it on their books as being
‘dirt cheap,’ but they were not to let it. Then she could always
say that it was already let if anyone came. But Mrs. Robinson—your
friend, I mean—managed to see it when Elsa was out. She took it
before the other could stop her. Elsa Hardt must have been furious!
But what could she do? She had to let it go. But since she has
come to England she has found that her pursuers have caught her
scent, and she is at her wits’ end what to do.”

“But I don’t see——”

“Sh!” Poirot’s hand was on my arm. “I hear a sound.”

We listened intently. Someone was moving in the sitting-room. A
low murmur of voices reached our ears.

“Wait here,” whispered Poirot.

He crept out of the room. A minute later I heard a scuffle and a
short cry. I rushed out to his assistance. In the center of the
room, Poirot was struggling with a tall, dark man. Another man,
stout and elderly, was standing by the window. As I appeared, the
first man broke away and dashed for the door. But I was too quick
for him. I had my revolver out and I covered him.

“Hands up!” I cried.

The man obeyed, with a muttered oath. At that moment the door
opened and the police, headed by Japp, burst into the room.

“Caught them, Japp?” cried Poirot.

“We’ve got the lot of them,” replied the Inspector. “And the
lady, too!”

He pointed to a woman who was standing in the doorway. It was
Mrs. Robinson. But it was not the Mrs. Robinson I had met at
Parker’s. This woman had dark hair and was several years older.

“Elsa Hardt!” cried Poirot.

“Yes,” she said, “you have won this time, M. Poirot. But there
will be another time!”

She was led away by the police.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we walked back to our own flat, “that
was a most exciting business. But there are still several things
I don’t understand. For instance, why did you think the papers
were in this flat?”

“Because Elsa Hardt would not have stayed here so long if they had
not been here. She was waiting for her Japanese friends to come
and fetch them. And then, when she was forced to let the flat to
your friends, she had to leave the papers behind. She was probably
intending to come back for them later, but she found that she was
being watched. So she had to wait until her friends arrived and
then they could all come together and search for the papers. They
were hidden in the coal-lift, by the way. I found them there this
morning.”

“And what about the other Mrs. Robinson?” I asked. “The one I met
at Parker’s?”

“Ah,” said Poirot, “that is the most interesting part of the whole
story. She was not Mrs. Robinson at all. She was—but here she is!”

We had reached our own door, and a lady was waiting for us. It was
the fair-haired Mrs. Robinson.

“Oh, M. Poirot,” she cried, “have you got them?”

“Yes, madame,” said Poirot, handing her a small packet. “Here are
your jewels.”

“My jewels!” I gasped.

“Yes, Hastings. This lady is not Mrs. Robinson, but Mrs. Gerald
Parker. She and her husband have been helping me in this little
matter. They were very anxious to get their jewels back—they were
stolen some months ago—and they thought that Elsa Hardt might have
them. So they pretended to be the Robinsons and took the flat.
It was a very clever idea, was it not?”

I looked at Poirot in amazement.

“Then the story about the cheap flat——”

“Was all a part of the plot, Hastings. I told you that it was a
curious story!”

At midnight, then, we descended our unusual staircase. The scullery
door was unlocked, and we made our way into the pitch-dark flat.
Poirot led the way with a small electric torch. We established
ourselves in the drawing-room, a pleasant enough apartment and
rather daintily furnished. We waited in silence for several hours.
It was about half-past three that a sound like a faint scratching
at the front door became audible. My heart began to beat a tattoo
against my ribs. Poirot’s hand was on my arm, and I felt him give
a quick squeeze. The scratching continued, and then, after what
seemed to me an age, there was a click and the door opened softly.
The ray of a dark lantern flashed round the room. My hand closed
firmly on my revolver.

In the faint light, I could distinguish the figure of a man, and
it seemed to me that I also saw a second figure behind him. They
moved with the utmost caution.

One of them was evidently searching for something. He went straight
to a bureau and I heard the sound of a key being turned in a lock.

“Now!” whispered Poirot.

I sprang forward, my revolver ready, and Poirot’s electric torch
revealed a tall dark man in the act of opening a drawer of the
bureau. At the sight of us he uttered an oath and reached for his
pocket.

“Hands up!” I cried, “or I shoot!”

The man gave a snarl of baffled rage and held up his hands. His
companion, a smaller man, stood beside him.

“I’ve got them, Poirot!” I cried exultantly. “Keep them covered
whilst I ring for the police.”

“One moment, Hastings,” said Poirot’s voice behind me.

I looked round in surprise. Poirot was not looking at the two men
at all. He was standing by the window, his head slightly on one
side as though listening.

“What is it?” I asked.

“The police, Hastings. I think I hear them. They are coming up in
the lift.”

He ran to the door and opened it. Two men in plain clothes entered.

“Mr. Poirot?” said one of them.

“At your service, Inspector. You are just in time. Here are our
friends.”

The two men were handcuffed and led away. Poirot followed them
to the door.

“A good night’s work, Inspector,” he said.

“Yes, sir. We’ve been looking for those two for some time. They’re
a pretty pair!”

When they had gone, Poirot returned to the drawing-room. He seemed
to be in a state of great excitement.

“Now for the cream of the jest, Hastings!” he cried. “Look!”

He went to the bureau and opened the drawer which the first man
had been about to search. From it he took a small, leather-bound
despatch-box. He opened it with a key which he took from his
pocket.

“_Voilà!_” he cried, and held up a packet of papers. “The Naval
plans!”

“Poirot!” I gasped. “Then Mrs. Robinson——”

“Is Elsa Hardt, of course. I knew it from the first. The auburn
hair, the blue eyes—and then the name! Stella—a star. It was all
so clear!”

“But how did you know the plans were here?”

“Because she told you so herself, Hastings! Don’t you remember her
story? The flat was ‘dirt cheap’—no premium—and she had to buy the
furniture for fifty pounds! Why? Because the plans were hidden in
one of the pieces of furniture, and she had to make sure of getting
them! She and her ‘husband’—who was no doubt her brother—had been
