living here for six months as ‘Mr. and Mrs. Robinson’ whilst they
waited for a chance to get the plans away safely. Then, when they
thought the coast was clear, they pretended to ‘find’ the flat
and move in as a ‘newly married couple.’ It was a very clever
scheme, but they did not account for Hercule Poirot!”

“But why did she tell us about it at all?” I asked.

“Because she is a woman, Hastings! She could not resist the
temptation of bragging about her ‘luck.’ And then, of course, she
wanted to account for her presence here in case any of her former
acquaintances should see her. It was a risk, of course, but she
is a woman who loves risks.”

“And the two men?”

“They were no doubt agents of some foreign Power who had also
discovered the secret of the flat. They were after the plans, too.”

“It’s wonderful, Poirot!” I cried. “Simply wonderful!”

Poirot smiled modestly.

“It was a small thing,” he said. “A very small thing. But it had
its points. And now, my friend, let us return to our own flat. I
think we have earned our repose.”

It was a few minutes past twelve when we cautiously made our
way down the lift-shaft to the second floor. Poirot had already
loosened the bolt, and we stepped into the dark scullery of the
Robinsons’ flat. I felt my heart beating with excitement as we
crept through the silent rooms.

“We will wait in the drawing-room,” whispered Poirot. “It
commands the front door and the hall.”

He led the way, and I followed him. The flat was shrouded in
darkness, and every sound seemed magnified a hundredfold. We
crouched behind a large sofa, and waited. The minutes dragged
by like hours. I began to wonder if Poirot’s theories were
correct, or if we were on a wild-goose chase.

Suddenly, a faint sound reached my ears—the soft click of a
key in the lock. I felt Poirot’s hand on my arm, a silent
warning to remain still. The front door opened slowly, and
a dark figure slipped into the hall. It moved with the
stealthy grace of a cat, heading straight for the small
study where we knew the Robinsons kept their private papers.

The intruder was a woman. Even in the dim light, I could
make out the graceful curve of her figure and the glint of
auburn hair. She was dressed in dark, practical clothes,
and she carried a small electric torch which she used
sparingly.

We watched as she began to methodically search the desk.
She seemed to know exactly what she was looking for, and
her movements were quick and efficient. After a few minutes,
she uttered a low cry of triumph as she drew a thick
envelope from a hidden compartment.

“Now!” whispered Poirot.

I sprang up, my revolver levelled at the intruder. “Hands
up!” I commanded, my voice sounding strangely loud in the
stillness of the room.

The woman spun around, her eyes wide with terror. The
torch dropped from her hand, its beam rolling across the
floor. In the sudden glare, I saw her face clearly. It was
not Mrs. Robinson. It was Elsie Ferguson.

At twelve o’clock precisely, we crept cautiously into the coal-lift
and lowered ourselves to the second floor. Under Poirot’s
manipulation, the wooden door quickly swung inwards, and we climbed
into the flat. From the scullery we passed into the kitchen where
we established ourselves comfortably in two chairs with the door
into the hall ajar.

“Now we have but to wait,” said Poirot contentedly, closing his
eyes.

Suddenly he started into an attitude of attention. A low,
whistling noise was audible from somewhere below us. It was
followed by a dull thud.

“The lift,” whispered Poirot. “But this time it is from the
ground floor.”

We waited. The lift came to rest on the second floor, and we
heard the wooden door into the scullery being cautiously
manipulated. Then there were footsteps in the kitchen, and a
man’s figure appeared in the doorway. He was a small man with
the typical face of the Japanese, and he was carrying an
electric torch in his hand. Its beam fell on Poirot and myself.
He uttered a low, guttural exclamation and his hand went to his
pocket. But I was too quick for him. My revolver was leveled
at his head before he could move.

“Drop it,” I commanded.

The man’s hand fell to his side. He stood there, motionless,
his eyes fixed on the weapon in my hand. Then, with a sudden,
agile movement, he turned and dashed into the hall.

“After him, Hastings!” cried Poirot.

We were just in time to see him disappearing through the front
door. We followed him down the stairs and out into the street.
But he was too quick for us. He had a car waiting at the
corner, and he had jumped into it and driven off before we
could reach him.

“A pity,” said Poirot, as we turned back towards the Mansions.
“But it cannot be helped. Let us return and see what he was
after.”

We re-entered the flat and Poirot at once began a systematic
search of the rooms. He did not seem to find what he was
looking for, however.

“It is very strange,” he murmured. “He must have been looking
for the papers, and yet there is no sign of them here.”

Suddenly he paused in front of a small, inlaid cabinet in the
drawing-room.

“Wait a moment, Hastings. This is interesting.”

He was pointing to a small, secret drawer which he had just
discovered. It was empty.

“You see?” he said. “Someone has been here before us. The bird
has flown, and the nest is empty.”

“But who could it have been?” I asked. “Mrs. Robinson?”

“Or someone else,” said Poirot enigmatically. “Come, let us
return to our own flat. There is nothing more to be done here
to-night.”

Hours passed. I felt myself nodding, but Poirot sat as if carved
out of stone. Suddenly he touched my arm. A slight sound had come
from the direction of the front door. We both listened
breathlessly. The door was being opened with extreme caution.
Soft footsteps moved along the hall, and then stopped. A light
flickered for a moment and then went out. Silence followed. My
heart was beating with a series of heavy thuds against my ribs.
I felt Poirot’s hand on my arm once more. Slowly he led the way
out into the hall, then he suddenly switched on the light. I had
my revolver ready, but there was no need for it. A tall,
beautifully dressed woman stood in the doorway, staring at us in
utter amazement. It was not Mrs. Robinson, but the friend she had
mentioned—Elsie Ferguson!

“What are you doing here?” she demanded, recovering herself after
the first moment of surprise.

“I might ask you the same question, Madame,” Poirot replied
suavely. “And also why you are in possession of a latchkey to this
flat?”

“I have every right to be here,” she said haughtily. “I am a friend
of Mrs. Robinson’s and she asked me to come and fetch some papers
she had forgotten. But who are you, and what are you doing in her
flat at this time of night?”

“I am Hercule Poirot,” my friend announced with a bow. “And I am
here because I am interested in certain—naval plans—which I believe
are hidden in this flat.”

I saw the woman’s face change. For a moment she looked as if she
were going to faints, then she pulled herself together.

“I don’t know what you are talking about,” she said. “I must ask
you to leave at once.”

“On the contrary,” Poirot replied, “it is you who will have to
accompany us to the police station. I have already communicated
with Inspector Japp, and he is waiting for us outside.”

I did not follow his example. My heart was beating high with
excitement. Somewhere—close at hand, perhaps—lurked the notorious
international spy, Elsa Hardt!

The time passed slowly, and my thoughts went back to Mrs. Robinson.
What was her husband? An accomplice? A mere tool? Or did he know
nothing of his wife’s real character?

My reflections were interrupted by a low, soft sound from the
scullery. I saw Poirot’s eyes open. He was instantly alert. From
the scullery came the noise of some one climbing cautiously
through the door. A moment later, a dark figure passed across the
kitchen doorway. Poirot and I followed withcat-like steps.

The figure, which was that of a man, moved into the hall, then
stopped for a second. In another minute he was inside the drawing-room
and we were after him.

The man had a small electric torch in his hand which he was
flashing about the room. Suddenly he gave a low cry of satisfaction,
and stooped down to a small writing-table in the corner. As he
did so, I switched on the light and Poirot and I sprang upon him.
A short struggle ensued, but we were too much for him, and soon
we had him securely bound on the floor.

He was a swarthy, dark-haired man, and he glared at us with eyes
that were full of hate.

“The Japanese gentleman, I presume?” said Poirot politely. “And
this, if I am not mistaken, is what you were looking for?”

He held up a small, sealed packet which he had taken from the
man’s pocket.

“And now, Hastings, you may telephone to Scotland Yard and ask
for Inspector Japp.”

Hours passed. I had just reached that stage of drowsiness when
it seems almost impossible to keep one’s eyes open, and yet I knew
perfectly well that I was not asleep. A slight noise from the
direction of the scullery aroused me. Someone was moving there.
My hand stole towards my revolver, but Poirot’s fingers closed
over it, and he whispered in my ear:

“Not yet. Do not move.”

A moment later the door of the kitchen opened and someone entered.
By the light of a small electric torch I could see a man’s figure
moving towards the dresser. He seemed to be feeling about with
his hands. A drawer was pulled out, and then I heard a low whistle.
Suddenly, from the hall beyond, there came the sound of a key
turning in the lock. The man in the kitchen heard it also, and,
as he did so, he switched off his torch and crouched behind the
table.

“The Robinsons are early!” breathed Poirot into my ear.

The front door was opened and then closed again. Someone walked
along the hall and entered the room where we were. A light was
switched on.

The man by the table rose to his feet. He was a small, dark,
foreign-looking individual.

The woman who had just entered the room was Elsa Hardt!

There could be no mistaking that auburn hair and those blue eyes.
She was dressed in a dark coat and skirt, and she carried a small
black bag in her hand.

For a moment the two stood staring at one another. Then the woman
spoke:

“So you’ve got here first, have you? Where are the papers?”

“I haven’t got them,” replied the man. “I thought you had them.”

“Liar!” cried the woman. “You’ve found them and you’re going to
double-cross me. Give them up, I tell you!”

She took a step towards him, but the man laughed and pulled a
revolver from his pocket.

“Stay where you are, my girl. I’m not such a fool as all that. If
anyone’s double-crossing, it’s you. You’ve been here six months,
haven’t you? You and that husband of yours. You had plenty of
time to find them.”

“But we didn’t. We’ve searched every inch of the place. They’re
not here, I tell you.”

“You’re a liar! Valdarno told me he’d hidden them in the coal-lift.”

“Well, we’ve searched the lift, and they’re not there.”

“Then you’ve found them and moved them.”

“I haven’t, I tell you! I’ve been looking for them ever since I
came here.”

The man laughed again.

“Well, you won’t look much longer. I’m going to have those papers
if I have to kill you for them.”

He raised his revolver. At the same moment Poirot’s hand closed
over mine.

“Now!” he whispered.

I sprang forward, my revolver in my hand.

“Hands up!” I cried.

The man turned, and as he did so I fired. The bullet went wide,
but it served its purpose. The man dropped his revolver and fled
towards the kitchen door. I followed him, but he was too quick
for me. He dashed into the scullery and out through the coal-lift
door. By the time I reached it, he was already halfway down the
shaft.

I turned back to the kitchen. Poirot was standing there, a smile
on his face. The woman had disappeared.

“She’s gone!” I cried. “We must catch her!”

“Let her go, Hastings. We have what we want.”

He held out a small packet of papers.

“Where did you find them?” I gasped.

“In the place where Valdarno hid them. In the hollowed-out handle
of the coal-lift.”

“But how did you know?”

“It was simple, my friend. Valdarno was a clever man, but he was
also a simple one. He knew that the coal-lift was the one place
in the flat that was never thoroughly cleaned. And he was right.
For six months Elsa Hardt and her husband searched this flat, but
they never thought of looking in the one place where the papers
actually were.”

“But Mrs. Robinson? Who was she? And why did she tell us that
story about the flat?”

“Ah, that is where the cleverness of Elsa Hardt came in. She knew
that the American Secret Service were on her track, and she knew
also that they would be looking for a woman with auburn hair and
blue eyes. So what does she do? She finds a woman who resembles
her in every particular—even to the colour of her hair—and she
induces her to take the flat. Then she herself takes another flat
in the same building, and waits for her opportunity. She knew
that, sooner or later, the woman who resembled her would be
mistaken for her, and that the American Secret Service would be
led off on a false scent. And she was right. You yourself,
Hastings, were completely deceived.”

“But the story about the flat being cheap?”

“That was also part of the plan. It was necessary that the woman
should be induced to take the flat, and what better way than to
offer it to her at a ridiculously low rent? It was a clever
scheme, and it would have succeeded but for one thing.”

“And what was that?”

“The little grey cells of Hercule Poirot!”

The hours passed slowly. The flat was silent, but for the ticking
of a clock and an occasional rattle from the street below. I found
myself nodding several times, but always I recovered myself with
a jerk. Poirot, on the contrary, seemed to be sleeping peacefully,
his head on his chest, but I knew his ears were as alert as any
watchdog's. It must have been nearly four o'clock when a faint
scraping sound from the direction of the scullery brought me to
full attention. I felt a light touch on my arm; Poirot was awake
and signaling for silence. We waited, breathless, as the sound
repeated itself—the unmistakable noise of the coal-lift being
operated. A moment later, the door to the kitchen creaked, and a
dark, muffled figure stepped into the room, holding a shaded
electric torch.

To me, the waiting appeared endless. I was terrified of going to
sleep. Just when it seemed to me that I had been there about eight
hours—and had, as I found out afterwards, in reality been exactly
one hour and twenty minutes—a faint scratching sound came to my
ears. Poirot’s hand touched mine. I rose, and together we moved
carefully in the direction of the hall. The noise came from there.
Poirot placed his lips to my ear.

“Outside the front door. They are cutting out the lock. When I give
the word, not before, fall upon him from behind and hold him fast.
Be careful, he will have a knife.”

I nodded, my heart beating in a perfect fever of excitement. At
last, the lock began slowly to turn. A moment or two later, the
door was softly pushed open. A man stepped across the threshold,
followed by a woman. Poirot gave the word. I sprang upon the man,
who had no chance to resist, and as I did so, Poirot’s electric
torch flashed out. I saw a dark, swarthy-faced foreigner, and
beside him, a woman with a white face and a great mop of auburn
hair. I recognized her at once—Mrs. Robinson!

Slowly the door was pushed open and a man entered. For a minute
he stood quite still, then he began to move forward as if he knew
exactly where he was going. Poirot made a low signal, and I sprang
upon the intruder. I had him. He was a small man, but he fought
with the strength and agility of a wild-cat. He had a knife in his
hand, and I felt it rip my sleeve as I struggled with him.

“The lights, Poirot!” I shouted. “Turn on the lights!”

The room was flooded with light, and I saw that I was holding a
thin, dark-faced man, a Japanese from his appearance.

He had some papers in his hand, which he was trying to tear up,
and Poirot had him by the wrist.

“Not yet, my friend,” said Poirot quietly, as he took the papers
from the man’s hand. “They are too important.”

“Where did he get them from?” I asked, after we had made our
prisoner secure.

Poirot did not answer. He was busy searching the room. From the
back of a small bureau, he drew out a roll of papers.

“_Voilà!_” he said. “They were hidden in here.”

“But how did he know where they were?” I asked.

“The Japanese are very well served. No doubt Elsa Hardt has her
agents.”

“But Elsa Hardt—Mrs. Robinson, I mean—what has become of her?”

“She went out for her evening walk, and she has not returned,”
said Poirot. “But come, my friend, we must go and give this
gentleman in charge. I have a taxi waiting at the corner.”

The prisoner was duly handed over to the police, and then Poirot
turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of the case?”

“I think it’s a very remarkable one,” I said. “But I can’t quite
see why the Robinsons should have had the flat at such a cheap
rent. I mean, Elsa Hardt and her brother——”

Poirot laughed.

“Wait a minute, Hastings. There are several points to be cleared
up. For instance, who was the woman who told Mrs. Robinson that
the flat was let? Who was Elsa Hardt?”

“She was Mrs. Robinson, of course,” I said.

“Was she?” said Poirot. “I think we will go and see Mrs. Robinson.”

“But she has disappeared!”

“Has she? We shall see.”

The next morning, at Poirot’s request, I went to see Mrs. Robinson.
I found her in the flat, looking as charming as ever.

“Oh, Captain Hastings!” she cried. “I’m so glad to see you. Such
a dreadful thing has happened. The flat was broken into last night,
and someone tried to steal our furniture!”

“Your furniture?” I asked.

“Yes, the bureau in the dining-room. It’s been all broken to
pieces. It’s too bad!”

I tried to comfort her, and then Poirot appeared.

“Good morning, Madame,” he said. “I have some news for you. The
man who broke into your flat has been caught.”

“Oh, I’m so glad!” cried Mrs. Robinson. “Who was he?”

“He was a Japanese,” said Poirot. “And he was looking for some
papers that were hidden in your bureau.”

“Papers? What papers?”

“The Naval plans that were stolen from Washington six months ago,”
said Poirot.

Mrs. Robinson looked at him in amazement.

“Naval plans? But how did they get into our bureau?”

“They were hidden there by Elsa Hardt,” said Poirot.

“Elsa Hardt? Who is she?”

“She is a very clever international spy,” said Poirot. “And she
is also very like you, Madame. In fact, she is so like you that
she was able to pass herself off as you.”

“As me?”

“Yes. You see, Madame, the plans were hidden in that bureau, and
Elsa Hardt wanted to get them. But she knew that the flat was
being watched by the American Secret Service. So she hit upon a
very clever plan. She took the flat under your name, and then she
waited for an opportunity to get the plans. But she was afraid that
if she stayed there too long she would be caught. So she decided
to find someone who was very like her to take the flat off her
hands. And she found you.”

“But how did she find me?” asked Mrs. Robinson.

“Through the house agents,” said Poirot. “She went to them and
told them that she wanted to sublet her flat at a very low rent.
She knew that would attract a lot of people. And then she waited.
Every time someone came to see the flat, she looked at them. If
they were not like her, she told them that the flat was let. But
when you came, she saw that you were exactly what she wanted. So
she let you have the flat.”

“But what about the woman I met on the stairs?” asked Mrs. Robinson.

“That was Elsie Ferguson,” said Poirot. “She was Elsa Hardt’s
accomplice. She was there to make sure that no one else got the
flat before you did.”

“I see,” said Mrs. Robinson. “But what has become of Elsa Hardt?”

“She has disappeared,” said Poirot. “But I think we shall find
her.”

He turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of my little theory?”

“I think it’s wonderful!” I cried. “But how did you know that
Mrs. Robinson wasn’t Elsa Hardt?”

“Because, my friend, Elsa Hardt is a very clever woman. And a
clever woman would never have been so foolish as to tell you that
story about the flat. She would have known that it would arouse
your suspicions.”

I felt a little deflated, but I had to admit that Poirot was right.

“But there is one thing I don’t understand,” I said. “Who was the
man who was inquiring about the occupants of No. 4?”

“That,” said Poirot, “was the man who broke into the flat last
night. He was an agent of the Japanese Government. He had found
out where the plans were hidden, and he was determined to get them.”

“I see,” I said. “It’s all very clear now. But what about the
furniture? Why did Elsa Hardt sell it to Mrs. Robinson for fifty
pounds?”

“Because she wanted to make sure that Mrs. Robinson stayed in the
flat,” said Poirot. “If she had given it to her for nothing, Mrs.
Robinson might have been suspicious. But by selling it to her, she
made it seem like a genuine bargain.”

“I see,” I said. “Well, Poirot, you’ve done it again!”

“It was a very simple case, Hastings,” said Poirot. “But it had
its interesting points.”

He turned to Mrs. Robinson.

“And now, Madame, I think we must leave you. I have some business
to attend to.”

We left the flat and went back to our own.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we sat down. “That’s another case
finished. But there’s one thing that still puzzles me.”

“And what is that, Hastings?”

“Who is the real culprit? I mean, who was the person who actually
stole the plans?”

Poirot looked at me with a smile.

“That, my friend, is a very interesting question. And I think I
can answer it.”

“Who was it?” I asked.

“It was Elsa Hardt,” said Poirot. “But she did not work alone.”

“Who worked with her?”

“Her brother,” said Poirot. “Or rather, the man who passed as her
brother.”

“And who was he?”

“He was a man named Gerald Parker,” said Poirot.

“Gerald Parker!” I gasped. “But he’s a friend of mine!”

“I am sorry, Hastings,” said Poirot. “But it is true. Gerald
Parker was the man who planned the whole thing. He was the one
who stole the plans, and he was the one who used Elsa Hardt to
get them out of the country.”

“But why did he tell me that story about the flat?” I asked.

“Because he wanted to throw us off the scent,” said Poirot. “He
knew that if he told us a story that seemed a little bit suspicious,
we would be so busy investigating it that we wouldn't think of
suspecting him.”

“I see,” I said. “He was very clever.”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “But not quite clever enough for Hercule
Poirot!”

And with a little chuckle, he settled himself in his chair and
closed his eyes.

The lock had now been completely removed, and a man’s hand and
forearm came through the hole and turned the handle of the door.
The door opened and a man slipped into the hall. He was a small,
dark man, and he seemed to be breathing hard. Poirot nodded his
head, and I prepared to spring.

“No, wait!” hissed Poirot.

The man had moved along the hall and was standing outside the door
of the second bedroom. He seemed to be listening. Then he produced
a small electric torch and flashed it into the room. It was
evidently empty, for he passed on to the next.

Suddenly, a loud and terrible cry rang out through the flat, and
the next instant the intruder came rushing out with a yell of
terror. I sprang upon him, and together we fell on the floor. In
the struggle he was unable to use his knife, and I had him
overpowered and his hands tied behind his back before he could
well realise what had happened.

The man was almost dead with fright, and his face was of a sickly
yellow.

“What was that?” he gasped, shivering. “The ghost—the ghost!”

I looked up. In the doorway stood a tall and terrifying figure
robed in white. I felt a cold chill run down my spine, and for a
moment I was as much alarmed as our prisoner.

“It is only the maid, Hastings,” said Poirot’s voice, and I saw
that he was doubled up with laughter. “_Tiens_, what a superb
figure she makes! It is no wonder that the poor little man was
frightened out of his wits.”

The figure moved and resolved itself into a tall, raw-boned woman
clothed in a night-gown. She was certainly not a prepossessing
sight.

“What is it?” she asked. “What’s the matter? Who are you?”

“It is all right,” Poirot assured her. “We have just caught a
burglar. He was trying to get into the flat. If you will go and
call the porter, I will look after him till the police arrive.”

The woman looked at us suspiciously for a moment, and then went.

“And now,” said Poirot, turning to our prisoner, “perhaps you will
tell us who you are and what you were looking for?”

The man shook his head and remained silent.

“As you like,” said Poirot. “I will tell you, then. You were looking
for some papers—naval papers—stolen from Washington some months
ago. Is it not so?”

The man gave a start of surprise.

“You know, then?” he gasped.

“I know a good deal,” Poirot replied. “I know that Elsa Hardt is
in London, and that she is living in this flat. I also know that
you are not the only person who is looking for her.”

The man looked at him with a puzzled expression.

“Who are you?” he asked.

“My name is Hercule Poirot. And now, as the porter is arriving with
a policeman, I will hand you over to their care.”

I felt my blood tingled as we waited. The scratching ceased, and
I saw a small thin circle of light on the hall floor. The next
moment, the door was noiselessly pushed open, and a man entered
the hall. I felt Poirot’s signal, and I sprang upon him. I had him
fast, but not before he had managed to give a low, piercing whistle.
Before I could prevent him, Poirot had run to the door and, I saw
him seize someone who was apparently about to enter. With a gasp
of astonishment, I realized that it was a woman. Poirot held her
by her wrists.

“_C’est bien_!” he said with satisfaction. “I’ve got her too.
Light the gas, Hastings, will you? Now then, let’s see who our
uninvited guests are.”

The man was a dark-complexioned fellow, but as for the woman, her
identity was a complete surprise to me. It was Mrs. Robinson’s
friend—Elsie Ferguson!

“What does this mean?” she gasped. “Let me go! Who are you?”

“Hercule Poirot, at your service,” he said with a low bow. “And
this is my friend, Captain Hastings. I see that you have brought
the tools of your trade with you.”

He pointed to a small bag of burglar’s tools which lay on the
floor.

“I—I don’t know what you mean,” she stammered. “I—I came to see
Mrs. Robinson.”

“At one o’clock in the morning? And after having cut out the lock
of the door? Your friendship for the lady must be very great!”

She did not reply, and Poirot turned to me.

“Fetch the police, Hastings, will you? I think we can safely leave
the rest to them.”

In a short time, we had the satisfaction of seeing our two captives
safely in the hands of the law.

“But what does it all mean?” I asked when we were once more in our
own flat. “Was Elsie Ferguson Elsa Hardt?”

Poirot shook his head.

“No, no, Hastings. I will explain it all to you in the morning.”

We waited. A second later there was a click and the door opened.
A dark figure appeared in the doorway.

“_Maintenant_!” cried Poirot.

I sprang. My man was small and light, but he had the agility of
a cat. He was round and had his hands at my throat before I could
do anything. Then, as I felt myself going, he suddenly let go and
fell in a heap on the floor.

“_Bon_!” said Poirot, who was standing over him with his heavy
cane. “I think that will do for him. He is still unconscious. No,
it was not a knife after all, but a very nice little pistol. Now,
what can I do for you, Madame?”

For a woman was standing in the doorway, her face white and her
eyes staring at us with horror. It was the Mrs. Robinson of the
party at Gerald Parker’s.

“What—what is the meaning of this?” she gasped.

“That is what we were about to ask you,” replied Poirot politely.
“If you would be so good as to step inside——”

Mrs. Robinson obeyed. She was trembling from head to foot.

“My husband,” she whispered. “Where is my husband?”

“He is in the bedroom, is he not? We have not disturbed him.”

“In the bedroom? But—but he isn’t here! He went away this evening!”

“Indeed! Then I suppose he is at Gerald Parker’s?”

“How—how did you know?”

“Because he is Gerald Parker,” Poirot said with a smile.

“Gerald Parker!” I cried. “But I have known Parker for years!”

“Precisely, my friend. And it was his habit of constantly changing
his flat that first attracted my attention. He was the one who
found this flat, was he not? He was the one who told us the
remarkable story of its cheapness. And he was the one who, when
I made inquiries, I found had been living here for six months—under
the name of Robinson!”

“But why—why?” I asked.

“Wait. Madame will tell us, I think.”

But Mrs. Robinson only shook her head.

“I don’t know. I don’t know anything about it. Gerald—John—told
me we were to move here, and that I was to tell everyone we had
only just come. He said it was a joke. I didn’t understand, but
he told me I must do as he said.”

“A joke!” Poirot’s voice was hard. “I think not. A very grim joke
for some people. And now, Madame, if you will excuse us, I think
we will go and find your husband—or rather, Gerald Parker.”

He led the way out of the flat and up the stairs.

“What does it all mean, Poirot?” I asked, as we reached our own
flat.

“It means, my friend, that Gerald Parker is the person we are
looking for. He is the one who stole those Naval plans.”

“But—but the description! Elsa Hardt! The auburn hair and the blue
eyes!”

“Precisely. Elsa Hardt. Only you see, Hastings, Elsa Hardt is not
Mrs. Robinson. She is—someone else.”

“Then who is she?”

“She is the person who was coming to this flat to-night—the person
who was to meet the Japanese gentleman here. She is—Elsie
Ferguson!”

Presently there was a rending sound, and a little circle of light
appeared through the door. It was extinguished immediately and then
the door was slowly opened. Poirot and I flattened ourselves
against the wall. I heard a man’s breathing as he passed us. Then
he flashed on his torch, and as he did so, Poirot hissed in my ear:

“_Allez_.”

I sprang upon him and together we came to the ground. I have always
prided myself on my physical strength, but it was with no little
difficulty that I succeeded in pinioning him. Poirot assisted me,
holding his light whilst he kept a watchful eye for any other
would-be intruder. We had just succeeded in trussing him up
securely when we heard a faint sound from the flat above.

“Quick, Hastings,” Poirot whispered. “Up by the coal-lift—I will
remain here.”

He helped me into the lift and I began the ascent. I reached the
second floor in time to see someone come out of the flat and enter
the lift. I caught a glimpse of a woman’s face, and, to my horror,
it was that of Mrs. Robinson! I followed her in the other lift as
she descended. She got out at the ground floor and hurried through
the entrance hall. I followed her. A car was waiting at the
pavement and she entered it. I was just in time to see a man also
inside, and, as the car drove off, I caught a glimpse of his face.
It was Gerald Parker!

I was dumbfounded. Was it possible that Parker—the man who had
told me all about the Robinson’s flat—could be an accomplice? I
stood staring after the car, my head in a whirl.

“_Eh bien_, Hastings? Have you caught the lady?”

It was Poirot’s voice, and I turned to find him at my elbow.

“No—she got away in a car,” I replied. “And Poirot—it was Gerald
Parker who was with her!”

Poirot nodded.

“I thought as much,” he said. “Come, we must return to the flat.”

“But the man we have tied up?”

“He is still there—and Inspector Japp is with him. I took the
precaution of telephoning to him before we left.”

We re-entered the flat to find Japp and two of his men in charge
of our prisoner. The man was a dark, sinister-looking individual
who scowled at us with impotent rage.

“Who is he?” I asked.

“One of the gang,” replied Japp. “But where are the others?”

“The others have escaped,” said Poirot. “But I think we shall find
them before long. Come, Hastings.”

He led the way out into the street. I was still in a state of
bewilderment.

“But what does it all mean, Poirot?” I asked. “What was Gerald
Parker doing with Mrs. Robinson?”

“All in good time, Hastings. All in good time. First we must find
where they have gone.”

He called a taxi and we were soon driving towards the West End.
Poirot appeared to be deep in thought.

“It is a curious case, Hastings,” he said at length. “A very
curious case. But I think I begin to see the light.”

“I wish I did,” I remarked.

“Wait, my friend, wait. You will see everything clearly soon.”

We stopped at a small hotel in a quiet street off Piccadilly.
Poirot dismissed the taxi and we entered the building.

“Is Mrs. Robinson here?” Poirot inquired of the clerk.

“Yes, sir. No. 10 on the first floor.”

We went upstairs and Poirot knocked at the door. It was opened by
Mrs. Robinson. She looked surprised and a little alarmed when she
saw us.

“Why, Captain Hastings! And Monsieur Poirot! What brings you here?”

“We have come to see you, Madame,” said Poirot, entering the room.
“And also Mr. Parker.”

Gerald Parker was sitting in an armchair by the fire. He rose as
we entered.

“Hullo, Hastings! What’s the meaning of this?”

“The meaning is very simple,” said Poirot. “I have come for the
Naval plans which were stolen from Washington six months ago.”

Mrs. Robinson turned pale.

“I—I don’t know what you mean,” she stammered.

“Oh, yes, you do,” said Poirot. “You are Elsa Hardt, are you not?”

The woman burst into tears.

“It’s no use, Elsa,” said Parker. “He knows everything.”

He turned to Poirot.

“You’re a clever man, Monsieur Poirot. How did you find out?”

“It was the flat that first attracted my attention,” said Poirot.
“The fact that it was being sublet at such a low rent suggested
that there was something wrong. And when I heard that Mrs. Robinson
had been told it was let when it wasn’t, I began to suspect that
someone was anxious to keep people away from it. Then there was
the description of Elsa Hardt—tall, fair, auburn hair—which tallied
exactly with that of Mrs. Robinson. It was clear that she was
using the flat as a hiding-place for the stolen plans.”

“But what about Gerald Parker?” I asked. “How does he come into
it?”

“Mr. Parker is also a member of the gang,” said Poirot. “It was
he who told you about the flat, Hastings, in the hope that you
would mention it to someone who might be interested. He wanted to
get rid of the plans and he thought that by letting the flat to
someone who was above suspicion, he could do so without being
suspected himself.”

“But why did he tell me?” I asked.

“Because he knew that you would be sure to tell me, Hastings! He
wanted to use me as a sort of guarantee of the respectability of
the tenants.”

“I see,” I said. “And what about the man we caught in the flat?”

“He was another member of the gang who had been sent to fetch the
plans. He didn’t know that Elsa Hardt had already taken them.”

“Well, you’ve beaten us, Monsieur Poirot,” said Parker. “Here are
the plans.”

He handed a packet of papers to Poirot.

“I think Inspector Japp will be interested in these,” said Poirot.
“And now, Hastings, I think we may go home. It has been a long
night.”

As we walked back to our flat, I couldn’t help feeling a little
mortified. Once again Poirot had been right and I had been wrong.

“But how did you know that Elsa Hardt was Mrs. Robinson?” I asked.

“It was the name, Hastings! The name Stella—which means a star.
And Elsa Hardt—Hardt is the German for heart. A star and a heart—it
is a well-known symbol in certain circles. I knew then that I was
on the right track.”

I sighed. Poirot’s logic was always so simple—when he explained it
to you.

“But what about Elsie Ferguson?” I asked. “Where does she come in?”

“She was merely a friend of Mrs. Robinson’s,” said Poirot. “She
had no idea what was going on.”

“I see,” I said. “Well, it’s been a most interesting case, Poirot.”

“Yes, Hastings. A most interesting case. And now, let us go to
bed. I am tired.”

And so ended the mystery of the cheap flat.

The End.

I leaped upon the man from behind and bore him to the floor. For
a moment he was taken by surprise, but then he began to struggle
with the most incredible ferocity. I felt a stinging pain in my
arm as his knife found its way through my coat-sleeve, and I
realized that I was in for a tough struggle. But the man was small
and thin, and I was just beginning to think that I should get the
best of him when Poirot’s voice sounded behind me:

“Keep him so for a minute, Hastings. I’ve got him now.”

I saw Poirot’s hand holding a small bottle. He was unscrewing the
top, and I realized what it was.

“Don’t!” I cried, but even as I spoke, the man uttered a stifled
shriek.

I saw Poirot’s hand with the small bottle in it, and I was about
to protest when I saw that he was merely using some kind of
disinfectant on my arm.

“_Mon Dieu_, what a man you are!” laughed Poirot. “You should have
seen your face when you thought I was going to use vitriol!”

I was too surprised to speak. Poirot had the intruder’s hands
firmly in his, and he was already slipping the handcuffs on.

The man turned his head towards me. He had a dark, thin,
un-English-looking face, and his eyes were gleaming with hatred.

“I’ll pay you out for this!” he said, and his voice had a curious
foreign accent. “I’ll get my revenge!”

“_Tais-toi_, my friend,” said Poirot calmly. “You’ve done enough
harm for one night. Now, Hastings, let us see what our friend was
looking for.”

He went into the drawing-room and switched on the light. The room
was in a state of the most incredible confusion. The chairs and
sofas had been ripped open, and the floor was strewn with horsehair
and stuffing. The intruder had evidently been looking for something
hidden in the furniture.

“_Tiens_,” said Poirot, “he seems to have been in a hurry. But I
think we shall find what we want in the dining-room.”

He led the way into the dining-room, where the same scene of
destruction met our eyes. But Poirot did not seem to be interested
in the furniture. He went straight to the sideboard and began to
examine the various articles upon it.

“Ah,” he said at last, “I think this is it.”

He held up a small, silver-mounted biscuit-box. It was a very
ordinary-looking object, but Poirot seemed to be immensely
pleased with it. He unscrewed the top and began to feel about
inside.

“_Voilà!_” he cried, and he drew out a small, folded packet.

He opened it and disclosed a number of thin, blue papers.

“The Naval plans!” I cried.

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “And now, Hastings, we will take our
friend to the nearest police station.”

“But what about the Robinsons?” I asked.

“Oh, the Robinsons! We shall find them at the police station, too,
I expect. Or at any rate, I can tell you where they are.”

“But they were in the flat this afternoon!”

“My dear Hastings, I think you will find that the people you saw
this afternoon were not the Robinsons at all. They were—shall we
say—substitutes?”

“But I saw them myself!”

“You saw a tall, fair woman with auburn hair, and a man who was—what
was it you said—‘betwixt and between.’ Exactly. And you jumped to
the conclusion that they were the Robinsons. But they were not. They
were Elsa Hardt and her brother.”

“But what about the real Robinsons?”

“The real Robinsons? Oh, they were—well, they were just ordinary
people who were looking for a flat. And they found one—at eighty
pounds a year. A very cheap flat, Hastings! Too cheap, in fact.”

“I don’t understand.”

“It’s quite simple, really. Elsa Hardt and her brother had the
Naval plans, and they wanted a safe place to hide them until they
could dispose of them. They chose this flat, which they took in the
name of Robinson. But then they found that the American Secret
Service was on their track, and they had to leave in a hurry. They
couldn’t take the plans with them, so they hid them in the
furniture. But they knew that they would have to come back for them
sooner or later. So they hit on the ingenious idea of subletting the
flat at a ridiculously low rent. They knew that there would be
plenty of applicants, and they could choose the ones that suited
them best. They wanted someone who was—well, shall we say—easily
deceived? Someone like our friend Mrs. Robinson. They knew that if
they let the flat to her, they could come back whenever they liked
and—well, do what they have done to-night.”

“But how did they know that she would be out to-night?”

“They didn’t. But they knew that she would be out sometime. And
they were watching the flat. When they saw her go out this
afternoon, they knew that their chance had come. They probably had
a key to the flat, or they may have used the coal-lift, as we did.”

“But what about the man I caught? Who was he?”

“He was a Japanese agent, I imagine. He had probably been watching
the flat, too, and he saw his chance when the others went out. He
didn’t know where the plans were hidden, so he had to search the
whole place.”

“But how did you know all this, Poirot?”

“My dear Hastings, it was the rent! Eighty pounds a year for a flat
in Montagu Mansions! It was impossible! And then there was the
furniture—fifty pounds for beautifully furnished rooms! It was
too much! Or rather, it was too little! And then there was the
story of the friend who said the flat was let when it wasn’t. It
was all very suspicious. So I made a few inquiries, and I found
that the flat had been taken six months ago by a Mr. and Mrs.
Robinson. And that was just the time that Elsa Hardt disappeared
from Washington. It was all very simple, really.”

“You are wonderful, Poirot!” I cried.

“_Mais oui_,” said Poirot complacently. “I have my little methods.
But come, Hastings, let us go to the police station. I have a great
desire to see Elsa Hardt again. She is a very clever woman, and I
admire her—in a way.”

We took our prisoner to the police station, where we found Inspector
Japp waiting for us. He was immensely pleased with our success, and
he congratulated Poirot warmly.

“You’ve done it again, M. Poirot!” he cried. “I don’t know how you
do it, I’m sure.”

“It is very simple, my friend,” said Poirot. “You have only to use
the little grey cells.”

“And what about Elsa Hardt?” I asked.

“We’ve got her,” said Japp. “She and her brother were caught trying
to leave the country this evening. They’re in the cells now.”

“Can I see her?” I asked.

“Certainly, if you like,” said Japp.

He led the way to the cells, and I saw a tall, fair woman with
auburn hair sitting on a bench. She looked up as we entered, and
her eyes met mine.

“So,” she said, and her voice was cold and hard. “You have caught
me at last.”

“Yes, Elsa,” said Poirot. “The game is up.”

“I suppose so,” she said. “But I shall get my revenge, M. Poirot.
You may be sure of that.”

“I have no doubt of it,” said Poirot. “But in the meantime, I think
you will find that the English prisons are very comfortable.”

We left the police station and walked back to our flat. It was a
beautiful night, and the stars were shining brightly.

“A wonderful night, Hastings,” said Poirot. “And a very successful
investigation.”

“Yes,” I agreed. “But I still don’t understand one thing.”

“And what is that, my friend?”

“How did you know that the plans were in the biscuit-box?”

“I didn’t,” said Poirot. “But it was the only thing in the room
that hadn’t been smashed to pieces. So I thought it was worth a
look.”

I laughed.

“You are wonderful, Poirot!” I said again.

“_Mais oui_,” said Poirot. “I am Hercule Poirot. And now, my
friend, let us go to bed. I am very tired.”

And so ended the mystery of the cheap flat. It was one of the most
curious cases that Poirot ever investigated, and it showed once
again the amazing power of his little grey cells.

I sprang forward and caught the man by the throat. I am no novice
in the art of wrestling, and my grip was a good one. He struggled
violently, and I saw the gleam of a knife in his hand. I caught
him by the wrist and wrenched it from him. He gave a sharp cry,
and then subsided. Poirot turned on the lights.

“Good work, Hastings. Now let us see our captive.”

He was a dark, foreign-looking man, and his face was distorted
with rage.

“_Eh bien_,” said Poirot politely. “Your little plan has not
exactly succeeded, has it? Perhaps you would like to tell us what
it is? Or perhaps you would like to see the police? They are only
around the corner, you know.”

The man glared at us, but made no reply.

Poirot chuckled.

“I think I can tell you,” he said. “You are a friend of the
gentleman who died in Washington—Luigi Valdarno, is he not? No
doubt you were together in the little robbery which he took it
upon himself to commit. And you thought that if you came to London
you might find the lady who has the papers. You have tracked her
down to this flat, and you thought that while she was out you
could search for them at your leisure. Is that it?”

The man’s eyes were narrow and his lips were drawn back in a sneer.

“_C’est ça_,” said Poirot, with a nod of satisfaction. “I think
we may leave our friend to the police. If you would kindly ring
up the station, Hastings?”

“Wait,” I cried, as a sudden thought struck me. “The lady who has
the papers—Mrs. Robinson—she isn’t in the flat, is she?”

“No,” said Poirot, “she is not. I saw to that.”

“But then—who is in the flat?”

“No one,” replied Poirot. “I saw them all go out this evening. And
I have a key of my own, you see.”

“Then—who was the woman I saw this afternoon?”

“That was Elsa Hardt,” said Poirot. “She had come to see the flat,
no doubt. And she was dressed in a way that would attract attention.
She wanted to be seen. You see, Hastings, the whole thing was a
trap. The flat was taken in the name of Robinson—a very common
name—and it was let at a ridiculously low rent to attract the
right kind of tenant. The idea was to find someone who resembled
Elsa Hardt—someone with auburn hair and blue eyes. And then, you
see, when the Japanese gentleman—or whoever it was—came to London,
he would find Elsa Hardt living in the flat. Only it wouldn’t be
Elsa Hardt at all. It would be Mrs. Robinson. And Mrs. Robinson
would have the papers.”

“But—I don’t understand,” I said. “Why should they want Mrs.
Robinson to have the papers?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “the real Elsa Hardt wanted to get rid of
them. She knew she was being watched, and she wanted to find
someone who would take the papers off her hands—someone who would
be suspected instead of herself. And what better way than to find
someone who resembled her and who was living in the very flat she
had occupied?”

“But—how did she know about Mrs. Robinson?”

“She didn’t,” said Poirot. “She just waited for the right person
to come along. And Mrs. Robinson was the lucky one. She has the
auburn hair and the blue eyes, and she was looking for a flat.
It was all very simple.”

“But the papers,” I persisted. “Where are they?”

“Ah,” said Poirot, “that is the question. We must find them before
Elsa Hardt does.”

He began to search the room, but it was not until he had moved
a heavy oak chest that he found what he was looking for. A small
packet was taped to the underside of the chest. Poirot tore it
off and opened it. Inside were several sheets of paper covered
with technical drawings and figures.

“The Naval plans!” he cried. “Success, Hastings! Success!”

“But what about Elsa Hardt?” I asked. “She’s still at large.”

“Not for long,” said Poirot. “I have already communicated with
Japp, and he is even now on her trail. Come, let us go and find
him.”

We left the flat and made our way to the police station. Japp was
waiting for us, and he was in a state of great excitement.

“We’ve got her!” he cried. “She was trying to leave the country on
the midnight boat-train from Victoria. We caught her just as she
was stepping onto the train.”

“And the brother?” asked Poirot.

“We’ve got him too,” said Japp. “He was with her.”

“Good work,” said Poirot. “And now, Japp, I think we have earned
our sleep.”

But as we walked back to our flat, I couldn’t help feeling a little
disappointed.

“So it was Elsa Hardt after all,” I said. “I was hoping for
something a bit more—well, more interesting.”

Poirot smiled.

“My dear Hastings,” he said, “truth is often less interesting than
fiction. But it is truth none the less. And in this case, the truth
was that Elsa Hardt was a very clever and very dangerous woman.
She almost succeeded in her plan, but she forgot one thing.”

“What was that?” I asked.

“She forgot,” said Poirot, “that Hercule Poirot was in London.”

And with that, he turned into the entrance of Montagu Mansions and
began to mount the stairs.

I sprang forward and, as I did so, the man gave a cry and turned
upon me with a knife in his hand. But Poirot had already caught
him from behind, and in a few moments we had him down. He was a
small, dark, wiry man, with a very determined face. Poirot took
from his pocket a pair of handcuffs, and he snapped them on the
prisoner’s wrists before the fellow could recover from his
surprise.

“Well done, my friend,” said Poirot, wiping his brow. “Now let us
examine him.”

He turned on his own torch and we saw that the prisoner was indeed
a foreigner. He was dressed in a dark suit, and had a soft felt hat.
Around his waist he wore a leather belt, in which were a number of
small pockets. Poirot went to work at once, and his eyes fairly
sparkled as he drew out several small packets from the belt. He
opened them and then looked up at me with a triumphant smile.

“_Voilà_, Hastings! The missing Naval plans!”

“The Naval plans!” I cried. “Then—then, Mrs. Robinson was Elsa
Hardt after all!”

“Not so fast, my friend,” said Poirot, shaking his head. “Wait
until we have had a little talk with this gentleman.”

He turned to the prisoner and said in a very quiet voice:

“Now, my friend, what have you to say for yourself? Who sent you
here to-night?”

The man looked at him with a sullen expression and did not answer.

“It is as I thought,” said Poirot. “He will not speak. But it does
not matter. I think I know who sent him.”

He rose to his feet and beckoned to me.

“Come, Hastings, we must leave him here for a few minutes while we
go and talk to the Robinsons.”

“The Robinsons!” I cried. “But—but they are in bed!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And they will be very surprised to see
us, I think.”

We went into the bedroom where we found Mr. and Mrs. Robinson
fast asleep. Poirot woke them up and, when they saw us, they were
indeed very surprised.

“What is the meaning of this?” cried Mr. Robinson, starting up in
bed. “Who are you, and what are you doing here?”

“I am Hercule Poirot,” said my friend, bowing politely. “And this
is my friend, Captain Hastings. We have just caught a man who was
trying to rob your flat.”

“To rob our flat!” cried Mrs. Robinson, her eyes wide with terror.
“Oh, John, I told you there was something queer about this place!”

“Wait a moment, my dear,” said her husband. “Let us hear what M.
Poirot has to say.”

Poirot told them what had happened, and then he said:

“And now, Mr. Robinson, I have a few questions to ask you. First of
all, how did you come to hear of this flat?”

“We heard of it from a friend of ours,” said Mr. Robinson. “A Miss
Elsie Ferguson.”

“Elsie Ferguson!” I cried. “But she was the one who told you it was
already let!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And that is very interesting, is it not?
Now, Mr. Robinson, did you ever meet a Miss Elsa Hardt?”

Mr. Robinson shook his head.

“No, I don’t think so. Why do you ask?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “I have reason to believe that Miss Elsa
Hardt is the person who is really responsible for all this.”

He turned to Mrs. Robinson and said:

“And now, Madame, I have a question to ask you. Do you happen to
have any auburn-haired friends?”

Mrs. Robinson looked at him in surprise.

“Why, yes,” she said. “Elsie Ferguson has auburn hair. But what has
that to do with it?”

“A great deal, I think,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will excuse
us, we must go and look for Miss Ferguson.”

We left the Robinsons and went back to the hall where we had left
the prisoner. But to our surprise, he was gone!

“Gone!” I cried. “But how? He was handcuffed!”

“He must have had a key,” said Poirot, looking very annoyed. “I
ought to have thought of that. But it does not matter. We shall find
him again, I think.”

He went to the window and looked out.

“Ah!” he said. “There is a car waiting outside. I think we had
better go and see who is in it.”

We ran down the stairs and out into the street. There was a car
there, and as we approached it, a woman’s face appeared at the
window. It was Elsie Ferguson!

“Stop!” cried Poirot. “I want to talk to you, Miss Ferguson.”

But the car started off with a jerk and disappeared round the
corner.

“Quick, Hastings!” cried Poirot. “We must follow them!”

We jumped into our own car, which was waiting nearby, and set off
in pursuit. The chase lasted for several miles, but at last we saw
the other car stop outside a small house in a quiet street.

“This must be it,” said Poirot. “Stay here, Hastings, while I go
and see what is happening.”

He got out of the car and walked up to the house. I watched him
as he disappeared inside. A few minutes later, he came out again,
accompanied by a woman. It was Elsie Ferguson!

“I have found her, Hastings!” he cried. “And she has something to
tell us.”

We all went back to the flat, where Poirot made Elsie Ferguson
sit down and tell us her story.

“I didn’t want to do it,” she said, sobbing. “But she made me. She
threatened to kill me if I didn’t.”

“Who made you?” asked Poirot.

“Elsa Hardt,” said Elsie Ferguson. “She’s my sister. She’s the one
who stole the Naval plans. And she’s been using me to help her.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And why did she want the Robinsons to have
the flat?”

“Because she wanted to use it as a hiding-place for the plans,”
said Elsie Ferguson. “She knew that no one would suspect the
Robinsons, because they were so respectable.”

“And what about the man we caught to-night?” asked Poirot.

“That was Gerald Parker,” said Elsie Ferguson. “He’s one of Elsa’s
accomplices. He was the one who told the Robinsons about the flat.”

“Gerald Parker!” I cried. “But he’s a friend of mine!”

“I’m afraid he’s not a very good friend, Hastings,” said Poirot.
“He’s been working with Elsa Hardt all along.”

“And where is Elsa Hardt now?” asked Poirot.

“She’s at her flat in Mayfair,” said Elsie Ferguson. “She’s
waiting for Gerald to bring her the plans.”

“Then we must go and see her at once,” said Poirot.

We drove to Mayfair and found Elsa Hardt’s flat. Poirot knocked on
the door and it was opened by a tall, beautiful woman with auburn
hair.

“Miss Elsa Hardt, I presume?” said Poirot.

The woman looked at him with a cold expression.

“Who are you?” she asked.

“I am Hercule Poirot,” said my friend. “And I have come to arrest
you for the theft of the Naval plans.”

The woman’s face turned pale.

“I don’t know what you’re talking about,” she said.

“Oh, I think you do,” said Poirot. “And I have your sister, Elsie
Ferguson, here to prove it.”

Elsie Ferguson stepped forward and the woman’s face filled with
rage.

“You traitor!” she cried, lunging at her sister.

But Poirot was too quick for her. He caught her by the wrists and
held her fast.

“It’s no use, Miss Hardt,” he said. “The game is up.”

He turned to me and said:

“Well, Hastings, I think we have solved the mystery of the cheap
flat. And we have also caught a very dangerous criminal.”

“But what about Gerald Parker?” I asked.

“Oh, we shall find him, too,” said Poirot. “I have already
telephoned Inspector Japp, and he is on his way here now.”

And so the mystery was solved. Elsa Hardt and Gerald Parker were
both arrested and sent to prison, and the Naval plans were
returned to the American Government. As for the Robinsons, they
decided to move out of the flat and find somewhere else to live.

“I’m glad we’re leaving,” said Mrs. Robinson. “I never did like
that place anyway.”

“And I’m glad we’re leaving, too,” said Poirot. “I don’t think I
could have stood another night in that coal-lift!”

I sprang forward with a suddenness that would have done credit to
a tiger, and my arms were round the man’s neck. He struggled
violently, and I saw the flash of his knife as he tried to use it
upon me. But I had my grip on his throat, and in a few moments I
was holding him by the collar, whilst Poirot sat calmly upon his
legs. Then I gave a cry of surprise.

“The porter from downstairs!” I ejaculated.

“Precisely,” returned Poirot. “I told you he was a man of few words,
and I find that his disposition is even more suspicious than I
imagined.”

The man gave a snarl of fury. He was indeed a most unpleasant
looking individual.

“I’ll have the law on you for this,” he muttered. “What’s the
meaning of it?”

“The meaning is,” said Poirot calmly, “that you were about to
commit a burglary. And I also imagine that you will find yourself
somewhat closely questioned about certain Naval plans when we
hand you over to the police.”

The man gave a start of terror.

“It’s a lie,” he cried. “I don’t know nothing of no Naval plans.
And I weren’t going to commit no burglary. I just thought that
this flat was being used for a purpose it shouldn’t be, and I came
up to investigate. That’s all.”

“Well, you’ll have plenty of time for investigation where you’re
going,” said Poirot with a chuckle. “Now, Hastings, just run out
and fetch the police.”

While we were waiting for their arrival, Poirot explained his
deductions.

“It was perfectly simple,” he said. “I was convinced from the first
that there was something wrong with that flat. The rent was too
cheap, and the story of the lady who said it was let when it wasn’t
was very suspicious. Then there was the description of Elsa Hardt,
which tallies exactly with that of Mrs. Robinson. It seemed more
than probable that she and her husband were in some way connected
with the theft of the Naval plans. I suspected that they were
using the flat as a hiding-place, and that they had chosen it
because it was cheap and because it was in a large building where
they would be less likely to be noticed. But then there was the
porter. He was always hanging about the entrance, and he was
evidently a very suspicious character. I began to think that he
might be in league with the Robinsons. But when I found him
trying to break into the flat to-night, I saw that I was wrong.
He was evidently after the plans himself.”

“But how did he know where they were?” I asked.

“Ah, that I cannot tell you. But no doubt he had his own methods
of finding out.”

When the police arrived, they took the porter into custody, and
Poirot and I returned to our own flat.

“Well,” I said, as we sat over our late supper, “it’s been a most
exciting night. But I’m still a bit puzzled about Mrs. Robinson.
Do you really think she’s Elsa Hardt?”

“I think it’s more than likely,” said Poirot. “But we shall know
for certain when we’ve had a talk with her to-morrow.”

We sprang together, Poirot with a quick movement enveloped the
intruder’s head with a light woollen scarf whilst I pinioned his
arms. The whole affair was quick and noiseless. I twisted a dagger
from his hand, and as Poirot brought down the scarf from his eyes,
whilst keeping it wound tightly round his mouth, I jerked up my
revolver where he could see it and understand that resistance was
useless. As he ceased to struggle Poirot put his mouth close to
his ear and began to whisper rapidly. After a minute the man
nodded. Then enjoining silence with a movement of the hand, Poirot
led the way out of the flat and down the stairs. Our captive
followed, and I brought up the rear with the revolver. When we were
out in the street, Poirot turned to me.

“There is a taxi waiting just round the corner. Give me the
revolver. We shall not need it now.”

“But if this fellow tries to escape?”

Poirot smiled.

“He will not.”

I returned in a minute with the waiting taxi. The scarf had been
unwound from the stranger’s face, and I gave a start of surprise.

“He’s not a Jap,” I ejaculated in a whisper to Poirot.

“Observation was always your strong point, Hastings! Nothing
escapes you. No, the man is not a Jap. He is an Italian.”

The Italian, who Poirot revealed to be the brother of the murdered Luigi Valdarno, sat in dejected silence as we drove toward the station. Poirot turned to me, his eyes shining in the dim light of the taxi. "You see, Hastings, the 'Mrs. Robinson' you met was playing a most ingenious part. She knew the stolen plans were concealed in No. 4—hidden there by Luigi before his death—but the flat was already occupied by a real Mrs. Robinson who had been there for six months. To gain access, our 'charming bride' and her accomplice used the name Robinson to avoid suspicion, posing as new tenants to their friends while they used the coal-lift—the very one we used—to enter the flat when the real occupants were out. She is the one the American Secret Service seeks; she is Elsa Hardt."

Poirot gave an address in a quiet street in Bayswater. As the taxi rattled through the night, he turned to me, his eyes gleaming with a sudden green light. “The mystery of the cheap flat, Hastings, was a most ingenious ‘blind.’ The real Elsa Hardt needed a place to receive her Japanese visitors, but she also knew she was being hunted by the American Secret Service and the vengeful kin of Luigi Valdarno. Her masterstroke was to find a pair of innocents who bore a striking resemblance to herself and her accomplice, and install them in the very flat that was marked. While the pursuers focused their attention on the blameless Robinsons, the real spy was free to operate from a distance. However, there was one person who knew the Robinsons’ movements perfectly—the woman who had first suggested the agency to them, and who later tried to frighten them away when she realized the Italian was already closing in on the building.”

The taxi sped through the darkness. Poirot leaned back, his eyes gleaming with a peculiar satisfaction. “You see, Hastings, the affair was always one of identity. The woman you met at Gerald Parker’s, the so-called Mrs. Robinson, played her part with consummate skill. She knew that the friends of the murdered Valdarno were seeking her, and she needed to establish herself in a way that seemed entirely transparent. What better way than to involve a friend of the police—yourself—in the ‘mystery’ of her new home? She calculated that if I investigated the ‘cheap flat,’ I would find only a young couple and a curious rental agreement, thereby giving her a clean bill of health. But she was too clever; she forgot that Hercule Poirot looks beyond the obvious.”

The taxi came to a halt outside a small, discreet house in a
quiet street. Poirot led the way inside, and we were immediately
met by Inspector Japp of Scotland Yard. Our captive was handed
over to a couple of plain-clothes men, and Poirot beckoned us
into a small sitting-room. “This gentleman,” he explained,
indicating our late prisoner, “is the brother of the murdered
Luigi Valdarno. He came to England with one object—to find the
woman who had lured his brother to his death and stolen the
precious Naval plans. That woman is Elsa Hardt. He had traced
her to Montagu Mansions, and was convinced that she was living
in No. 4 under the name of Mrs. Robinson.”

“We drove in silence for some time, the Italian sitting between us, his eyes gleaming with a mixture of fear and rage. At last Poirot spoke. ‘You see, Hastings, the mystery of the cheap flat is solved. It was a bait—a bait to attract a couple who should exactly resemble the original occupants. The real Elsa Hardt and her brother wished to find doubles who would occupy the flat and receive the “attentions” of those who were searching for them. What could be simpler? An advertisement, a ridiculously low rent, and the thing is done. The Mrs. Robinson you met—the innocent bride—was merely a tool, a double. The woman who had lived in No. 4 for the past six months, she was the true Elsa Hardt.’”

We got into the taxi, and Poirot gave the driver an address in St.
John’s Wood. I was by now completely fogged. I did not like to ask
Poirot where we were going in front of our captive, and strove in
vain to obtain some light upon the proceedings.

The taxi stopped at a large house standing in its own grounds.
Poirot led the way up the path and rang the bell. A man-servant
opened the door.

“I wish to see Mrs. Robinson. She is here, I think.”

“The lady has only just come, sir.”

“I know. Tell her that I have brought her a message from No. 4
Montagu Mansions.”

The man-servant showed us into a small sitting-room and left us.
A few minutes later a woman entered the room. She was tall and
slight, with a mass of auburn hair.

“You have a message for me?” she asked.

Poirot bowed.

“I have, madame. From your friend, the Italian.”

The woman started and her face grew deathly pale.

“I do not understand,” she began.

“_Oh, si, madame_,” Poirot said. “You understand very well. He has
confessed.”

“The coward!” she hissed.

Poirot turned to me.

“Hastings, would you be so good as to step into the hall and ask
the man-servant if he would mind fetching a taxi for this lady.
She is going with us to Scotland Yard.”

The woman’s hand went to her bosom, but Poirot was too quick for
her. He caught her wrist.

“No, Elsa Hardt! No!” he said sternly. “The game is up. We have
the papers.”

The taxi stopped before a small detached house standing in its own
garden. We got out, and Poirot paid the man. Then, with a gesture
to our prisoner to follow, he walked up the gravel path to the
front door and rang. I followed him and waited for what should
happen. The door was opened by a trim maid, and as she saw Poirot
she stepped back with a little cry of recognition.

“Is Miss Hardt at home?”

“She is in the drawing-room, sir.”

Poirot walked straight in, and we followed him. A girl was sitting
at the piano, her fingers idly straying over the keys. She turned
round as we entered, and I saw at once that she was the image of
Mrs. Robinson, only that her hair was a darker shade of auburn.
Beside her stood a man, and as he saw our prisoner, he uttered a
quick exclamation of surprise.

“Elsa Hardt,” said Poirot, “I think you know this gentleman. He
is the brother of Luigi Valdarno.”

The girl turned white to the lips.

“What do you want?” she gasped.

“The papers,” replied Poirot. “The papers that were stolen from
Washington six months ago.”

“I have not got them,” she cried. “I do not know what you mean.”

“It is useless,” said Poirot. “Valdarno here has told us
everything. He came to England to find you and to avenge his
brother’s death. He found you to-night.”

“He would have killed me!” she cried.

“Undoubtedly,” agreed Poirot. “But I saved you. In return, I
demand the papers.”

The girl looked at the man by her side. He nodded. With a sigh of
relief, she crossed the room, and, after a moment’s hesitation,
handed Poirot a small packet.

“They are all here,” she said.

“I will see to that,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will excuse
me, we will leave you. I have no doubt that you will find much to
say to each other. Come, Hastings.”

He led the way out, and I followed him, still in a state of
bewilderment. When we were once more in the street, I turned to
him.

“But Poirot, I don’t understand. Who is Mrs. Robinson? And what
about the flat in Montagu Mansions?”

Poirot laughed.

“_Mon cher Hastings_, it is very simple. The Robinsons are a
perfectly innocent couple who were used as a screen by Elsa Hardt.
She and her accomplice, the man we saw with her just now, had
taken the flat at Montagu Mansions under the name of Robinson.
They were using it as a safe place to hide the papers. But when
the American Secret Service began to get on their track, they
realised that they must move. They could not take the papers with
them, so they hit upon the ingenious plan of subletting the flat
at a ridiculously low rent to another couple of the same name.
Any inquiries for ‘the Robinsons’ would thus be met by the presence
of the real Robinsons, while Elsa Hardt and her friend were living
comfortably in St. John’s Wood.”

“But the furniture?” I asked.

“Ah, that was the cleverest part of the whole thing! The papers
were hidden in one of the pieces of furniture—probably the
wardrobe. By selling the furniture to the new tenants for a nominal
sum, they ensured that it would remain in the flat, where they
could come and fetch the papers at their leisure when the coast
was clear.”

“But how did you find out where Elsa Hardt was living?”

“By following the maid,” replied Poirot simply. “I knew that she
was in the habit of visiting her mistress every Sunday, and it was
an easy matter to have her shadowed.”

“And the Italian?”

“Ah, that was a stroke of luck! I had already suspected that
someone was looking for Elsa Hardt, and when I saw him break into
the flat to-night, I knew that I had my man. He was convinced that
she was still living there, you see.”

“Well,” I said, “it’s certainly a most remarkable case. But tell
me, Poirot, how did you know that the papers were in the furniture?”

Poirot smiled.

“Because, my friend, when I examined the flat on Sunday, I found
a small hole in the back of the wardrobe which had evidently been
made quite recently. And inside the hole was a cavity just large
enough to hold a small packet of papers. _Voilà tout!_”

“And the true culprit?” I asked. “Was it Elsa Hardt?”

Poirot nodded.

“Yes, it was Elsa Hardt. She was the one who stole the papers and
murdered Luigi Valdarno when he threatened to betray her. A very
dangerous woman, Hastings—but not quite clever enough for Hercule
Poirot!”

At last we drew up before a small detached villa. As we got out of
the taxi, Poirot turned to me and whispered:

“You know, Hastings, I am much interested in this case. Let us see
who is living here.”

He walked up the steps and rang the bell. A middle-aged woman
opened it. She was quite different from the type of person I had
expected. She had a kind, motherly face and was dressed in a neat
black gown.

“Wait here, Hastings,” said Poirot, “I am going to speak to this
lady.”

He disappeared into the house, and I was left alone on the doorstep
with our captive. He was a small, dark man with a nervous and
agitated manner. He seemed to be in a state of great terror.

“What is the meaning of all this?” I asked him. “Who are you?”

“I am an Italian,” he replied in a low voice. “My name is Luigi.”

“Luigi!” I exclaimed. “But I thought you were dead.”

“I am not dead,” he said. “I was only wounded. I managed to escape
from the hospital and come to England. I wanted to find Elsa
Hardt.”

“And did you find her?”

“Yes,” he said. “I found her. She is living here.”

At that moment Poirot reappeared. He looked very grave.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have something to tell you. Elsa Hardt is
in this house.”

“Then why are we waiting?” I cried. “Let us go in and arrest her.”

“It is too late,” said Poirot. “She is dead.”

“Dead!” I exclaimed. “How did she die?”

“She was murdered,” said Poirot. “And the murderer is in this house.”

He turned to the Italian.

“Come,” he said. “We must go in and see what has happened.”

We followed him into the house. In the sitting-room, we found a
woman lying on the floor. She was tall and fair, with auburn hair.
It was Mrs. Robinson.

“Mrs. Robinson!” I cried. “Is she Elsa Hardt?”

“No,” said Poirot. “She is not Elsa Hardt. She is the woman who
was pretending to be Elsa Hardt.”

“Then who is Elsa Hardt?”

“Elsa Hardt is the woman who murdered her,” said Poirot.

He turned to the middle-aged woman who had opened the door.

“This is Elsa Hardt,” he said.

“But she doesn’t look like the description,” I protested.

“Descriptions are not always accurate,” said Poirot. “And Elsa
Hardt is a very clever woman. She knew that the American Secret
Service was looking for her, so she changed her appearance. She
dyed her hair and put on a different dress. She even changed her
name. She called herself Mrs. Robinson.”

“But then who was the woman we saw in the flat?” I asked.

“That was the real Mrs. Robinson,” said Poirot. “She was a poor
woman whom Elsa Hardt had hired to play the part. Elsa Hardt wanted
someone to take her place in the flat so that she could stay here
in peace. She chose Mrs. Robinson because she looked a little like
her. She gave her the flat at a very low rent on condition that
she stayed there and didn't see anyone. But Mrs. Robinson was
indiscreet. she went to a party and met Captain Hastings. And she
told him about the flat. Elsa Hardt heard about it and she was
afraid that she would be discovered. So she decided to kill Mrs.
Robinson.”

“But why did she kill her here?” I asked.

“Because she had invited her here for tea,” said Poirot. “She
knew that Mrs. Robinson would come because she thought Elsa Hardt
was her friend. And when she was here, Elsa Hardt killed her.”

“And what about the Italian?” I asked.

“He is the man who was working with Elsa Hardt,” said Poirot. “He
was the one who stole the papers. But Elsa Hardt cheated him. She
took the papers and ran away. He followed her to England and tried
to find her. He thought she was in the flat, so he went there to
kill her. But he found us instead.”

“It is a very strange story,” I said.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “It is a very strange story. But it is true.”

He turned to Elsa Hardt.

“You are under arrest,” he said. “For the murder of Mrs. Robinson.”

The woman did not say anything. She only looked at Poirot with a
look of hatred in her eyes.

“Come, Hastings,” said Poirot. “We must go and call the police.”

As we walked out of the house, I turned to Poirot.

“You are a very clever man, Poirot,” I said.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “I am a very clever man. But I could not have
done it without your help, Hastings.”

I felt very proud.

“And what about the papers?” I asked.

“The papers are here,” said Poirot. He drew a packet from his
pocket. “I found them in Elsa Hardt’s bedroom.”

“You are a marvel, Poirot,” I said.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “I am a marvel.”

We walked down the street, and as we did so, I thought of the
strange events of the last few days. It was indeed a very unusual
case.

The taxi drew up at a small house in a quiet street. There were no
lights in the windows. We descended and walked up the little
garden path. Poirot rang the bell. After a minute or two, a light
showed through the fanlight and then the door was opened cautiously
by a woman in a dressing-gown.

“What is it? What do you want?” she asked in a thin, nervous voice.

Poirot bowed.

“I believe that I have the pleasure of addressing Miss Elsa Hardt?”

The woman’s face went white.

“I—I—don’t know what you mean.”

“_Allons_,” said Poirot gently. “It is useless. This gentleman is
one of the many who would be interested to see you. You see, he
has been looking for you—for some time. Perhaps it would be better
if we went inside?”

The woman hesitated for a moment and then led the way into a
small, shabbily-furnished sitting-room. Poirot motioned our
prisoner into a chair and then turned to the woman.

“Now, Miss Hardt, we have come for those papers.”

“I haven’t got them. I don’t know what you are talking about.”

“It is no good, Elsa,” said the man in the chair suddenly. “They’ve
got us. It’s all up.”

The woman’s face changed. She turned on him like a tigress.

“You fool! You miserable, white-livered hound! To give in like
this! If you’d only held your tongue——”

“It wouldn’t have been any use,” said the man dejectedly. “They
know too much.”

Poirot stepped forward.

“Exactly. And now, the papers, please.”

With a gesture of despair, the woman went to a small writing-desk
and taking a packet of papers from a secret drawer, handed them
to Poirot.

“Thank you,” he said with a bow. “And now, I think, we will leave
you. This gentleman,” indicating our prisoner, “will remain with
us for the present. I don’t think you will be troubled by him again.”

As we were walking away from the house, Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? It was quite simple after all.”

“Simple! I don’t understand a word of it! Who is this man? And
what has it all got to do with Mrs. Robinson and her flat?”

Poirot chuckled.

“I will tell you. To begin with, the man is Luigi Valdarno’s
brother. He came to England to find Elsa Hardt and the papers
which he knew she had stolen from his brother. He didn’t know
where she was, but he knew that she had taken a flat in Montagu
Mansions under the name of Robinson. That was why he was
inquiring about the occupants of No. 4.”

“But Mrs. Robinson isn’t Elsa Hardt!” I cried.

“Exactly! That was the mistake he made. You see, Elsa Hardt and
her brother—who is really her husband—took the flat six months
ago under the name of Robinson. They were the original ‘Robinsons.’
But after a while, they began to get nervous. They knew that both
the American Secret Service and the Valdarnos were on their track.
So they hit upon a very ingenious plan. They would find another
couple of the same name, who looked somewhat like them, and get
them to take over the flat. Then, if anyone came looking for ‘the
Robinsons,’ they would find the innocent couple instead of the
real ones. They even went so far as to pay part of the rent and
provide the furniture, so as to make the flat more attractive.
They chose our friends, the Robinsons, because they were young
and inexperienced and not likely to ask questions. And because
Mrs. Robinson, with her auburn hair, was a very good double for
Elsa Hardt.”

“But how did you find out where Elsa Hardt was?” I asked.

“Ah, that was where the little Elsa Hardt made her mistake. She
couldn’t resist the temptation of keeping an eye on the flat to
see how her plan was working. It was she whom we saw coming out
of the flat on Sunday afternoon. I followed her, and found out
where she was living. The rest was easy.”

“And the man we caught in the flat?”

“That was Luigi’s brother. He had managed to find out that ‘the
Robinsons’ were living in No. 4, and he had come to try and get
the papers. He didn’t know, of course, that they weren’t the real
Robinsons. When we caught him, I told him that I knew who he was
and that if he would take us to Elsa Hardt, I would see that he
didn’t get into any trouble with the police.”

“I see,” I said slowly. “It was a clever plot.”

“Yes,” said Poirot, “it was clever. But it had one flaw. It did
not take into account the intelligence of Hercule Poirot!”

I looked at him. He was preening himself like a peacock.

“And what about the other suspects?” I asked. “Gerald Parker and
Elsie Ferguson?”

Poirot shrugged his shoulders.

“They were merely ‘red herrings,’ as you say in England. Gerald
Parker was a friend of the Robinsons, and Elsie Ferguson was the
one who tried to warn them—though she didn’t know it—that the flat
was already ‘let.’ It was all very simple, Hastings, once one had
the key!”

The taxi stopped before a small detached house in a quiet street
not far from Lord’s. Poirot paid the man, and as he drove away
beckoned to us to follow him. He did not ring at the door, but
opening the gate, led the way into the garden. As he did so, he
gave a low whistle.

A tall man stepped out from the shadow of the house.

“Is that you, Poirot?”

“Yes, Japp. Have you got them?”

“Safe and sound. They were just going.”

“And the lady?”

“Oh, she’s here too. Bit of a surprise for her, I fancy!”
