Japp chuckled.

“Wait here a moment, Hastings. I will go and prepare them.”

He was back in a moment and signed to us to follow him. We went
into a small sitting-room, and there, to my intense surprise, sat
my host of a few nights ago, Gerald Parker, and beside him—the lady
I had known as Mrs. Robinson!

She was no longer the charming little bride of a few nights ago.
Her face was white and her eyes were hard and glittering. She
reminded me of a beautiful, trapped animal.

“Well, Mr. Parker,” said Poirot smoothly, “and what have you to
say to us? You have played your part with much skill. The little
story of the flat was most artistically done.”

Parker did not answer. He sat with his hands in his pockets and
his chin on his chest, a picture of sullen defiance.

“But the game is up,” continued Poirot. “We know all. You are not
Gerald Parker, but a very clever international thief, and this
lady is not Mrs. Robinson, but Miss Elsa Hardt, late of Washington,
U.S.A. We have also the pleasure of presenting to you your late
colleague, Signor——” Poirot paused, and then added with a polite
bow to our captive: “I do not know your name, Monsieur, but I have
no doubt it is an alias.”

The Italian broke out into a torrent of words, but Poirot stopped
him with a wave of the hand.

“_Assez, assez_. It is all very clear. You were the friend of
Luigi Valdarno, were you not? And you thought that Elsa Hardt had
stolen the papers from him. You followed her to England, and you
meant to have your revenge. It was you who sent the various
applicants to the flat at Montagu Mansions, hoping that one of
them would find the papers for you. When that failed, you decided
to take matters into your own hands. You did not know that the
real occupants of the flat had been kidnapped and their places
taken by Miss Hardt and her accomplice.”

“Kidnapped!” I cried. “But I saw them myself at Parker’s the other
night.”

“You saw Elsa Hardt and the man who calls himself Parker. The real
Mr. and Mrs. Robinson were safely disposed of some days before.
It was a clever idea, Hastings, was it not? To take the flat at
a ridiculous rent, and so ensure that a constant stream of people
should be coming to see it. It would be a most effective way of
getting rid of any unwanted observers.”

“But the papers?” I asked. “Where are they?”

Poirot smiled.

“Ah, that is the most interesting part of the story. Miss Hardt,
it appears, has a taste for curios. Among the furniture which she
bought for fifty pounds was a very old and curious-looking bureau.
In a secret drawer of that bureau, which I have no doubt was
skilfully constructed for the purpose, the papers were hidden.
The bureau was sent to this house two days ago. Am I not right,
Mademoiselle?”

Elsa Hardt did not answer. She only stared at him with those hard,
glittering eyes.

“It was a well-laid plan,” said Poirot, “but you forgot one thing.
You forgot that even the most insignificant of men may have a
friend who is—Hercule Poirot!”

We alighted at the door of a small house standing back from the
road. A returning wayfarer, slightly drunk, was lurching along the
pavement and almost collided with Poirot, who said something
sharply to him which I did not catch. All three of us went up the
steps of the house. Poirot rang the bell and motioned us to stand
a little aside. There was no answer and he rang again and then
seized the knocker which he plied for some minutes vigorously.

A light appeared suddenly above the fanlight, and the door was
opened cautiously a little way.

“What the devil do you want?” a man’s voice demanded harshly.

“I want the doctor. My wife is taken ill.”

“There’s no doctor here.”

The man prepared to shut the door, but Poirot thrust his foot in
adroitly. He became suddenly a perfect caricature of an infuriated
Frenchman.

“What you say, there is no doctor? I will have the law of you. You
must come! I will stay here and ring and knock all night.”

“My dear sir——” The door was opened again, the man, clad in a
dressing-gown and slippers, stepped forward to pacify Poirot with
an uneasy glance round.

“I will call the police.”

Poirot prepared to descend the steps.

“No, don’t do that for Heaven’s sake!” The man dashed after him.

With a neat push Poirot sent him staggering down the steps. In
another minute all three of us were inside the door and it was
pushed to and bolted.

“Quick—in here.” Poirot led the way into the nearest room switching
on the light as he did so. “And you—behind the curtain.”

“Si, signor,” said the Italian and slid rapidly behind the full
folds of rose-coloured velvet which draped the embrasure of the
window.

Not a minute too soon. Just as he disappeared from view a woman
rushed into the room. She was tall with reddish hair and held a
scarlet kimono round her slender form.

“Where is my husband?” she cried, with a quick frightened glance.
“Who are you?”

Poirot stepped forward with a bow.

“It is to be hoped your husband will not suffer from a chill. I
observed that he had slippers on his feet, and that his dressing-gown
was a warm one.”

“Who are you? What are you doing in my house?”

“It is true that none of us have the pleasure of your acquaintance,
madame. It is especially to be regretted as one of our number has
come specially from New York in order to meet you.”

The curtains parted and the Italian stepped out. To my horror I
observed that he was brandishing my revolver, which Poirot must
doubtless have put down through inadvertence in the cab.

The woman gave a piercing scream and turned to fly, but Poirot was
standing in front of the closed door.

“Let me by,” she shrieked. “He will murder me.”

“Who was it dat croaked Luigi Valdarno?” asked the Italian hoarsely,
brandishing the weapon, and sweeping each one of us with it. We
dared not move.

“My God, Poirot, this is awful. What shall we do?” I cried.

“You will oblige me by refraining from talking so much, Hastings.
I can assure you that our friend will not shoot until I give the
word.”

“Youse sure o’ dat, eh?” said the Italian, leering unpleasantly.

It was more than I was, but the woman turned to Poirot like a
flash.

“What is it you want?”

Poirot bowed.

“I do not think it is necessary to insult Miss Elsa Hardt’s
intelligence by telling her.”

With a swift movement, the woman snatched up a big black velvet
cat which served as a cover for the telephone.

“They are stitched in the lining of that.”

“Clever,” murmured Poirot appreciatively. He stood aside from the
door. “Good evening, madame. I will detain your friend from New
York whilst you make your getaway.”

“Whatta fool!” roared the big Italian, and raising the revolver he
fired point-blank at the woman’s retreating figure just as I flung
myself upon him.

But the weapon merely clicked harmlessly and Poirot’s voice rose
in mild reproof.

“It is a wise precaution, _mon ami_, to remove the cartridges from a weapon before handing it to a man of such—shall we say—volatile temperament,” Poirot remarked with a dry smile. “You see, the little grey cells, they must always be one step ahead. And now, Miss Elsa Hardt, the game is truly at an end. You were clever, yes, but you made one fatal error: you appealed to the one passion in London that is more obsessive than crime—the passion for a cheap flat! By masquerading as ‘Mrs. Robinson’ at the house of our friend Mr. Parker, you hoped to establish a fresh identity and a believable history for your presence in Montagu Mansions. You chose the name of the actual tenants of No. 4, knowing they were a quiet couple, thinking that if anyone inquired, the porter would confirm that ‘the Robinsons’ had lived there for six months. But to claim a rent of eighty pounds when the market demands three hundred and fifty—ah, that was the ‘miracle’ that invited the scrutiny of Hercule Poirot! You are the true culprit of this piece, the thief of the Naval plans and the murderer of the unfortunate Luigi Valdarno.”

“I took the liberty of removing the cartridges from my friend’s
revolver while we were in the taxi,” Poirot explained mildly. “It
is a wise precaution when dealing with such impulsive
temperaments. And as for you, Elsa Hardt, your career as a
secret agent is at an end. Japp!”
The “drunk” whom we had encountered in the street stepped into
the room, remarkably sober and followed by two other men.
“Good work, Poirot,” he said, as he moved towards the woman.
“We’ve been looking for her and her ‘brother’ for some time.
The ‘brother’—otherwise known as the accomplice who assisted
in the theft of the Naval plans—is currently being attended to
in the hall by my men.”

“I took the liberty of removing the cartridges, Hastings. I have a great horror of the ‘big bang’—it is so very un-neighborly. And now, if you would be so good as to pick up that velvet cat, we shall find within it the stolen Naval plans that have caused so much trouble. You see, the scheme was of a most cold-blooded ingenuity. Elsa Hardt, whom we see before us, knew that the friends of the murdered Valdarno would be seeking her across the Atlantic. To protect herself, she and her accomplice took the flat at Montagu Mansions under the name of Robinson. They then offered it at an absurdly low rent, waiting for a couple to apply who matched their own physical description—particularly a woman with that beautiful auburn hair. The innocent Stella Robinson was to be the sacrificial lamb; she was intended to move into the flat so that when the Italian avengers arrived, it was she who would have paid the price for the crimes of the true culprit, Elsa Hardt, while the spy herself vanished with the spoils. It was a clever trap, and even the seemingly accidental meeting with Elsie Ferguson was part of the design to make the Robinsons feel they had secured a prize they could not possibly refuse.”

“Calm yourself, Hastings,” said Poirot with a mild reproof. “I took the liberty of removing the cartridges from your revolver before we left our own flat. As for this gentleman, he is no assassin, but a devoted cousin of the late Luigi Valdarno who has been assisting me in this little comedy to frighten the truth out of Miss **Elsa Hardt**. You see, the mystery of the cheap flat was quite simple. The ‘Robinsons’ who had lived there for six months were Elsa and her accomplice. They knew the pursuit was closing in, so they moved here to St. John’s Wood, but they needed to leave someone at the old address to mislead their pursuers. They specifically sought out an innocent couple named Robinson to take over the lease, ensuring that any vengeful Italians or government agents would waste their time watching the wrong people. The true culprit in the theft and the murder of Valdarno was indeed **Elsa Hardt**, who used the name and the very appearance of the woman she intended to use as a decoy.

“A little precaution, Hastings. I took the liberty of removing the
cartridges from your revolver while we were in the taxi. I have a
great horror of bloodshed. And you, monsieur,” he turned to the
Italian, “I will ask you to hand over that weapon. You have served
your purpose in frightening the lady into a confession, but your
vengeance must be left to the law.” The Italian, crestfallen,
surrendered the pistol. At that moment, the “drunk” we had
encountered on the pavement—who was, of course, none other than
Inspector Japp—stepped into the room, followed by two other
plain-clothes men. “Good work, Poirot,” said the Inspector,
clapping a hand on the shoulder of the man in the dressing-gown.
“We’ve been looking for this couple for some time. They’ve been
using the Robinson identity as a clever screen while they waited
for the right moment to pass on those plans.”

“Never will you trust your old friend, Hastings. I do not care for
my friends to carry loaded pistols about with them and never would
I permit a mere acquaintance to do so. No, no, _mon ami_.” This to
the Italian who swearing hoarsely. Poirot continued to address him
in a tone of mild reproof: “See now, what I have done for you. I
have saved you from being hanged. And do not think that our
beautiful lady will escape. No, no, the house is watched, back and
front. Straight into the arms of the police they will go. Is not
that a beautiful and consoling thought? Yes, you may leave the room
now. But be careful—be very careful. I——Ah, he is gone! And my
friend Hastings looks at me with eyes of reproach. But it was all
so simple! It was clear, from the first, that out of several
hundred, probably, applicants for No. 4, Montagu Mansions only the
Robinsons were considered suitable. Why? What was there that
singled them out from the rest—at practically a glance. Their
appearance? Possibly, but it was not so unusual. Their name, then!”

“But there’s nothing unusual about the name of Robinson,” I cried.
“It’s quite a common name.”

"Exactly, Hastings! A name so common that it would not attract attention. But you see, our 'charming' Mrs. Robinson was not a bride at all. She was Elsa Hardt herself! She had been living in that flat for six months, but she knew the net was drawing closer. She knew that the American agents and the vengeful Italians were looking for a 'Mrs. Robinson' who had occupied No. 4 since the Michaelmas quarter. So, what does she do? She stage-manages a 'move-in'! She goes to the party of an unsuspecting house-hunting enthusiast like Gerald Parker and tells a long, rambling story about a 'cheap flat' and a 'sudden stroke of luck.' If anyone were to inquire about a Mrs. Robinson at Montagu Mansions, she wanted them to find a 'new' Mrs. Robinson who had just arrived—an innocent bride—not the woman who had been hiding there for half a year with stolen naval plans! She even invented the story of Elsie Ferguson seeing the flat to make the 'luck' of her obtaining it seem more authentic and hard-won. It was a clever piece of psychological camouflage."

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “The name is the key. You see, Hastings, the woman you met at the house of Monsieur Parker—the ‘charming’ Mrs. Robinson—was not the innocent bride she appeared to be. She was, in fact, the dangerous Elsa Hardt herself! She and her accomplice had occupied No. 4 for six months as ‘the Robinsons,’ but when they realized the vengeance of Valdarno’s friends was imminent, they devised a plan of singular cruelty. They sought to find another couple, also named Robinson and of similar appearance, to take their place and receive the blow intended for them. The story she told you of ‘just finding’ the flat was a fabrication intended to test your credulity and lead us into becoming her unwitting pawns. She assumed that a pretty face and a tale of a lucky find would blind us to the truth. It was she who stole the Naval plans, and it was she who orchestrated the death of Luigi Valdarno!”

“Precisely, Hastings. The name was a common one, chosen for its very
ordinariness, but it was the discrepancy of time that was my
guide. The porter at Montagu Mansions was very sure: the tenants
of No. 4 had been there for six months. Yet the lady told you a
tale of a bargain found only yesterday. Why? Because she is, in
fact, Elsa Hardt. She had been in that flat for six months,
hiding. But she knew the Italian, the vengeful associate of the
murdered Valdarno, had tracked her to London. She needed to
establish a new, ‘innocent’ identity. She staged that little scene
at Mr. Parker’s—the story of the ‘cheap flat,’ the ‘miracle’ of the
rent, and the imaginary competition with Elsie Ferguson—all to
interest you, and through you, me. She wanted me to be present
when the Italian struck, to capture him as a ‘burglar’ and thus
remove the threat to her life, while she remained the ‘charming’
and ‘innocent’ Mrs. Robinson. She even invented the ‘cheap’ rent
to explain why she would be so anxious to move in. It was a
masterpiece of deception, but she forgot that I, Hercule Poirot,
check the facts. I visited the agents; there was no flat at eighty
pounds. She had been paying the full rent all along. She was the
culprit, Hastings, playing a double game to save her skin and keep
her spoils!”

“Precisely,” cried Poirot. “It was the very commonness of the name that was its attraction. But there was more than that. Elsa Hardt knew she was being hunted by both the law and the vengeful comrades of the man she had betrayed. She needed a ‘double’—someone who would occupy the flat at Montagu Mansions, use the name Robinson, and match her own general appearance. By installing the innocent Mrs. Robinson there at a nominal rent, she created a perfect decoy. Any pursuers—like our Italian friend—would find only a harmless young bride, while the real Elsa Hardt remained safely hidden in St. John’s Wood, using the flat merely as a clearing-house for her stolen documents. It was Elsa Hardt who had been the tenant for six months, as the porter said, but she sublet it to the Robinsons to provide herself with a human shield. It was a masterpiece of cold-blooded calculation, utilizing the very ‘cheapness’ of the flat to lure a suitable couple into the trap, and even perhaps influencing the movements of people like Elsie Ferguson to ensure the stage was set just so.”

“Exactly, Hastings! It is because it is a common name! Now, consider the logic: The people who had lived in No. 4 for six months were named Robinson. The agents were instructed to find another couple named Robinson to take over the lease at a nominal rent. Why? Because as long as ‘the Robinsons’ occupied No. 4, any inquiries from the authorities or the postman would appear perfectly normal. The spies—the real Elsa Hardt and her companion—could slip away, leaving a perfectly innocent ‘double’ in their place to act as an unconscious screen. They chose the Robinsons we met at Parker’s because of their name, and because Mrs. Robinson’s appearance was sufficiently similar to Elsa Hardt’s to deceive a casual glance from the porter. It was a stroke of genius! The cheap rent was the bait to ensure the real Robinsons moved in immediately and stayed there, effectively burying the trail of the stolen Naval plans. Our charming Mrs. Robinson was merely a pawn; the true culprit, the mastermind who stole the plans and arranged this elaborate masquerade, is the woman you just saw—the real Elsa Hardt.”

“Ah! _Sapristi_, but exactly! That was the point. Elsa Hardt and
her husband, or brother or whatever he really is, come from New
York, and take a flat in the name of Mr. and Mrs. Robinson. Suddenly
they learn that one of these secret societies, the Mafia, or the
Camorra, to which doubtless Luigi Valdarno belonged, is on their
track. What do they do? They hit on a scheme of transparent
simplicity. Evidently they knew that their pursuers were not
personally acquainted with either of them. What then can be simpler?
They offer the flat at an absurdly low rental. Of the thousands of
young couples in London looking for flats, there cannot fail to be
several Robinsons. It is only a matter of waiting. If you will look
at the name of Robinson in the telephone directory, you will
realize that a fair-haired Mrs. Robinson was pretty sure to come
along sooner or later. Then what will happen? The avenger arrives.
He knows the name, he knows the address. He strikes! All is over,
vengeance is satisfied, and Miss Elsa Hardt has escaped by the skin
of her teeth once more. By the way, Hastings, you must present me
to the real Mrs. Robinson—that delightful and truthful creature!
What will they think when they find their flat has been broken
into! We must hurry back. Ah, that sounds like Japp and his friends
arriving.”

A mighty tattoo sounded on the knocker.

“How did you know this address?” I asked as I followed Poirot out
into the hall. “Oh, of course, you had the first Mrs. Robinson
followed when she left the other flat.”

“_A la bonne heure_, Hastings. You use your grey cells at last.
Now for a little surprise for Japp.”

Softly unbolting the door, he stuck the cat’s head round the edge
and ejaculated a piercing “Miaow.”

The Scotland Yard inspector, who was standing outside with another
man, jumped in spite of himself.

“Oh, it’s only Monsieur Poirot at one of his little jokes!” he
exclaimed, as Poirot’s head followed that of the cat. “Let us in,
moosior.”

“You have our friends safe and sound?”

“Yes, we’ve got the birds all right. But they hadn’t got the goods
with them.”

“I see. So you come to search. Well, I am about to depart with
Hastings, but I should like to give you a little lecture upon the
history and habits of the domestic cat.”

“For the Lord’s sake, have you gone completely balmy?”

“Not at all,” replied Poirot. “But I have a fancy for this
particular cat. Examine the lining, my friend. You will find it
most—instructive.” He handed the toy over to the bewildered
Inspector. “And so, Hastings, the mystery of the Cheap Flat is
resolved. The woman you have just arrested, the mistress of this
house who posed as the ‘first’ Mrs. Robinson, is none other than
the international spy Elsa Hardt. She sought an innocent double to
die in her stead, nearly sacrificing your ‘delightful’ young bride
to the vengeance of the Mafia in order to save her own guilty neck.
She played her part with great cunning, even managing to mislead
the likes of Gerald Parker and Elsie Ferguson, but she did not
account for the ‘little grey cells’ of Hercule Poirot. Come, my
friend, let us leave Japp to his search. I find that, after all, I
prefer my own chair to the furniture of Montagu Mansions. And as
for the real Mrs. Robinson—I think she will find that eighty pounds
a year was a very small price to pay for a story she can tell her
grandchildren!”

“Not at all,” replied Poirot with a flourish. “I merely wish to point out that this particular cat has swallowed a most valuable meal. If you will rip open the lining, Japp, you will find the stolen Naval plans for which the American Government is so anxious. As for Elsa Hardt, she played her part with some skill, using the name of the innocent Robinsons as a shield against her own past, but she forgot that Hercule Poirot has a nose for the unusual. Even a ‘dirt cheap’ flat has its price, and in this case, it was the price of her own capture. Come, Hastings, let us return to our own home. I find that I have a sudden craving for a cup of chocolate, and perhaps a small _biscuit_ to celebrate the triumph of the little grey cells.”

“Not in the least, my good Japp,” said Poirot, his eyes twinkling with a sudden mischievous light. He took a small penknife from his pocket and, with a deft movement, slit open the stitching of the black velvet cat’s underbelly. From the interior, he drew forth a thin packet of papers, closely covered with fine writing and diagrams. “Here, my friend, are the stolen Naval plans that have caused so much international agitation. Elsa Hardt was indeed a formidable opponent, but she made the mistake of underestimating the ‘little grey cells’ of Hercule Poirot. She sought to hide her identity behind a name as common as Robinson, using the innocent Stella Robinson as a shield against her past. But as I told you, Hastings, the stars give light—and in this case, they led us straight to the truth.” As Japp stared in speechless admiration at the recovered documents, Poirot turned to me with a flourish. “And now, _mon ami_, let us return. I find myself suddenly possessed of a great desire for a cup of chocolate. It has been a most fatiguing, yet remarkably satisfactory, adventure of the cheap flat.”

“Not at all,” Poirot replied with a flourish. “I am merely indicating where your elusive plans are to be found.” With a swift movement, he ripped open the lining of the black velvet cat, and a packet of thin, crackling papers fell onto the table. Japp let out a whistle of pure astonishment as he realized the value of the prize. “The Naval plans! You’ve done it again, Moosior Poirot!” As the Inspector bustled away to complete the arrest of the woman known as Elsa Hardt—who had so cleverly utilized the common name of Robinson to mask her trail and had used the innocent Stella Robinson as a shield against her enemies—Poirot turned to me with a look of supreme satisfaction. “You see, Hastings, the ‘dirt cheap’ flat was a very costly venture for the lady in question. She hoped to lose herself in a sea of Robinsons, but she did not account for the ‘little grey cells’ of Hercule Poirot. And now, let us go; I have a sudden craving for a cup of hot chocolate, and I must confess that even I, Poirot, find the midnight air of London a trifle chilling to the bones.”

Poirot chuckled and handed the velvet cat to the bewildered inspector. “In the lining, my friend Japp, you will find the stolen Naval plans. Elsa Hardt was a clever woman, but she did not count on the ‘little grey cells’ of Hercule Poirot. She was the true culprit who stole the papers in Washington and fled to London, using the innocent Stella Robinson and her husband as unwitting shields against the vengeance of the Italian society. It was a cold-blooded scheme; had the assassin succeeded, it would have been the real Mrs. Robinson who paid the price for Elsa Hardt's crimes. As for our friend Gerald Parker and the elusive Elsie Ferguson, they were but minor actors in a drama they did not understand. Come, Hastings, let us return to our own flat. I find that I have a great desire for a cup of chocolate and a little quiet reflection on the many meanings of the name ‘Robinson’.”

“The cat,” declaimed Poirot, “was worshipped by the ancient
Egyptians. It is still regarded as a symbol of good luck if a black
cat crosses your path. This cat crossed your path to-night, Japp.
To speak of the interior of any animal or any person is not, I
know, considered polite in England. But the interior of this cat
is perfectly delicate. I refer to the lining.”

With a sudden grunt, the second man seized the cat from Poirot’s
hand.

“Oh, I forgot to introduce you,” said Japp. “Mr. Poirot, this is
Mr. Burt of the United States Secret Service.”

The American’s trained fingers had felt what he was looking for.
He held out his hand, and for a moment speech failed him. Then he
rose to the occasion.

“Pleased to meet you,” said Mr. Burt.
